Shareholder: "Half capable of nothing, and the rest capable of anything." THE Height of Presumption—Breaking into a house and waking up the master of it to assist you in carrying your booty down stairs. A WITTY lawyer once asked a boarding-house keeper the following question : "Mr. M ,if a man gives you five hundred 'pounds to keep for him, and dies, what do you do? Do you pray for him?" "No, sir," replied Mr. M—, "I pray for another like him?'

A BROAD MARGIN. —Little Susie : " Effie, what is a marriageable age?" : " Anywhere between fourteen and death," HE " Will you marry me ?" She : No." He : Whom are you going to marry ?" She: "I shall marry whom I please." He : " Well—you please me ! ' _

WHEN something is very difficult to understand," said the distinguished professor of biology, "it is called science; when it is impossible, it is called philosophy." MRs. DIMPLE "Would your husband leave you very much if he were to die?' Mrs. Grayise : Not much more than now. He leaves me six nights out of the week as it is." THE old maxim that "man proposes" is contra- dicted by certain spinsters of uncertain age, who only wish he did. FRIEND to Mr. D. (who has married a second time) : "How are you getting on?' Mr. D. : "First-rate, and more settled-like. You see, when my first wife was living, we never seemed to know exactly who was master in the house." Friend : "I suppose that now you are master ?" Mr. D. : "Not thit way; my wife is boss." INCOMPETENCE PUNlSHED.—lianerly : "Do you think the law has any right to punish a man for trying to commit suicide 7" Austen: "Not unless he fails." A YOUNG man was found tricking at cards, and the players pitched him out at a first-floor window. Being picked up by a friend, he blustered a good deal, and said, "What would you advise me to do under the circumstances?" "Not play cards again except on the ground floor," replied the candid friend. - - - -

She seems to have everything there is a-going." TIIE ditlerence between having a tooth drawn by a professional man and having it knocked out by a fall on the pavement is only a verbal one. The one is dental—the other accidental..

Tommy—" But she's going to give me a penny for telling you. THE APOLOGY SUFFICED.—" I have never given you credit for knowing very much, madam," said a blunt old bachelor, "but—" "Sir," she interrupted, "do you wish to insult—" "But," he continued, "I have always admired your grace and beauty." "I accept your apology," said the lady. As old woman who was injured in a railway collision was advised by her friends to sue the railway company for damage.. "No," she said; "I've had damage enough, already without suing for more. I'd need sue them for repairs, I think." div.head: CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: CAPITAL" CHAT.

Now the Liberal party have taken in hand the "mending or ending" of the House of Lords, it may not be without interest to notice the policy which the Long Parliament adopted with regard to that venerable institution. It was not so drastic as is commonly supposed, for though the House of Commons voted the House of Lords to be "useless and dangerous," and abolished it accordingly, yet an act was passed allowing the Peers to retain their titles, and rendering them eligible for election in the House of Commons.

One of the Lords who promptly took advantage of this permission was the Earl of Salisbury, the lineal ancestor of the present Marquis, who, no doubt, under similar circumstances, would give the House of Commons many further exhibitions of his powers as " a master of flouts and gibes and sneers." The Earl of Salisbury of that day was also a member of the Council of State of forty-one mem- bers.

Mr. Justice Gnntham has been very unfortunate in his public utterances. On Saturday in a speech to his employes at the harvest home at Barcombe, in Sussex, he accused supporters of the Government of doing all they could to injure landowners and farmers, to set class against class, and said the Ministry owed its life to the which existed in some places between the farmer and his labour, ers. The learned judge claimed that he was not trenching on politics in making these assertions ; but I hear that the speech will be brought before Parliament, particularly as at the time he delivered it the judge was on the rota for the trial of election petitions.

The old and the new Radicalism are splitting asunder in South-west Ham., and Mr. Keir Hardie will have to fight for his seat. Neither he nor his Radical opponent will get it, however, as a Tory will slip in and carry off the spoils. Ostensibly it , is trades union members who have seceded from the Radieal mass of voters in the constituency, and in the true spirit of the older Radicalism they have sought out a capitalist who represents Radical prin- ciples. Rumours of dissensions have been long current in South-west Ham, and the selection of an employer of labour by the working men, instead of a direct labour candidate, shows that there are middle-class influences in operation behind the working-class deputations who waited upon the candidate. Another result of the split will be that the seat in North-west Ham will be lost to the Liberals also, as the extreme Radical party in that constituency will avenge its colleagues in the South-west Division by running a candidate in opposition to the sitting Liberal, Mr. Grove. Thus two seats are likely to be gained by the Tories ; for, although Mr. Hardie was not professedly a Govern- ment supporter, he kept the enemy out of the constituency.

--- One is quite interested to find l‘lr. Frederic Harri- son discussing the unexpected question of the late Lord Beaconsfield's place in literature. A hasty pprson might be led into saying that the author of "Vivian Grey " has ceased to have any place in literature. Nobody talks about his books, and scarcely anybody seems to purchase or read them. It seems very odd nowadays that any publisher should have been willing to pay ten thousand pounds for " Lothair."

Mr. Harrison commits himself to the statement that "in the next century little will be heard of Lord Beaconsfield, the Jingo Prime Minister, but some of Benjamin Disraeli's pictures of English imiety and the British Parliament may still amuse awl instruct our descendants." The nevels have had an enduring political effect, this critic declares; they have real historical value, they are full of wit and vivacious originality.

It was not expected that the scheme prepared by the committee of the M.C.C. for regulating the county championship would give entire satisfac- tion, and there are cricketers who maintain that the mere condition of each county playing eight out and eight home matches will not suffice. They urge that it should have been insisted that every county should play once, at any rate, against each of the others. Probably this will be arranged, and it would puzzle the critics of the M.C.C. to adopt a more excellent course. The inclusion of Hamp- shire has given great satisfaction. Devonshire may be added to the list another year.

The resignation by Mr. Charles Spurgeon of the pastorate of the Greenwich Tabernacle has not ex- cited any surprise among his friends, who know that the less famous son of the great Baptist preacher has never been really strong. Except his failing health, and the necessity for spending the winter in the South of France, there is no reason for Mr. Spurgeon's retirement. He is on the best of terms with his large congregation, has done excel- lent work in South East London, and his compul- sory withdrawal from the duties he has discharged so faithfully for nearly fifteen years is deeply regretted.

--- Little as we know in England about the Czar's illness, yet we know more than his own people in St. Petersburg. A bit of news that has never reached the Russian capital yet, is well known in our Royal family, is that the Princess Alix of Hesse is averse to mounting the Throne of Russia. Time after time she refused the proposals of the Czare- witch before his pertinacity overcame her reluc- tance. Is it possible that in this we have a clue to the conflicting reports about the attitude of the rzarewitch, including the alleged painful scene with his father? The devotion of the Princess is limited to the renunciation of her family's tradi- tional religion, for she has openly declared that she never can be a Russian at heart. It is not only the constant fear of the assassination of her husband that she dreads, but the secrecy and privacy of movement inevitable to the position are abhorrent to her. The Queen has in the "Court Circular" stated that the Princess has gone to Livadia at, the express wish of the Czar and Czarina,and this there- fore must be accepted as the true explanation of her long journey.

I understand that the additions made to our quadron in Chinese waters in consequence of the state of affairs in the Far East are very much more numerous than was at first supposed, and that the list of vessels under orders to join Admiral Fre- mantle's fiag which was published on the day 'after the much-discussed Cabinet Council would be more nearly correct if it were doubled. The battleship Gibraltar (or the St. George, a vessel of the same class) from home. the ./Eolus from the Mediterran- ean, the Pigeon and the Redbreast from the East Indian squadron, are the vessels whose names were first published. But to these have now been added the Crescent, a vessel said to he a sister ship to the Gibraltar, the Edgar, a first-class cruiser, and the Sparton, a second-class cruiser—both vessels built since 1889, and both ordered to China from the Mediterranean. It may be said roughly that these additions more than double the effective force of the China squadron. The • force of marines des- patched the other day from Liverpool across Canada was intended for these vessels. I hear also that the Admiralty, on the principle of not chang- ing horses while crossing the stream, has decided that, Admiral Fremantle. whose term of command is just about to expire,shall remain at his post for the Present. It is quire obvious that this large squad- .nn is not intended solely for the protection of British subjects in China, for the four or fire most powerful of the vessels could not get within many miles of any of the foreign settlements, except the comparatively small and unimportant one of Cheefoo. The settlements for the most part are at nonsiderable distances up comparatively shallow rivers, which are quite inaccessible to large war- ships Clearly, Admiral Fremantle is expected to have other work for his force. What this is I have already indicated more than once.

THE DOUBLE LIFE:

trey, at the very time that the great trouble hap. pened." " Negwyn ? George Negwyn ?" repeated Gir- alda, in astonishment, remembering the name, "I have heard of him, Mrs. Pumpton. If I could only find him !" "Peggy 'll know where he is, if any one knows,ff observed the housekeeper, not noticing the emotioft of her young guest. "Then let us set out at once," cried Giralda, feverishly eager. "It is this Negwyn who alone can prove papa's innocence. Mamma has adver- tised and offered rewards for his address, but she could never discover him. Oh 1 Mrs. Pumpton, Providence is surely guiding me through all these dark paths." "We will start as soon as you shall have had your tea, Miss Giralda," said the housekeeper, rising. "Just lie back in the chair and rest, while I prepare your supper." She went to a wall closet and brought out a clean cloth, which she spread on the small round table and she then set out upon it a pot of jam, a goodly pot of butter, a seed-cake, a portion of roasted fowl, and finally a plate of cold muffins and a small copper tea-kettle. "I always take my meals alone here," she ob- served, setting on the kettle to boil, and preparing to toast and butter the muffins. "I shouldn't be able to manage the servants a week if I were to eat with them. They'd think I was no better than they," and she smiled humorously. "There's nothing like keeping up your dignity." By the time the tea was made the muffins were fully prepared, and Mrs. Pumpton wheeled Gir- alda's chair to the table and proceeded to wait upon her.
OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. By the Author of " DARKWOOD."

CHAPTER XXXVIII. SEEKING REFUGE. This accident and flood of fortune So far exceed all instance, all discourse, That I am ready to distrust mine eyes, And wrangle with my reason, that persuades me To any other trust. SHAKESPEARE. Lord Trevelyan's distressful cry did not reach the ears for which it was intended. Half wild with excitement Giralda had plunged into the shrubbery, not knowing nor caring whither she went. To get away from the park, and the mock- ing face and voice of her enemy, was the one idea that possessed her. She had, however, not progressed far in her wild flight through those trackless shades, when a woman's figure darted out into her very path- way, and a woman's hand caught her by the arm, bringing her to an abrupt halt. The figure and the band belonged to Mrs. Pump- ton, the housekeeper at the Park. Giralda looked at her in a bewildered way, recog- nizing her, and strove to break from her detaining grasp. "Let me go! Let me go!" she panted, trembling like a deer brought to bay. " He told me to be- gone." " I know it !" cried Mrs Pumpton, all excite- ment and tears. "I heard it all, Miss Giralda I was looking for you, knowing that you had gone to walk in the shrubbery alone. I came upon you at the glade at the moment my lord did. How his lordship raged! And Mr Geoffrey's alive! Thank God my prayers are answered !" The good woman sobbed in very excess of joy. " And you are Mr. Geoffrey's daughter!" she continued, clinging to Giralda's hand. "I might have known it by your bonny eyes! I wonder I never suspected it! How blind I have been Don't tremble so, my poor lamb. You've got a friend in me." The housekeeper's tone of hearty kindness soothed Giralda's nerves, and she fell upon the good soul's ample bosom and wept convulsively. "It is so hard to bear 1" she sobbed. "Papa is safe, and they cannot harm him; but Lord Tre- velyan will never be assured of papa's innocence 1 Oh, Mrs. Pumpton, I have hoped for so much, and now—" "There! there !" said the worthy housekeeper, soothing the maiden as if she had been a child. "It will be all right some day, Miss Giralda. Don't go to crying yourself sick, my poor lamb. Think of Mr. Geoffrey, and the rest of them. Don't lose your courage now at this late day." Thus adjured, Giralda began to grow calmer. "You must come into the house now, Miss Gir- alda," said Mrs. Pumpton, who was brimming over with joyful importance at the prospect of aiding, even indirectly, her beloved Mr. Geoffrey. "No, you won't see anybody," she protested, as the girl began to object. "You shall go into my quiet little room, and we'll talk up about your go- ing away there at our leisure." Giralda yielded to the woman's persuasion, and the two, hand in hand, threaded the dark shrub- bery, crossed the shaded lawn, and gained the housekeeper's room, in the rear wing of the man- sion, without being seen. The glazed door of Mrs. Pumpton's room stood invitingly open, but there was no light save the faint glow emitted by the few embers in the grate. The housekeeper stirred the fire, closed the doors and shutters, and lighted a lamp. "Sit down here, Miss Giralda," she said, draw- ing forward a red-covered easy. chair. "I've locked the door, and no one can intrude upon us. How pale you are, poor lamb 1" She sat down at a respectful distance, while Giralda leaned back in her chair, her weary soul refreshed and strengthened by the good woman's tender kindness and sympathy. "You mustn't take my lord's words to heart," said the housekeeper. "As long as your papa 's safe, you needn't care what my lord says or does. He 's no better than a raging tiger when he 's aroused. Lord Adlowe's very cunning, and knows just how to stir him up. I wonder, Miss, that, being the daughter of poor Mr. Geoffrey, you dared to come to the Park at all." "When I came here I came only in answer to Lord Trevelyan's advertisement," explained Giralda wearily. "I did not know that papa was was his nephew, or that papa had ever been called Geoffrey Trevelyan. I knew nothing of this terrible secret. When his lordship took me up to London, I saw mamma, and she told me all. And then it was I dedicated myself to the task of clearing my father's name." "And quite right, too, Miss Giralda," said Mrs. Pumpton, wiping her eyes. "But there's DO use trying to soften my lord's heart against poor Mr. Geoffrey. I little knew what interest you had in it when I begged you to speak a good word for my poor, wronged young master. And he's alive, as I suspected! I wonder if he remembers me?" "You may be sure dear Mrs. Pumpton, that he remembers all his old friends." "That I may. He had the truest, kindest heart. He was the noblest fellow that ever lived—so true, so gay, so honest. He was like the apple of my eye, Miss Giralda. Now I know why I loved you so much from the first." "I must go away from here at once, this very night," said Giralda, dearily. "Where can I go, Mr. Pumpton? Papa has left home, and found a safe refuge elsewhere. Our home is broken up, I

"Sit down, Mrs. Pumpton," said Giralda, for the first time noticing that but one plate was laid. "I will not eat alone." With some difficulty she persuaded the good woman to sit down with her and share the repast. "How are we to perform the journey ? " asked Giralda, as the meal progressed. "On foot ? " "No, Miss; on horseback. My lord gave you a horse, and you must use it. There's a horse in the stable I always ride over to the village, for I can't abide this road in a waggon. I can bring the horses back when I come." "But," said Giralda, "I fear you will get your- ' self into trouble by befriending me, dear friend. My uncle may discharge you on your return—" "Let him," said the housekeeper, setting her lips together firmly. "He can't live without me, Miss. Why, the house would be all at six and sevens in no time. He'd scare away all the ser- vants with his tempers, if it wasn't for me. His lordship discharge me ! " and she laughed good- humoredly at the preposterous idea. "He wouldn't try it.' iz'upper was eaten' and Mrs. Pumpton then sug- gested a change from Giralda's bright dress to some- thing of sober hue. "I'll slip up to your room, Miss," she said, "and bring down what you are likely to want. Lock the door during my absence." She hastened away immediately, and soon re- turned, fully dressed for her journey, and with her arms laden with Giralda's effects. "Here's your travelling-bag, Miss, with a change of under-garments' and your pocket-book in it," she explained. "Here is your black silk suit to wear, and your hat in place of that opery thing you had on in the shrubbery.'' "Did you see my uncle, or Lord Adlowe ?" asked Giralda, hastening to dress. "No, Miss. They are out scouring the road for you, so Sarah the house-maid says. We can't get away too soon. What my lord can want of you. after the way he spoke to you, I can't see. May be he wants to urge you to marry Lord Adlowe." "Won't they see us on the road ?" asked Giralda In a tremor. "We won't go on that road," was the reply, "We'll try the bridle-path down the other side of the hill. Trust in me, Miss, and keep up your courage." Giralda was quickly ready. Mrs. Pumpton packed up a luncheon, which included a bottle of wine, and then covered her fire and extinguished the light. The glazed door was then unlocked, and the two, with beating hearts, stole out on the lawn. The shadows still lay thickly over the out- door scene, not a star being visible. The fugitives crept toward the stables in silence. "There's no one out here now," whispered the housekeeper, as they entered the stable yard, "The men have gone in to their supper." The stable door was open. A big lantern hung on the wall lighted the interior of the stable, and the woman, peering in, saw the bases in their stalls." She saddled first Giralda's mare, and then a stout brown mountain pony for her own twe, end led the two animals out to the horse-block in the stable yard. Giralda mounted quickly. The bouseteeper followed her example, and the two rode silently mit of the yard, crossed the rear end of the lawn, and rode into the shadow of a tall coppice which screened the stables from the mansion. You want a firm seat and a steady hand now, Miss Giralda," said the housekeeper, in an under- tone. "This is a rugged path, so rugged that they won't dream of our being on it. I never rode on it but once, and then I was in haste to visit my dying sister, and the road was impassable by reason of the freshets." With much inward trembling Giralda followed her leader. The path, narrow at best, was rugged enough. The branches of trees brushed the travellers as they rode along, occasionally almost sweeping them from their seats. The descent was steep—so steep that it was quite impossible to maintain an upright position. But gradually the evening shadows cleared, and the stars showed themselves in full splendor through the clear, frosty air. "We shall have a cold night for the season," said Mrs. Pumpton, picking her way carefully. "All the better for the horses, though, Miss Giralda. You can begin now to see the path ahead 1" Giralda fancied that she discerned the path winding in and out like a thread among the cop- pices, and losing itself for a space' only to become apparent a little later, crossing the stony barrens and ridges in its continual descent, until it was lost in the distance. " We are surely safe from pursuit on this path 1" she said, with a sigh of relief. "You were right, Mrs. Pumpton. They won't think of searching for us here." _ _ _

think." "Of course you'll go right to your mother," sug- gested the housekeeper. Giralda's cheeks flushed painfull. "I cannot," she said, in a smothered voice. "There are reasons, Mrs. Pumpton, which you will know one day, why I can't go to mamma. My dear, dear mother !" and her tones treinbled. "I understood,' said the housekeeper. "She's an actress, you told me once, and don t want you with her. Quite right. A theatre is no place for a young girl like you. I can't understand, though," she added, "how Mr. Geoffrey came to marry a play-actor, begging your pardon, Miss. Has your mamma no relations?" "None to whom I can go." "And you have no other friends to go to?" "None but Lord Grosvenor," replied Giralda, blushing. "He is my promised husband, Mrs. Pumpton. I will go to him. I can easily walk to the Eyrie, and he will tell me what to do.' "Not for worlds V cried Mrs. Pumpton, in alarm. "Its out of the question for you to go to the Eagle's Eyrie. Mr. Geoffrey's daughter must not compromise her name by sucn an unguarded step, and people would talk if you sought refuge there. No one must say anything ill against the daughter of the future Marquis Trevelyan. Leave the matter to me, Miss Giralda. I will try and think of a refuge for you." The good woman became thoughtful. She had S morbid fear of the old marquis, but her love for her former nursing. Geoffrey Trevelyan, out- weighed that fear- There was nothing she would not do, no sacrifice she would not make, for Geof- frey Trevelyan or his child. "You cannot stay in the village alone, that's clear," she murmured. "You would be at Lord Adlowe?s mercy there. You cannot go to the Ey- rie. You cannot stay there. What you want is a quiet secluded place, where no one can find or harm you, and where you can stay until you can write and get letters from your parents." "Yes," that is what I want," said Giralda, oagerly. " The more secluded the place, the safer I shall feel." "The towns and villages won't do," mused Mrs. Pumpton. "A young girl alone in a country town excites gossip. Ah I I have it." Her face brightened up, and she drew nearer to Giralda in sudden excitement. "1 know the very place for you, Miss Giralda," she exclaimed. "There was a farmer's daughter who lived at the Park many years ago—a plain. faced, honest, homely creature that everybody liked. She left, on falling heiress to a farm of her uncle's—a queer old place on the Burnt Did you ever hear of them?" Giralda replied in the negative. "The Burnt Downs is a desolate district, cov- ered with gorse that is annually burnt over, from some cause or other," explained Mrs. Pumpton. "It is about a mile in breadth, and some three miles in length. The only house on it is Peppy Willsey's, the woman I was speaking of. Lord Adlowe would never trace you there." "Is it far from here?" asked Giralda. "Over thirty miles. It's over twenty miles north-east of Ilamptunwold, the seat of the great Earl of 11-in pen—" "1 u ih go there," said Giralda, hastily, decided by vie mention of the nearness of her mother's country home. "Do you think the woman will deceive me ?" " I know she will. She is always kind to those in trouble, although many think her a cold- heartel w :fo an. She had a dippolus,uient once, and that changed her. She was engaged to Geo_. aLroe .'let of Lord Acil:)kve laid Mr, _Coal-

_ Mrs. Pumpton was puffing heavily with her un- wonted exertion, and her reply was incoherent. "Lord Grosvenor was to call upon me at the Park in the morning, "continued the young girl, with another sigh unlike the first. "What will he think to find me gona ? He will be so anxious, so frightened. I wish I had left a message for him.' "Your message, Miss Giralda, would have been first delivered to my lord," said the houseke?per, in a wheezy voice. "There ain't a servant at the Park but would give their souls right up, if it would satisfy his lordship in his tearing moods! lam the only person you can trust. Wild horses wouldn't tear your secret from me! When you get to Pegg's, you could drop Lord Grosvenor a line, you know, Miss, and one of his thorough- breds would make nothing of the distance to the Burnt Downs." At this juncture" in the conversation a closer attention to the ruggedness of the path became necessary, and a silence ensued. Giralda lived over again, in her own thoughts, the events of the evening—her interview with her young lover—and the interview which had fol- lowed that happy one, shrouding her present in darkness. "Will the wrong ever be made right?" she asked herself, with a wild glance upward at the calm stars. "Will justice ever be done in this world ?" The night deepened. The hill, or mountain, on which Trevelyan Park was perched had been safely descended. The mountain paths had given now into a wider road, which was, however, full of unpleasant inequalities, and which also in many places dangerously skirted precipices and pitfalls. The fugitives halted to rest their horses, and to look upward at the Park. Lights were flashing from every window of the mansion, and gleamed from the stables. "They have discovered that we have taken the horses," said Mrs. Pumpton, "but they have not discovered which way we went. They will nat. urally think," she added, "that we have made for the Eagle's Eyrie." They looked a while longer, and then turned and rode forward on their lonely journey through that desolate region and the desolate night. And up on the heights, in the great mansion, in Giralda's deserted room, the old marquis was kneeling, his grand head, with its clustering white curls, bowed in utter anguish, his rugged, massive features wet with bitterest tears, and his voice call- ing vainly upon Giralda to return, protesting that ; he loved her and trusted her through all. _And out on the ruazed mountain roads. with
f-
plenty of assistants, Lord lidlowe, full of vengeful hatred, rode swiftly to and fro, searching for the maidia who he had sworn should be his wife! ( To be continued.)

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

The fashions for the autumn and winter promise to be in no wise behind their predecessors in pretti- ness, while in many ways they are more stylish. Skirts are to be full, with a good sweep at the back from large' rioh-looking, plentifully con- structed pleats. There is a slight spring at the sides, while the front falls with a most becoming flatness. The perfectly plain skirt has yet a further lease of life, and will figure triumphantly among the new fashions. It owes its prolonged existence to its becomingness to medium and small figures, and to its own grace and prettiness, as well as to its convenience and comfort.

As to bodices in general, there is but little change. The prettiest are rather full in front for evening wear, with soft filmy lace and chiffon, caught in either with ribbon or bands of the material, arranged in various ways, to suit various figures. As to sleeves, they continue to be the most impor- tant portion of the dress. Day dresses are plain, too, as to skirt, and tailor-made is popular. One lately seen was in a dark-green tweed mixture with braid round the skirt in undulating lines, a cutaway coat edged with braid, a vest of baby astrakan with plain brass buttons, revers of similar fur, a high fold over collar of fur, and a deep low one of old oopper-ooloured velvet. Black rep will be a stylish material for plain smart. walking dresses, but must be beautifully built up, with perhaps a vest of fur, and some jet and steel. The attractiveness of the winter hats is very great, and the fabricators have afforded abundance of choice. One beautiful toque I have seen was of velvet, edged with ostrich feathers, and trimmed with pom-poms and quills.

We are told by an authority of no less weight than Mr. Worth, that cashmere is to be worn again; indeed he has been making many gowns of that fabric; but he is said to be much disgusted with the English leaders of fashion, because, while accepting cashmere, they have refused to adopt draped skirts. Now it was purposely for draperies that the great man re-introduced the material, so he has been defeated on his own ground. One cannot be very sorry for him, however, for draped. ; skirts are certainly neither comfortable nor prac- tical for people who lead active lives. Except on the tallest figures, they look "bunchy," especially under winter wraps and coats. Moreover, they refuse to be held up out of the mud, and they crease wofully if one dares to sit on them. Long may the graceful and useful bell-skirt flourish amongst us .1 American fashion has set the seal of her approval upon the custom of going about at home with bare feet. As yet this practice is confined to the privacy of the boudoir, or to very informal morn- ings in the drawing-room. The fad (for I can call It by no other name) originated in bhe treatment of the celebrated German physician Kniep, who, among other things, required his patients to take a ran with bare feet every morning, no matter what the weather was. He was successful in his praotice, and it became fashionable to go to him, and hence to adopt his methods. Madame Sarah Bernhardt, it is said, spends her mornings, when alone, with bare feet. This fashion is not likely to be adopted by any but women who have pretty feet. It has already resulted in greater attention being given to the feet, and many persons have their toe-nails trimmed and polished as carefully as they do their finger-nails. Pretty coats are nowadays to be had in profusion for children of tender years. A particularly pleasing ono is made of art serge in a red-brown shade, with a touch of terra-cotta in its depths, and it boasts a loose zouave, edged with blue fox. These zonaves, by the way, are in some instances entirely of fur. On a bright blue coat one looks charming in caracule, and then again sealskin , forms another most successfully.

The right way to roll your umbrella is to take hold of the ends of the ribs and the stick with the same hand, and hold them tightly enough to pre- vent their being twisted while the covering is being twirled around with the other hand. Then your umt rolls will be as nicely closed as when you bought it, and the only wear and tear will be on cloth. It is twisting the ribs out of shape around the stick and fastening them there that spoils the umbrellas. Never hold the umbrella by the handle alone when you roll it up, and you find It will last longer and oost less for repairs. Yours lovingly, JENNIN.
Last year over four thousand five hundred million gallons of beer were drunk by the people of this world. The Patagonians are the tallest people in the world ; the shortest are the Laplanders.

Lady Sophia Cecil, who when a child was present at the famous dance in her mother's house in Brussels the night before the battle of Waterloo, has arrived at York from Edinburgh. Her ladyship is in the enjoyment of excellent health.

It is said that the Emperor Wilhelm, sitting out a dance with a young lady at a ball given by Prince Henry of Prussia, asked, " What would you say if I forbade naval officers to marry P" " Your Majesty," was the prompt reply, "that would be impossible.. Your navy would cease to exist.

All About the Body. Here are 19 facts about the human body, which ap- peared in the "Yorkshire Gazette " : Each ear has four bones. The stomach has four coats. Every hair has two glands at its base. - The sense of touch is dullest on the back. The globe of the eye is moved by six muscles. The cerebral matter is about seven-Pighths water. The normal weight of the liver is between three and four pounds. The human skeleton, exclusive of the teeth, consists of 208 bones.

Hair is very strong. A single hair will bear a weight of 1,150 grains. The colour of the skin depends on pigment cells in the inferior epidermis. The enamel of the teeth contains over 95 per cent, of calcerous matter. The wrist contains eight bones, the palm five ; the fingers have fourteen. The roots of the hair penetrate the skin about one- twelfth of an inch. The weight of the average-sized man is 140 pounds ; of the woman, 125. On an average the lungs contain about 280 cubic , inches, or nearly five quarts, of air. ' A woman's brain is larger in proportion to the weight of the body than that of a man. The longest, largest, and strongest bone in the human system is the femur, or thigh bone. The height of a fully grown man should be three and a half times that at his birth. There are in the human body 527 distinct muscles, of which 261 are in pairs.
Sciatica.

It is signalised by paroxysmal' pain in the buttock, the back of the thigh, the knee, the front, back, and outside of the leg, and the whole of the foot except the outer border. The pain may not be experienced in all these situations simultaneously, but in a bad case they all in turn come in for a share of its favours. The neuralgia may attack one leg or both. Very often as soon as it begins to get better in one leg the other is i attacked. The pain varies somewhat in character n different cases. It may be shooting, darting, screwing, commonly termed "indescribable." It may be more or tleisnsglcionngt,mbuuornig continuous or or of the peculiar nature which is or the pain may come on in paroxysms, lasting from a few minutes to the best part of a day. The limb Tay feel numb and aching, and when the pain is at its height there is a natural aversion to anythinc., in the shape of exertion. It does not make an invalid of a man or keep him in bed, but it certainly prevents him from enjoying life. A patient with sciatica wants no amusement; dinners, ball parties, and theatres are thrown away on him; and all he wants is to get home to his own fireside, where no one will speak to him or bother him. It is a disease not calculated to improve the temper. The pain may be temporarily alleviatid at night. but sleep is usually disturbed, and is broken and unrefreshing. The attack may be an acute one or may, under vigorous treatment, pass off in a few days; or, on the other hand, it may hang about for weeks, or even months. It is difficult to say what brings it on. Sit- ting on a stone seat or step, or on a damp cushion on the top of an omnibus, seem the favourite modes of pro- duction. Cold winds and draughts, especially when thinly clad, may excite it, anti blows or falls are often credited as exciting causes. It is predisposed to by a gouty or rheumatic tendency, and an old attack of syphilis may perhaps have something to say to it. It is chiefly a disease of middle life, the majority of cases occurring in men between the ages of forty and fifty. It is not often met with in women, probably be cause their petticoats serve to protect that particular region.— "The Family Physician."

div.head: SCOTCH MINERS STRIKE.
div.p: THE SCOTCH MINERS STRIKE.

The Scotch miners' strike ended on Monday, when the Fifeshire mem, the last to hold out, returned to the pits. The dispute, which began four months ago, has resulted in an enormous loss in wafzeA alone. Mr. Innes, one of the men's leaders, speaking at Dunfermline on Saturday, explained the situation. He said the reports received from the various districts showed that the majority of miners de4red to return to work on the masters' terms. He was bound to acknowledge that the back of the strike , had been broken, hut the coalowners liai paid a high I price for their victory.

div.head: DINING UNDER DIFFICULTIES.
div.p: DINING UNDER DIFFICULTIES.

The Portuguese in East Africa, in spite of all their fault, possess three good points. They are kind to their children, fond'of animals, and keep fine flower gardens. Pigeons, fowls, cats, dogs, pigs, and monkeys run all over the houses, without let or hindrance. Mr. H. H. Johnston, the traveller, was once dining at a house on the Zambesi, and had an uncomfortable time. The meals, well cooked and served,were,according to custom, all placed on the table at once. But the guests had hardly sat down when the pigeons flr,w in and settled on the boiled beans,the cat jumped on the table and stole his chop,a sow threatened to be troublesome till he bought peace by throwing her some food, and as the negro ser- vants passed in and out, fowls, dogs, and baboons at- tacked the plates and carried off half the meal. And all the. time the Portuguese host sat quietly by, merely say- " Poor little thing !" if a dish were broken by the babo.n, or the sow bit the baboon as the latter was about to partake of stewed pigeons.—" Little Folks."

div.head: AFRAID TO ENTER THE BRITISH
div.p: AFRAID TO ENTER THE BRITISH
MUSEUM.

i -- It is, says a writer n " Cassell's Saturday Journal," a curious fact that there are certain people who are positively unable to enter the British Museum. Extra- ordinary as this may sound it can be soon explained. Speaking to one who never dared enter any public library, the writer asked what there was in such institu- tions that was so repelling to him. "The excessive amount of learning," was the reply. " Directly I enter even a small private library, I begin at once to think of the number of books, then of the number of pages in these, the number of lines, and at last the number of words. Try it for yourself and you will gather some idea, if you can realise all this, what an awful, incalcul- able sum you are thinking of. It drives me nearly mad. The whole world of learning seems to press upon my brain, and I feel as if I must he out in the open air. If I were to stay in a big library for longer than ten minutes, I believe I should die of asphyxia." Another man who is a prominent solicitor declares solemnly that the British Museum is in reality nothing but a madhouse. "Go any day," he says gravely ; examine. the people reading there. They are all hopelessly Insane. The spirit of learning diffuses itself in the building and up- sets the equilibrium of one's brain. It's the State mad- house, and the authorities are cognisant of it !"

div.head: WHEN MEN ARE AT THEIR BEST.
div.p: WHEN MEN ARE AT THEIR BEST.

Dr. Beard states that from an analysis of a thousand representative men in all the great branches of the human family, he made the dis- covery that the golden decade was between forty and fifty, the brazen between twenty and thirty, the iron between fifty and sixty. The superiority of youth and middle life over old age in original work appears all the greater when we consider the fact that all the positions of honour and pres- tige, professorships and public stations, are in the hands of the old. Reputation, like money and position, is mainly confined to old. Men are not widely known until long after they have done the work that gives them their fame. Portraits of great men are delusions; statues are lies. They are taken when men have become famous, which, on the average, is at least twenty-five years after they did the work which gave them their fame. Original work requires enthusiasm. Men are at their best at that time when enthusiasm and ex- perience are almost evenly balanced. This period, on the average, is from thirty-eight to forty. After this the law is that experience increases, but enthusiasm decreases.

div.head: PARSON SURELY CALLS FOR A CONTRIBUTION.
div.p: PARSON SURELY CALLS FOR A CONTRIBUTION.

Once upon a time the Board of Commissioners sent to Parson Surely a circular letter, requesting him on a certain Sabbath to take up a contribution from his congregation for the benefit of Foreign Missions. The parson received the letter on the last of March; but he let the month of April slip by without calling for the contribution; but the month of May opened beautifully, and the good man announced to a few of the faithful, in advance, that on the first Sunday in May he should call for a contribution towards the work of carrying the Gospel Light into heathen lands. The day came bright and beautiful; and the people of the parish beheld something that sur- prised them something which they had never seen before. The parson seemed to be pleased— really delighted upon beholding the young damsels of his flock arrayed in new and gorgeous attire—new and flaming bonnets, and new and gaudy dresses! But the explanation was coming. For that very thing had he been waiting. "My friends ! " he said, sweeping his congrega- tion with those keen eyes, "I come now to the duty of asking you—each and every one of you— to give stomething towards the cause of our Foreign Missions.' Then he enlarged upon the cause ; the duty we owed to those of our brethren who had taken their lives in their hands, and gone out there, in savage lands, to carry the bread of life to dying souls. And, finally, when he had brought the whole thing down to the act then about to be consummated—the taking up of the contribution, he added:

"And now, my friends—and especially you, my my sisters—who have been so wondrously favoured by Providence—you who have appeared in new and brilliant plumage !—you have felt able to clothe yourselves in almost regal attire !—let the poor of the Lord share in your riches, and He will bless you. And, dear sisters— those of you who are noe pre- pared to respond to-day, may send to me on the morrow, and it shall be accounted unto you in thankfulness from many grateful hearts." Never before had such a contribution been taken in the church ! And, moreover, on the morrow fourteen women—young and old—sent to the parson goodly sums to be added to the gross amount. _ _
During the remainder of the season the women flaunted their new fashions boldly; for they had earned the right.

THERE is nothing purer than honesty; nothing sweeter than charity; nothing warmer than love; nothing brighter than virtue; and nothing more steadfast than faith. These, united in one mind, form the purest, the sweetest, the richest, the brightest, and the most steadfast happiness. SIB. GEORGE ROSE, once turning a corner, mune suddenly upon some young barristers who were in the act of aping his walk and gestures. "You mistake, gentlemen," said the good-natured wit, accosting them. "That is not the air of the Rose; it is only the stalk." HOTEL PROPRIETOR: "Yes, I want a clerk at once. What do you know about hotel keeping ? " Applicant " Know ? See here! Unless you've got four or five years to spare for a little chat, ask me what I don't know. It'll take less time. What do I know about hotel-keeping? Well, I should smile. I know it all—more than all. I could run forty hotels and play ten games of chess blindfolded. Why, man, I used to be a commercial traveller." HE DREW A BLANK.—She: "Do you also think, Frank, that marriage is a lottery ?" He: "Certainly not." She (agreeably surprised) : "And why not ?" He: "Simply because when one has drawn a blank in a lottery he can begin again, taking another ticket; but once drew a blank in marriage and you've got to stick there !" IT makes a great diflerence whether glasses are used erter or under the nose. If the former, the person can see and go straight ahead—if the latter, his head is rather apt to go where it can't see at all. A glass before the eye may make a man a philosopher—one before the mouth will most likely make him a fool. A QUESTION FOR A DEBATING SOCIETY.—The following question was lately put to a debating society.. There were a hundred ears of corn in a barn. A greedy rat carried them off to his nest, taking along three ears every time he left the barn. How many visits did he have to make to get the hundred ears? The president of the society answered, "Thirty-four visits -" but the secretary said that, inasmuch as two of the ears the rat took away were his own ears, he must have made a hundred visits. rou see, granama, we perrorave an sperms in the apex, and a corresponding aperture in the base and by applying the egg to the lips, and forcibly inhaling the breath, the shell is entirely discharged of its contents." "Dear me I" ex- claimed the old lady, "what wonderful improve- ments they do make. Now, in my younger days they just made a hole in each end and sucked." "It ain't any of your business as I know," she responded, tartly, "I might have beeh married a dozen times if I'd felt like providie for some poor, shiftless wreck of a man 1" He doesn't ask ladies if they want "single" tickets ahy more, heis afraid to. "I hear that your brother is given to sonuiam- bulism ? " "What's that ? " He walks in his sleep." "Well, that makes me smile. I guess you don't know my brother. He is the laziest white man in Texas. He would'nt walk in his sleep no matter how sound asleep he was. He is too lazy entiiely. I might not be surprised to hear that he had ridden in a street car in his sleep, but as for his walking that is out of the question. He doesn't walk when he is wide awake if he can help It." AN Irishman was once brought before a provin- cial magistrate on a charge of begging. After the magistrate had heard the evidence against the prisoner he sentenced him to three months' im- prisonment with hard labour, but as he was about to be removed from the Court he said: "Might I usk his Worship a question ? " "Well, what is it you want ? " said the magistrate. "Oh, I just wanted to ask your worship if I was to call you a silly old fool now what would I get done to ? " "Why, you impudent scoundrel, said the magistrate, "I should have you up for contempt of court and give you another three months." "But if I was only to think so, your worship, what then ? " "Oh, that Is quite another matter; I couldn't do anything to you for that." "Ah I sure, then I'll only think so, your worship,' said the prisoner.

A RUNCORN MAN KILLED AT WIDNES.
INQUEST AND FUNERAL.

Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coronor, conducted an inquiry on Friday afternoon at the Widnes Police Station into the circumstances connected with the death of James !Dudley, 28. Union-street, Runcorn, who was killed on Thursday morning at Gaskell Deacon's Works, Widnes. Superintendent Keighley attended on behalf of the police., and there were also present Mr. H. M. Richmond, governmmt inspector of factories and workshops, and Mr. H. V. Driffield, manager of Gaskell-Deacon's Chemical Works.—Evidence of identification was given by the father ot the deceased who said that his son was 21 years of age.—Henry Hatton, an employe at Gaskell-Deacon's deposed to the deceased being a shunter at the same works. Tne shunters were provided with long sticks to uncouple the waggons. There was a rule against •uncoupling waggons without sticks. On Thursday morning, about 930, two waggons were being shunted into a siding by au eng,ine The deceased had to unhook one of these, and when the watrgons reached him he put the long stick away and got under the buffers. Having un- hooked the waggons with his hands deceased shouted to the engine driver to go ahead. The waggons were on an incline. When be shouted to the driver, the engine and one waggon attached to it went ahead. The un- hooked waggon followed the engine. Peceased was standing straight up. When the driver saw the un- hooked waggon fallowing him he put the brake on. The buffers met and the deceased was caught between them. The driver did not know deceased was between the waggons.—John Dwyer and Richard Bevan also gave evidence. The latter was the engine driver and said that the deceased after uncoupling the waggons told him to go ahead. Witness had cautioned Hindley against going between the waggons.—AnswerMg Mr. Richmond witness said the brake of the waggon was down, but not pinned.—Having reviewed the evidence, the coroner observed that if the deceased had obeyed the yard regulations the accident would never have occurred.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." The funeral of the deceased tocik place on Sunday afternoon. The first portion of the burial service was conducted in the Halton-road Wesleyan Church,of which the deceased was a member. The body was then taken from the church to the cemetery and interred in the Nonconformist portion of the grounds. rhe procession was a very large one, and included, in addition to the relatives as chief mourners, about 30 members of the Runcorn Sons of Temperance, CO Odd fellows (Rose of Sharon Lodge), several °dicers from Halton-road con- gregation, and from Mill Brow Schools. Some of the members of the Halton-road Christian Endeavour Society., as well as representatives from other Friendly Societies, Joined the procession. The service at the graveside was conducted by the Rev. W. George. Many wreaths of ,exceptional beauty were placed upon the coffin, and the scene was a most impressive cne as the body was being lowerod. into its last resting place.

div.head: SEXTON SAVED FROM THE GRA.VE.
div.p: A SEXTON SAVED FROM THE GRA.VE.

The "Lancaster Guardian" reports a narrow 'escape of whighly respectable and intelligent man, Who was interviewed by its reporter. Mr. Samuel Fern, of :Brookhoese, Caton, near Lan- caster, is (says the reporter) well known to the-clergy and parishioners there, having been gravedigger at Brookbouse Church for -a number of years. life is up- wards of seventy years of age, which makes his -escape the more remarkable. He has, it appeared, died two strokes of paralysis, the latter of which, last year deprived him of the entire use of one side. It pretty generally agreed among medical men that this form of paralysis (called medically " hemiplegia," which means half-palsy) is uncura,ble, and Mr. Fern says that he had no use in his arms and-could not work. div.head: SICK NURSING LECTURE AT
div.p: SICK NURSING LECTURE AT
RUNCORN.

DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. The second course of lectures on sick nursing was opened on Friday afternoon in the Camden School Lowlands-road, a large audience being present., The Rev. Canon Wood occupied the chair. The occasion had been seized as one on which the prizes and certificates, gained at the recent examinations, might also be distributed. The Rev. Canon Wood, after reading a letter from Lady Brooke, in which that lady regretted that she could not be present to distribute the prizes, said that these lectures contained elements of great usefulness. Those who attended were not only made more fit to fulfil the duties of mothers, wives, and sisters, but were made much more useful to those at home and around them. They owed a debt of gratitude to Mr. Speakman and Mr. Hazlehurst, their county Council representatives for having begun the lectures. The County Council had provided a competent lecturer, syllabuses, prizes and certificates, but the gentlemen named had borne all local expenses, In view of the possibility that they might not always be represented on the County Council by those gentlemen and in order to place, if possible,the lectures on a permanent basis, it was thought desirable that a Committee of ladies should he appointed to carry on the work. He occupied the chair of that meeting because he was president of the Nurse Fund, and it was considered that the two might be com- bined. He agreed with this, and thought that much more benefit would be derived if the two were combined. He trusted that the work would not be confined to those who listened to Miss Watson. but the ladies who were instructed by her would use their in- structions for the benefit of others. (Applause.) The prizes and certificates were then distributed by Mrs. Wood to the following ladies :—Miss Clara-Anna Littler, Mrs. Elizabeth Cooper. Mrs. James Littler. Mrs. Parkinson, Miss A. M. Mack, Mrs. S. A. Davies, Miss M. M. Whiff!. Mrs. P. le Couteur, Mrs. Collier, Mrs. Mat- thews, Mrs. E. L. Davies, Miss Blanche Rowland, Mrs. Harrop, Mrs. J. Scragg, Miss M. A. Smith, Miss Carter, and Mrs. J. Mort. On the propositian of the Rev. T. Brackenburv, seconded by the Rev. W.George, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mrs. Woods for distributing the prizes. The Rev. Canon Wood in responding on behalf of his wife, expressed the gratitude they all felt towards those who had placed such an admirable room at their dispo- sal for the delivery of the lectures. A vote of thanks was also passed to the Chairman on the motion of the Rev. J. Stafford, seconded by the Rev. T. Bramall. Subsequently, the gentlemen retired, and Miss Watson proceeded with her lecture on "Pneumonia, bronchitis, and pleurisy." The followinz ladies were afterwards appointed a committee to make all necessery arrange- ments :—Mesdames F. J. Norman, T. Handley, J. Littler, W. Parkinson, Cameron. Davies, and le Couteur, Misses White, Annie Littler, A. M. Mack, B. Rowland, and Burton.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE.
ANECDOTES BY THE REV. NEWMAN HALL

Dr. Newman Hall, the great preacher, who has known Mr. Gladstone fOr twenty-five years. has been giving the "New Age" some very interesting reminiscences of the Grand Old Man. Althongh opposed to the ex-Premier's Home Rule policy Mr. Hall is very wrathful at the treat- ment meted out to him by ill-bred people of the "upper lasses." "I am indignant," he said, "at some of the spiteful things said of Mr. Gladstone, and evil motives attributed, because of differences of political opinion. At the last but one Handel Festival, when Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone went out during the interval,l saw two ladies very fashionably dressed go up behind him, one of whom hissed in his ear. I was some distance off by reason of the crowd. On returning to hear the second part of the oratorio, I heard a lady say, Didn't I hiss in his ear ?' I turned round and saw the same two ladies, and could not forbear saying in a loud voice, And you ought to be ashamed of yourself. We may not agree with Mr. Gladstone in politics, but we ought to honour him as one of the greatest men of the day, who has spent a long life in the service of his country.' The so- called ladies seemed somewhat crest-fallen.

div.head: TIIE JUBILEE SINGERS.
div.p: TIIE JUBILEE SINGERS.

" Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone once asked me to bring the Negro Jubilee Singers to their house to breakfast, and I took about eight or ten. The Gladstones had also in- vited some dozen aristocratic people, and the Jubilee Singers were sandwiched between them, and not placed altogether.. So that you saw in one place a well-known countess, and by her side a full-blown negress,all waited upon in an equal way. Mr. Gladstone engaged in con- versation on matters of interest to them, and showed a wonderful knowledge of negro character and history. After breakfast the singers sang for about an hour. Mr. Gladstone sat on the sofa,and his eyes were moist with emotion, while he seemed absorbed in the music. In the next morning's paper I saw that he went by special train at twelve o'clock to see the Queen at Windsor, and on the same afternoon made a great speech in the House of Commons. "He might well write as he does here," continued Dr. Hall, turning to a letter from Mr. Gladstone--' My daily life is a continual struggle, with immediate calls and unfulfilled engagements.' That was in 1878."

div.head: 70118 'BRIGHT'S RESIGNATION.
div.p: 70118 'BRIGHT'S RESIGNATION.

Resuming his reminiscences, Dr. Hall said :—" One morning I met John Bright in the street looking very downcas t. After greeting me, he said, • I feel very anxious, and should like a long talk with you, but I have not time now.' A few hours later his resignation was announced in the House of Commons. It was the day on which the bombardment of Alexandria took place, and when that was determined upon he with- drew from the Cabinet.

"The same evening I was in the gallery of the House of Commons and saw Mr. Gladstone sitting on the front bench busily engaged in reading despatches which were being continuously brought to him. Apparently he was absorbed in nothing but these, wheif suddenly he jumped up and exclaimed, I beg the hon. member's pardon; I did not say—. What I said was—,' and then he busied himself again in his despatches. "Presently the House rose, and going out into the Yard I saw Mrs. Gladstone in her victoria waiting for her husband. She kindly beckoned me to her, and we had several minutes' chat. Soon there was a bustle and much cheering, and out came Mr. Gladstone with a bunble of papers. I should have liked to linger and shake hands with him, but at such a crisis I thought it more polite and patriotic not to detain him, so I backed into the crowa, and they droveaway. "Next morning found this letter awaiting me : Downing-street, July 12, 1882. DEAR MR. NEWMAN HALL,—How rude you must have thought me! My sight grows welk, especially in recognition. I was in a great hurry,and rather avoided personal ing:ection, but had I seen who it was I should not have failed in greeting and asking how you did in these anxious and oppressive thnes. Pray forgive rne.— Faithfully yours, W. Z. GLADSTONE. "This is interesting," eaid Dr. Newman Hall, " as an illustration of Mr. Gladstone's courtesy to small people, and attention to little things. Under the cir- cumstances he might have taken no personal notice of the greatest in the land. Rather than let me think that he had overlookod me, you see, he wrote that note. Of course there was every reason why he should not have seen me. All my acquaintance with Mr. Gladstone deepens my sense of his religiousness, breadth of sym- pathy 4 large heartedness, conscientiousness, and wonder- ful intellect. He knows everything."

div.head: XL 0 LADSTONE't MIRVANTS.
div.p: XL 0 LADSTONE't MIRVANTS.

"Some time ago I was preaching in the North of England, and happened to stay at the house of a solicitor who had paid a recent visit to Hawarden, merely as a tourist. On his return he entered a carriage in which there was seated a woman with a very beautiful bouquet of flowers, which my friend admired. " ' Mr. Gladstone gave them to me,' said the woman. Oh,' replied my friend, how was that?' He was then told that every servant who left the Castle with a good character was invited to return and spend a week during the summer. used to be a servant there,' continued the woman, 'but left because I was going to be mar- ried. I have, however, just been staying there a week, and as I was leaving I met Mr. Gladstone in the garden. He asked me if I liked flowers, and when I said that I did Me gave me this bunch, which he had in his hand, saying, "Pray accept them."' I think that was very characteristic," added Dr. Hall. "Another incident was related to me at Wigan,by my host. A young girl of that town who was dying of con- sumption,was making a bookmarker for Mr. Gladstone's birthday. She became so much worse that she was afraid she would not live to finish it. She did, however, finish it, and her doctor sent it to Mr. Gladstone, telling him all the circumstances under which it was made. Immediately there came back a note of sympathy and a. basket of magnificent grapes from Mr. Gladstone's own vine."

div.head: VISIT TO • CROSSING-SWEEPER.
div.p: VISIT TO • CROSSING-SWEEPER.

"The other story," Dr. Newman Hall went on, "which I had in my mind happened when Mr. Glad- stone was Chancellor of the Exchequer, and was told me by Sir Francis Crossley. Sir Francis was one day dining with the vicar of St. Martin-in-the-Fields, to which church Mr. Gladstone used to go when living in Carlton House-terrace; it was then that he heard the story from the vicar. The vicar had recently been to see a cross- ing-sweeper in his parish who was ill. Asking him if anyone had been to see him, the sweeper replied, Yes Mr. Gladstone.' Which Mr. Gladstone,' asked the vicar. 'Mr. Gladstone,' repeated the poor invalid. 'But how came he to see you ?' inquired the vicar.'We!,' answered the crossing-sweeper, he always had a nice word for me when he passed my crossing, and when I was int there he missed me. He asked my mate, who has taken my place, where I was, and when he heard I was ill, he asked for my address, and when he was told he put it down on paper. So he called to see me." And what did he ?' aQked the vinar. Why, he read some Bible to me and prayed,' was the reply."

div.head: "DREADFUL AFFAIR" AT THE "ZOO.'
div.p: "DREADFUL AFFAIR" AT THE "ZOO.'

"A SERPENT'S DINNER." A dreadful affair is reported from the London Zoolo- gical Gardens. It is said that a boa-constrictor eight feet long was eating a pigeon when another serpent a foot longer began to eat the part of the pigeon which was still projecting from its friend's mouth. We under- stand, subject t, correction, that when a boa-constrictor begins to eat one end of a substance it continues to eat till the other end of the substance is reached, however distant it may be when the meal is begun. Mastication having already made the other end of the pigeon virtu- ally a portion of the body of the smaller serpent, the larger one, however much it may have regretted the misconception, felt itself bound, as the Irish say, "to eat all before it" till it came to its brother's tail. " Once begun," the reporter says, "the swallowing process would go on almost mechanically." Considering the tremendous nature of the digestive forces at work, we should be seriously lacking in charity if we judged hardly of this snake. A mere solecism, a slight breach of the civilities of the table—probably a competent jury of serpents, acquainted with the physical organization of their race, would acquit the boa-constrictor which is now " outside " the other of anything worse than this. The remorse which he must now feel as he lies, a little stiff but not really bilious, in his blanket,will no doubt be a sufficient lesson—teaching him, at any rate, if there be a third boa-constrictor ten feet long at the Zoo, never to begin a pigeon in his pres- ence.

div.head: WOMEN AND THE PARISH AND DISTRICT COUNCILS ACT.
div.p: WOMEN AND THE PARISH AND DISTRICT COUNCILS ACT.
MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

tra,ler the auspices of the Earlestown and Dis- tric:-, Womens' Liberal Association, a meeting was held in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom on Saturday evening, to hear an address by Miss Kate Jenkins, of London, on the Parish and District Councils Act. Mrs. Rawlins, of Rainhill, presided but there was only a moderate attendance. Mrs. Rawlins said that meeting though held under the auspices of the Women's Liberal Association was not a political meeting in any sense of the word, it was en- tirely educational. In anticipation of the first Parish and District Councils to be held in December, they, as an association, thought it was desirable, knowing the widespread want of knowledge as to the working of the Act, regarding voting, how to vote, and who could vote and who could sit on the Council and so on, that they should do what they could to enlighten the people as to the duties and privileges which the Act conferred on men and women before the elections took place. Con- ferences organized by the National Liberal Federation had been held in the South of England and in the Mid- land Counties for the purpose of instruction, and dele- gates had been asked to attend these meetings from the rural districts all round, and this call had been very well responded to and they had met with very satisfactory results. She was desirmus that the whole of the working classes should fully take to heart that this measure was intended to give them self government to a great ex- tent. It was like giving the people local parliament,and this was a thing they had wanted for a very long time. Now that women had such enormous benefits conferred, she could not urge too strongly on them the necessity for educating themselves in all tint had to do with this Act, and the nrevileges it conferred on them. Women could now vote and sit on the Parish Councilsand Urban and Rural District Councils, but not in the boroughs. Married women also could vote. (Hear, hear.) There- fore let women take the matter up and go thoroughly into it, as far as they could, and taking every advan- tage of learning what their powers were, and then they need never hesitate to use them for the good of the places in which they lived. There was an enormous scope for women's work, as in the case of the guardians where men and women together could do very much better than men alone. Their association would do all in its power to spread a knowledge of political instruc- tion in evJry district; it had begun very well, and was going on in a very promising and prosperous way. If women could not exercise the vote which they had for Parish and District Councils, how did they suppose they should exercise the frinchise which they hoped to have presently for Parliamentary elections? They must work hard, and put their shoulders to the wheel, and in that spirit let them help the men, then the men would help them, and they would in this way do much better work than they had done before. (Cheers.) Miss Kate Jenkins, of London, in a lengthy address, said the Parish and District Councils Act had been called one of the greatest Acts which had been passed during the 18th century, and if they surveyed the laws which had been passed for the benefit of the community at large, they would find that such was the case. It was the greatest reform which had been enacted since the great Reform Bill of 1832, and the Municipal Corpora- tions Act of 1835. They had made progress in many directions,and their educational progress was wonderful. It had been said that the Parish Councils Act was a very dry Act, it was, however, only the skeleton which they were to clothe with life and action. The Board of Guardians which had done so much work, was not to be done away with altogether. It would be reconsti- tuted to suit the times., and in future in the rural dis- tricts, the district councillors were going to take over the work of these bodies. Some people who were not progressive, and who did not wish to have reform,would say that these bodies had only changed in name, and that their work would continue the same, bat if they looked into it, they would see that the case was very much different. This Act was going to give self-govern- ment to the people, such as they had never before possessed. On the 14th December, she said, in every rural district in England and Wales, there was to be a parish meeting, which would be held at the democratic hour of six o'clock, when most men and women could come toge- ther. They would speak and -vote and pass resolutions, and discuss the affairs of the town or the village or any reform which they might require. She then went into minute detail with regard to the various provisions of the Act. Coming to the District Councils,she said the eouncil would take over the work of the sanitary authority of the Boards of Guardians, and also they would have some of the powers of the justices entrusted to them, to took after footpaths, and see that no encroachments were made on any common (loud cheers) and they would also have the powerto see that dwellings were in a proper sanitary condition. They often could not get the right people on the guardians, firstly, because of the plurality of voting and secondly because of the open voting: 'Under this new act how- ever, the elections would be on the principle of one man one vote, and the ballot. (Applause.) Hitherto in large towns, when land was wanted for special building pur- poses, for the public good, they had been compelled to give a fancy price for it,but in future, not a penny more than it was worth was to be paid for this land. The Chairman of the rural and urban district councils would be a magistrate in virtue of his office and this was a great step, which would make 1200 or 1400 popularly elected magistrates. There were going to be more guar- dians elected, and there was room for women on these Boards of guardians. She tad never met a man who was a guardian himself, who did not say that there ought to be women on every Board of Guardians. (Ap- plause.) After some remarks by Mr. Cordingley, Mr. G. W. Rawlins moved and Miss Ashcroft seconded a vote of thanks to Miss Jenkins.which was unanimously accorded. A like compliment having been paid to Mrs. Rawlins,the meeting terminated.

div.head: "PEACOCK" TEMPER.
div.p: "PEACOCK" TEMPER.

What is" peacock" temper ? In a professedly ver- batim report of Mr. Asquith's speech published in the columns of a contemporary on Tuesday, the Govern- ment was spoken of as having been accused of refusing so-called amendments to the Employers' Liability Bill in " peacock " temper. Can it be that the ears of the re- porter were mistaken, and that when Mr. Asquith said was " pique or temper ? "

GENIIRAL BOOTEE IN NEW YORE.—New York, Tuesday. —A great concourse of Sal'ratio nists with several bands, assembled in Union Square on Monday evening to wel- come General Booth. Later on a reception was held at the Carnegie Music Hall, attended by 5,000 persons. Much enthusiasm was displayed. General Booth, in addressing the assemb!age, briefly recounted the history of the Salvation Army.

The mpress of Austria has to give a written receip for the State jewels every time she wears them. and her Majesty, as a result, usually contents herself with a private collection, which is worth three hundred thou- sand pounds.
