div.head: IHE EXAMINEP, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27 1894. GOOD TEMPLAR ANNIVERSARY AT I IN SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA. EARLESTOWN.
div.p: IHE EXAMINEP, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27 1894. GOOD TEMPLAR ANNIVERSARY AT I IN SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA. EARLESTOWN.

The twen'r second anniversary of the Hope of Earle:q own lodge of Good Templara No. 1644, was celebrated on Saturday evening by a tea and enter- tainment, held in the Co-operative Hall, the head- quarters of the Lodge. Recently the membership of the lodge has gone forward by leaps and bound,, and within the space of a very few months it has drawn within its shelter, not only several gentle- men of good standing, not necessarily previously intem- perate, but a good number of others who this time last year would have laughed to scorn any suggestion that they should become members of the order, but who have now become useful members of the Society and are in a fair way of remaining such. The proceedings were initiated by an excellent tea to which about 140 persons were present. Several of the lady members of the order attending to the wants of the visitors. After tea the attendance was considerably augmented, the entertain- ment being presided over by Bro. E. J. George, who was ' supported by Bro. Rev. J. A. L-e, D.C.T., and G.C. of England; Bros.Q.M. Sergeant Mantle, D.C.T. ; Sergeant Roberts, D.T.S. ; G.Clarke, D.M. ; W.H. Dale, secretary, and the officers of the lodge were also present on the platform. The Chairman in the course of his address said he was once connected 4,ith a lodge for a considerable period. He was the Worthy Secretary, for two years and more a regalia with the letters W.S. and he thought he owed some at any rate,of his business aptitude to the business he learned in the lodge. (Hear, hear and applause.) The lodge,he said,taught them to be methodical and business- like. He was proud of his connection with the temper- ance cause, not of Good Templars only,or the Rechabites or Band of Hope, but of the temperance cause generally. He counted it a great honour to be a member of the temperance order, and he urged all those present, who were not members to give in their names that night for nomination. (Applause.)—Bro. W. H. Dale in submitt- ing his report for the year said the lodge was instituted on the lith October, 1872, in Mr.Corlett's room.Market- street, where it met weekly for about two years, and then removed to Mr. Clarke's room, Bridge-street, meet- ing there weekly until about two years ago, when they removed to their present quarters in the Co-operative Hall. Since their commencement they had initiated about 800 members, and although they had not that number on the books at the present time, as many had left by clearance card, and gone to other districts,some had left to join other temperance societies, and some were working as missionaries, and the fruits of their labours had not been in vain. They reported for the quarter ending October, 1893, a membership of 41 on the books, and for the quarter ending January, 1894, 40 members, a decrease of 1, April, 1890, 38, and al- though the tide seemed to be very much against them at the beginning of the year, the quarter commencing , Moy seemed to be the turning point, as at the end of , July they had 92 members on the books, an increase of 50. (Applause.) They had gone on initiating every lodge night since that time, and for the quarter ending October they had 140 members, being an increase of 48 on the previous quarter, or about 100 on the whole year. Money had been raised in the town fora new piano, and the money hal been spent in the town. (Ap- plause.) Bro. the Rev. J. A. Lee, D.C.T., briefly addressed the meeting, remarking that he thought the hops of the 1 future in connection with Good Templary, as in other temperance organisations, was with the young. He claimed for the Good Templar Order that it was the most perfect temperance organisation that the world has ever seen. It had the most perfect pledge ot any organisa- tion ; personal abstinence, non-providing of intoxi- cants, and the prohibiting of the sale of intoxicants. Ile concluded by exhorting all who had not signed the pledge to do so that night before leaving the room, and eive in their names to become members of the Hope of Earlestown lodge. (Applause.) During the evening a programme of vocal and instru- ental selections was submitted in a pleasing manner by the following :—Bros. W. Willis. W. Hudleston, W. Wil- son, George Clarke, and G. E. Warburton ; Sisters Cord- inelev. Roberts and Willis. A juvenile choir, under the conductorahip of Bro. G. Clarke gave one or two pleas- ing selections, and Bro. A. Haynes received applause for his performance on the fairy bells. The anniversary services were continued on Sunday morning, when Bro. Rev. J. A. Lee conducted special services in the Primitive Methodist chapel. There was a large congregation present, the preacher basing his diecourse on the text, Isiah xlvii. 4. The Primitive Methodist choir sang the anthem "The Lord is Bing," under the conductorship of Mr. Dickens. Another ser- vice WAS held in the Co-operative Hall in the afternoon, when the Rev. J. A. Lee again officiated.

(BY MR. H. WHITHAM). My last letter wa,A written at Worcester, Mass, and I had half determined to write no more, or at least, not to write until I could send to my friends in Warrington some better news as to my do- ings in the "Garden of the Lord," towards which it seemed my steps were again tending. After a fruit- less and wearying effort to find work in Worcester I felt myself forced to part, once again, from my I dear wife and little ones and go to the three girls I I had in San Francisco, hoping there to find matters more favourable. I have been wofully disappointed. Some of my friends urge that I ought net to write such doleful letters, as I but show myself up as an unsuccessful man. As nothing succeeds like success, the reverse must also be accepted, and a man who repeatedly proclaims to all the world his want of success and his repeated failures, but invites all the world to crash him still lower. I cannot say if this is good philosophy or not, but I do think it a duty to place before my friends and readers of the " Ex- aminer " generally, as fair a description of the state of things existing in this country as possible. I have stated already what the prospects of the labourer were in Worcester: how the streets were crowded with unemployed,and how at every factory notices were posted up "no help wanted." To get a job at anything required a "political pull," and,in fact, one had to be either a very great saint or a desperately great sinner to get within sight of the squirming dollar. I lay no claim to being even a moderate sort of a saint ; possibly my friends will acquit me of being a desperate sinner. 1 thought the journey from New York to Califor- nia called for no hurry, so I took the sea from the former place to Norfolk in Virginia. Slow riding, frequent stoppages, and now and again a tramp, gave me lots of opportunities for a talk with the 1 old southern slave-owners, and with the whilom slave. The condition of things in the Southern States is bad, desperately bad. The change from slavery to freedom has satisfied no party. True,they no longer have the slave market, nor the gibing auctioneer, nor yet the jeering purchaser, but, coloured man, and white man alike, are being unrelentlessly crushed by the heel of a tyranizing despot. Some of us call this despot "Capital," others give it various names. "What's in a name." The fact remains. I saw in all the southern towns
was in a more abject, dirty, squalor existing than

. _ -I- ever saw in either. the east end of London or in the worst parts of Manchester. I cannot dwell on this, although the subject of the south tempts me. It is sufficient to say that the changed system has left both planter and coloured man wretchedly poor,and its results are seen in the poverty-stricken farms one rides through. What is wanted in the southern State is money and order. The land is naturally rich, and will, lam told, grow anything. Minerals are also plentiful. There is great future for the South. but I am of opinion this can only follow in the steps of the reforming spirit of the age that now cries out for acceptance. Right on through Kentucky,Lousiana,up through the Middle States,and so on to San Francisco where I was pleased to meet my three girls, all looking well, and feeling well, until we sat down to talk things over, and then a change is seen. Awkward questions are asked," When are ma and the children going to come?" " When I get to work and earn money enough." Oh dear," What are you going to work at? Why there are thousands of men walki ing about the streets." What a splendid reception all the same the facts of life have to be met, and I turn out to seek work as a common labourer. After some five or six weeks marching and counter marching I come to the conclusion that employers decide me to be an :uncommon labourer and there- tore have no use for me. Says one "Are you a book- keeper ?" " No," " How old are you ?" "Just turned fifty." " Ah we never start a man at labouring over forty-fiva and I think we have nothing that will suit you, good-bye." I managed to get, in as cheap a fashion as poss- ible, out some 200 miles among the peaches, plums, and pears at Napa. I didn't have it all to myself here. Crowds of men I found still. After a couple of days, I managed to get a job making trays for drying fruit on. These trays are about three feet long by three wide. They are made by nailing two ends and two sides together, and then nailing fourteen boards across, five nails on each boards. One penny each is !paid. Two men will make fifty a day. I worked three days changed partners twice, and earned the overwhelming sum of Bs. On the Monday morn- ing no partner turned up, yet scores of men were lying around, but, they wouldn't face the job so the boss put me on the field to turn fruit that was dry- ing in the sun. The beat that day was 120 degrees out in the field. The work was all done kneel- ing. The ground was hard as a stone, at noon my poor knees were blistered badly. The sun had blistered my brains, and I quit work. At night a scarcity of fruit caused a dozen men to be let out. The next two days were passed in bed my back and legs being of no use. After this I tried to get a job about some stores. Well I started off back to Frisco not very elated with the doctrine of the "survival of the fittest." After another week spent in the city I determined to go out in the country again. Previous to doing this I ought to give an account ot the employment bureaus R 5 I found them in my rounds seeking work. These bureaus are quite an institution here. They are honest and otherwise. the "otherwise" being the more numerous. An "ad." will be put in the paper for fifty grape pickers. A charge is made according to the wage going to be paid. If a man gets a dollar and half a day's job,he pays the bureau a dollar and half. The agent will take men so long as they come for the fifty men job, so that when they arrive on the ground there may be a hundred men or more. It may have cost the men their last five dollars to get there. No matter, if they cannot give, or outbid, with the man bossing the job they must seek elsewhere, with the helpless feeling of knowing they are being robbed. Men in the coun- try arrange with these bureaus's to be always wanting' men, dividing the plunder with each other. I went around to these places a full week, and concluded to go again into the country on my own hook. This time I fixed upon Fresno over 200 miles from San Fran- cisco. This is in the very midst of the raisin and fig growing country. After about a week I got a job in a Tasin and fig packing place. The grapes are picked from vines standing about 3ft. high, and laid on trays to be dried into rasins by the sun. They are then gathered into boxes weighing each about 2001bs, loaded on waggons, and drawn by teams of ten and twelve mules to the packing place. They are then sorted, and graded, and packed into fifty pound boxes such as are seen in the shops. My work is lifting these boxes from the waggons and again into the cars. Of all the heavy labor I ever had in my life this takes the palm. I weighed 174 lbs when I started. and:if I stay at it long I shall be minus the 100 lbs. I wish some one would make me agent for a fig and rasin business. It is a big business here thousands of acres covered with vines and fig trees. To leave that part of my tale and talk about the labor. I think I may fairly say that I have had some experience in the labor question. I never really saw it until I came here. As seen here it is something to make the most optimistic shudder. To begin with, there is no Sunday. If you don't work Sunday, why,you don't work at all. The sun keeps right on and the labourer must do likewise. If I go out to pick grapes I get 3s. a day and my board, and to hear the latter described by some of the pickers, as I have done, would make a pig sick. It a picker you take a blanket with you—l have mine with me—and coil yourself up anywhere or anyhow. For mate you may have anyone of the thousand and one nationalities that encumber this evoluting globe. You needn't trouble about any valuables you may have, there are lots around only too willing to take care of them for you. I board and lodge in the usual American saloon which stands facing the railway dep6t. Into this hotel are passing day by day and every day hundreds of men each with his blanket on his shoulder, all seeking work, none daring to question the wage offered. I get ss. a day, and I pay £1 a week for sleeping and eating. Have I said enough? So far as I remember not one prophecy I have ventured to make since I came here has turned out wrong. I again venture before five years are over, either Republicanism or, its alter ego, protec- tionism will prevail against Democracy or free trade, or else the most bloody revolution the world ever saw will come about in the United States of ' America. Europe has dumped its poor and ignorant on this soil. It has also dumped a dollar-making unscrupulous class here. Between the two will come the tug of war. I don't suppose I shall stay here many days, the rain has set in to-day. This will spoil all grape picking, and so I shall have to move on again.

div.head: CATHOLICS AND THE LONDON SCHOOL
div.p: CATHOLICS AND THE LONDON SCHOOL
BOARD ELECTOR.

A concerted attack is being mad, upon Mr. T. P. O'Connor by the organ of Cardinal Vaughan in Eng- land and of Mr. Healy in Ireland. In the case of the " Irish Catholic," Mr Healy's paper, this is only part of a policy that has been pursued for a long time, apparently designed as a retaliation for con- demnation of Mr. Healv's habit of dragging into publicity internal conflicts of opinion among the Nationalists. The immediate cause of this renewed fusilade is the outspoken opposition of the" Sun" to Cardinal Vaughan's appeal to the Roman Catho- lics to support the Diggleites. Mr. O'Connor has advocated, on the contrary, a cordial alliance be- tween the Catholics and the Progressives, trusting to this co-operation to bring about, in due time, favourable consideration for Catholic claims by the Liberal party. Curiously enough, while Mr. O'Con- nor is denounced by the two organs referred to as an enemy of religion, the Catholic Bishop of Southwark and several priests have advocated the same policy,and no less than three or four Catholic candidates in South London have put in the fore- front of their programme an utter want of sym- pathy with Mr. Diggle and his policy. Indeed, one of these, a well-known priest, graphically said" I renounce Diggleism and all its works and pomps," so that, like the Church of England, Roman Catho- licism is speaking with very decided voice on the present contest.
It is announced that Messrs. Lynoch and Co., of Bir- mingham, have decided to e;tablish a cordite factory in the south of Ireland, subject to receiving Government unction.

The second ballots in Belgium on Sunday have ended in a decisive victory for the Catholic party. The Gov- ' velment will have a large majority in the Chamber. The Queen of Saxony maintains three physicians whose sole duty is to attend the ailments of the suffering poor. The tendency to embonpoint which so distresses Queen Margherita is probably due to her fondness for II Italian cookery, with its oils, spices, and pastry. She is especially 'fond of cakes fried in oil, spaghetti with cheese and olives, and when there are no foreigners present at the royal board the national cookery is al- ways in the ascendant, and garlic and onions literally "rule the roast." •

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT -WARRINGTON.

The local officer of the N.S.P.C.C. is causing great commotion among those persons who are neglect- ful of their children in Warrington. He has had a great number up recently and in the majority of the cases, he has obtained heavy convictions. The majority—or in fact all—of these cases of neglect are attributable to one source, and that is drink. If it were not for the irresistible temptations which are placed in the way of these parents they would pro- bably have looked after their children properly instead of wasting their time and money in drink- ing. Such cases as these are, surely, weighty argu- ments in favour of the temperance cause. It is a very Easy thing for people to say that it is "their own fault" for getting drunk, but with a public- house at almost every turn of the road, it is almost an impossibility for some people—many of whom have inherited the curse of the craving for strong. drink—to resist the temptation. The drink traffic has truly a great deal to answer for.

The summer season is now over and all the sum- mer entertainments are dropping off one by one. On Saturday last the Bands Association closed their season by a grand united gathering in front of the Town Hall. The association has had a most success- ful season,and large crowds have been present every time the bands have occupied the bandstand in the park. The proceedings on Saturday afternoon lust were very short,—too short in fact for most people. They however showed what progresshad been made in Warr- ington in instrumental music. There is now quite a number of very good bands in the town,and it is only fair to say that a great deal of this good work that has been done is duo to the exertions of the worthy hon. secretary, Mr. Joseph Taylor.

The danger of standing up in swing boats was very strongly emphasized by the fatality which occurred during the past week at Howard-street. The deceased young man with another of about the same age, would persist in standing up in the "boat" while it was going, in spite of everything that the man in charge said to them, and the result was a fatal accident. The coroner hoped that the accident would be a warning to young people to keep their seats while swinging, but I don't expect that the warning will have very much effect. A spice of danger seems to add to the attraction to some people. However, it ought to make the keepers of these swing-boats even more strict than they are at present in putting down the dangerous practice.

An interesting paper was read at the first meet- ing for the session of the Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday evening last, by Mr. T. May, F.EI.S.. upon local antiquities. The workings of the Ship Canal have laid bare quite a number of relics of ancient times, and Mr. May was good enough to explain all that was known of the history of the various articles found near Warrington. In read- ing the paper,one is surprised at the number of the articles found, which once again prove that this district has considerable archasological interest. It is interesting to know that Mr. May's opinion con- cerning the canoe found not far from Walton lock is that it dates from a period not later than the second century. The lecturer had a side-thrust at the Museum Committee, who, he said were not likely to be troubled with valuable antiquities, until they had made better provision for housing and showing them. He said that he nnderstood that the difficulty was owing to want of funds. It is to be hoped that all the relics of the district will not be lost to Warrington on this account.

There was a good number of enthusiastic politi- cians waiting in Sankey-street in front of the Con- servative Club and the Post Office on Wednesday night last to hear the result of the Birkenhead election. They had a long wait, however, for it was not until about ten minutes to twelve that the definite news came. The members of the Conservative Club were put in high spirits at about half-past ten, by two well-known young Tory bloods rushing along San- key-street and into the Club shouting "Lees is in by 730." At this "glorious news," loud and pro- longed cheers were raised in the Conservative Club at the crushing defeat of the Liberal candidate. The two young men alleged that they had received the news from the Central Station.

A local curate who is not of Brobdingnagianl dimensions was in the small crowd, and on hearing the news, his face lit up, and he exclamined with much gusto "That's good, that's good. I knew Lees would give Lever a good beating," and off he went home looking an inch or two bigger. He was evidently one of those "political parsons" of whom Tories express so much horror. Several of the Liberals present were rather sceptical with regard the large majority and they were further re-assured when no news had come to the Post Office. Towards twelve o'clock the news came from various sources that " Lever was defeated:by 106," which one man who had come from Liverpool said that "Lever was in by 9." The 106 majority for the Tory was, how- ever, confirmed, and the small crowd separated, Councillor Smethurst loudly asserting that he con- sidered the result to be practically a defeat for the Conservatives. _

div.head: MERLIN.
div.p: MERLIN.
SHIP CANAL

MANCHESTER RATEPAYERS AND THE CANAL. At Manchester, on Monday.a deputation, representing tillarge number of ratepaverslof Manchester,waited upon the Lord Mayor (Sir A.Marshall) to support a requisition suggesting that the eleven corporation representatives constituting the majority of the Ship Canal directorate should be elected to their seats directly by the ratepayers instead of being chosen by the City Council from their own number. Mr. F. Spence, who read the requisition. said that not a single signature to it had been obtained by solicitation, but all had been forwarded by post, in compliance with the simple request that if the proposal was approved the form might be returned signed. The loan of £5,000,000 of borrowed money to the Ship Canal by the corporation made it imperative that the city representatives on the directorate should be the ablest practical administrators the community could provide. Traffic on the canal was increasing so Wowly that unless a speedy change for the better took Place the company would be unable to pay interests on its borrowed capital, and a crisis must ensue. In that case help would have to come alone from the city of Manchester, and an agreement might be made which, instead of extricating the ratepayers from their burdens and perils, might commit them to a new and possibly disastrous involvement of the corporate finances. Of the present directors sent by the Corporation seven were aldermen. They were therefore practically irremovable, and out of touch with the ratepa.vers. They had not the necessary leisure to devote to Ship Canal matters, and the whole eleven were in business, which gave them no special fitness for controlling and managing the gigantic enterprise. It would he the truest and wisest course for the City Council to promote a Bill in Parliament em- powering them to hold an election of city representa- tives to the Canal Board simultaneous with the election of the School Board.

Mr. A. Forest said it was not derogatory to sav that their were corporation representatives on the Board who could not influence a single ton of traffic, simply because their business connections were not of a nature to brine. traffic to the canal. The ratepayers had to pay the piper and they had a right to call the tune by the direct elec- tion of members to the Canal Board. The Lord Mayor, in reply, said the Act of rarliament was obtained and the loan granted with the full consent of the ratepayers. So far the work had been done by the Corporation directors faithfully and capably. The memorialists to his mind had not advanced a satisfac- tory reason why any change should be made. The method they proposed was likely to lead to the election of outsiders, who had no time for the work, and who had hitherto shown no interests in the canal and its commerce. He could not see his way to calling a public meeting, but if they wanted one he would lend them the use of his parlour. THE CONDITION OF THE CANAL. A STRONG COMPLAINT.

At a meeting of the Altrincham Rural Sanitary Autho- rity, on Wednesday. Dr. Fox. medical officer, who is detained at Nantwich owing to a serious outbreak of measles, wrote calling special attention to the condition of the Manchester Ship Canal. All through Carringtcn and Partington, and even up to Latchford. it was an intolerable, disgraceful, and dangerous nuisance. The Sanitary Authority decided to write the Ship Canal Company on the subject.

WALES.
THE LATE REV. R. H. DIGNUM. - EXTRAORDINARY STATEMENTS.

An extraordinary paragraph appeared in some of Sat- urday evening's papers with reference to the late Rev.R. H. Dignum, who died at Partick on the 26th of August. For some years Mr. Dignum, who was a brother of Mr. John Dignum, of Penketh, was pastor of the Free Epis- copalian Church at Partick, but latterly he had been in failing health and died on the 26'h August and was buried on the 28th. Mr. John Dignum attended the funeral and superintended the arrangements. In Satur- day's evening papers, under the heading, "exhumation of a clergyman's body" appeared the following extra- ordinary paragraph :—" Yesterday, Mr. Nisbet, funeral undertaker, of Partick, received instructions to exhume the body of the Rev. R. H. Dignum, an Episcopalian minister belonging to Warrington. The man was found dead at Partick some weeks ago, and hurriedly buried as an ordinary pauper. On his friends in England hear- ing of it they Drdered the body to be immediately ex- humed." On seeing the above paragraph, Mr. John Dignum sent the following letter to the Press : Sir,—The paragraph which appears in the Press of Saturday is in its particulars utterly untrue. How such a statement comes to be made is absolutely inconceiv- able.

Mr. Dignum died suddenly, and was buried at the ex- pense of his own relatiqes in the Western Cemetery at Partick, Glasgow. The Orange lodge with which he had at one time been connected applied to have the remains buried in a portion of the cemetery set apart for the members of that lodge. Before this request was made the relatives had already purchased a lair, and the grave had been preparsd. A few weeks afterwards an applica- tion was made from the lodge to have the body exhumed and reinterred in their portion of the cemetery, and to their very earnest request as a favour the relatives gave their consent.—Yours, &c. (Signed)
JNO. DIGNUM.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Tuesday evening, in the Town Hall; Runcorn., , Mr. W. Handley presiding. There were also present; Messrs. S. Pope, H. G. Grice, T. Riley, and J. D. Jones, librarian and secretary. Mr. Jones submitted his cash statement for the month ended Oct. 16th, and also statistics relating to the issues from the library during the month of September. The library had been open 21 days, during which period the following numbers of hooks had been issued from the lending department :—Theologv 32, philosophy 5, science 81, history, Arc.. 133. poetry 12, fiction 1,420, miscella- neous 136, total 1,858. From the reference department 45 "miscellaneous" books had been issued. These figures showed a decrease in the refer.nce dvartment of five volumes compared with the same month last year, whilst in the lending department an increase of _ _

85 appeared. The aggregate number of books issued was 1,903.—Mr. Jones further reported that the following gifts to the library had been received from Mr. John Simpson :—Alderley's "Stephen Reinarx,Borthwich's, " Hymns from the land of Luther" Bunce's. "Life of Joliah Mason," Franzo's- " For the Right," Faber's " Mysteries of the Cabin i " (2 vols). " Bain on the study of character," Vaughan's " Age of great Cities," Cooke's "Rifted Cloud," Aiton's " Lands of the Messiah," Newsholme's " Hygiene." "Why I left the Church of Rome," (Felix) and Fouler's "Deductive Logic." The Buxton Library report for 1893-4 had also been received.—The Librarian's report was adopted. The question was raised of forming a library of musical works, and after some discussion it was decided on the motion of Mr. S. Pope, seconded by Mr. T. Riley that the matter be referred to the Books Selection Com- mittee for their consideration. The idea of organizing "half-hour talks with Library readers" was also mooted. Mr. Jones said he had al- ready been promised by two or three local gentlemen that they would undertake to deliver lectures of this nature to the frequenters of the Library.—Eventually the Librarian was instructed to preceed with the neces- sary arrangements for the lectures.
- The proceedings then terminated.

' Mr. Harry Pope, Greenway-road, Runcorn, was, amongst others, presented with an award by the Lady Mayoress on Saturday at St. George's Hall, Liverpeol, for having passed with honours in several subjects at the recent examinations in connection with the Liver- pool centre of the Trinity College of Music, London. COLLIER'S sell the best quality goods at lowest possible prices.—Advt. AN ARMY DESERTER AT RUNCORE.

Michael Morris, a young man, was on Saturday morn- ing charged at the Runcorn Police Court before Mr. Thomas Handley, with having deserted the Liverpool Regiment then stationed at Salford Barracks.—Defend- ant acknowledged the offence, and he was remanded te await an escort. COLLIER'S Is. BUTTER is tha gem in the market.—Advt. SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN. A service of song, entitled" Which was the Hero "was given on Sunday evening by the choristers in the Mariners' Church, Runcorn. Mr. G. E.Sutton conducted the choir, and the organ was presided at by Mr. T. Forster. There was a good attendance, and the render- ing of the various pieces was much appreciated. MEETING OF THE ST. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. On Sunday afternoon an open meeting was held in connection with this class, a large attendance of mem- bers and friends being present. Mr. B. Kniveton pre- sided. An interesting and instructive address was given by Mr. F. J. Norman, J.P., whose remarks were listened to with much attention. A programme of vocal and in- ' strumental music was rendered in very good style by various members of the class, and at the close the presi- dent gave a hearty invitation to all young men to join the class, the meetings:of which would be" brief,bright, . and brotherly." ODDFELLOWSHIP AT RUNCORN. A meeting of the members of the Rose of Sharon Lodge of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows was held on Saturday evening. Bro. James Jackson pre- sided, and in the course of the business, an emblem of the Order was presented to Bro. Ernest Douglas for his three years' service as an officer of the lodge. Bro. Massey remarked that the recipient had performed his work well, and had given general satisfaction to the members. He wished Bro. Ernest Douglas much success in his new sphere of labour at Fleetwood. A very enjoyable two hours' entertainment WU given on Friday evening in the Greenway-road Board School to a large and appreciative gathering of boys and girls. Limelight views, of the principal cities and buildings in the British Empire, as well as pictures of the most notable persons were thrown upon a arge screen. The descriptive readings were given by the heodmaster, Mr. J. F. Moulton, whilst the lantern oper- ator was Mr. T. Bowyer. COLLIER'S FRESH IRISH DAIRY BUTTER, Uld. per lb.is excellent.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1894.

SINCE the publication of Mr. The Licensing ri vrLADSTONE'S famous letter on Controversy.- licensing reform the question of the relative merits of the Gothenburg system and local veto has been one of the most absorbing topics of the day. This is a remarkable indication of the influence which the veteran statesman still commands, even though he is in retirement. What BismAucx is in Germany GLADSTONE is in England. Both of these eminent men have left the active work of politics in younger hands, but both of them still possess an authority, based on past services, which is sufficient to influence the opinion of their countrymen to a material extent. As might be expected, one of those who have entered most strenuously into the contro- versial fray over the temperance question is Mr. CAINE. Mr. CAINE is all for local option and all against the Gothenburg system. He does not appear to have realised, as most other people have done by this time, that the two methods of reform are not antagonistic but supplemental. In his opinion the Gothenburg systena "is a quack remedy, about as useful in getting . rid of the evil of drunkenness as a smell of Eau de Cologne is for a bilious headache." In support of this unqualified denunciation he declared that Gothenburg itself is more drunken than any town in the United Kingdom. While in Liver- pool 1,800 persons per 100,000 of the population are charged with drunkenness, the proportion in Gothenburg is 4,400. This seems pretty conclu- sive against that, the method of reform which is I advocated by the BISHOP of CHESTER, Mr. GUAM- REMAIN, and Mr. GLADSTONE, but there are one or two considerations which should not be neg- lected. In the first place,it is alleged that,drunken as Gothenburg undoubtedly is, it was no more drunken before the adoption of the present sys- temin the second place,there are modifications of the system,some of which may be an improvement upon the original form. And, then again, there is room for inquiry as to the fashion in which the police of the Swedish town enforce the laws relat-7 ing to drunkenness. It is notorious that in some English towns the police, by a little additional strictness in the discharge of their duties, could greatly increase the number of drunken cases which are cited before the magistrates. It may be that in Gothenburg the laws are more rigid or more rigidly administered than in England, and this would, of necessity, have a very marked effect upon the statistics. It is clear from all this that what is now needed is more complete and exhaustive evidence than as yet at hand as to the working of the Gothenburg method in the coun- tries in which it has been tried. The advocates of tha system would be well in obtaining reliable in- formation of this kind Until they do so local veto is bound to hold the first place in the minds of temperance reformers in this country. It is a reform which has been debated for years, which has been embodied in a Bill promoted by a res- ponsible government, and which has behind it a solid body of enthusiastic supporters.
IT would seem from the latest European Peace. news that the death of the CZAR

of RUSSIA, may be announced at any moment. The CZAR recently travelled from St Petersbury to Livadia with the intention of pro- ceeding to the island of Corfu, the genial climate of which, it VMS thought, would promote his recov- ery. But the final stages of this journey have now been abandoned in consequence of the r apid development of his Majesty's ailments, and his condition is now reported to be hopeless. The death of a CZAR is not at any time a common- place event, but the demise of the present ruler of 'Russia in the existing state of Europe may be fraught with the most momentous results. There appears to be a vague but general feeling that the great war which has been so often predicted may break out at any time. This feeling is probably illue to the fact that the great military powers of the Continent are now in the highest degree prepared for war. They have furbished and perfected their fighting machines until it seems as though they could carry the process no further. If there be any truth in the saying that the "Sight of means to do:ill deeds makes ill deeds done," the rulers of Europe are at the present time' under a powerful temptation to " Cry" Havock, and let slip the dogs of war." The Czar is credited with having been a great restraint upon all warlike enterprizes which would endanger European peace. He has been, of course, too potent a factor in the situation to be ignored ; and, indeed, so long as he resolutely set his face against war, a continuance of peace was practically insured. Will his suc- cessor be of an equally pacific disposition? That is the question which will be in the mind of every politician of Europe upon the death of the CZAR. Time alone will give a decisive answer, but there is no questioning the fact that in the past the CZARS have on the whole been more famous as disturbers than as preservers of the peace.

THERE are people who seem to The People and the Land find pleasure in declaring that . English agriculture is on the brink of ruin, that land is rapidly returning to its original state of uncultivation, and that what is needed to redeem the country is the acceptance of the extreme agrarian policy of Tory landlords. To those who are of this way.of thinking,a reading of the reports of the two day's conference of the

linglish Land Colonisation Sooiety, held this week in London, might be usefully commended. They would there find it very clearly demonstrated that the evils from which English agriculture isauffer- ing are almost entirely due to the perniciousland system built up by Tory landlords in the peat, and that the remedy is to be found—is already being found—in Radical legislation and methods. Eng- lish land is not yet played out, and there seems to be good reason to believe that, as was declared by one of the speakers, this country might still pro- duce sufficient wheat for home use and even a surplus for export if need be. Take as an instance the change which was made on one farm in Wiltshire. A few years ago this farm was cultivated in the old style, and the total number of men who drew a more or less pre- carious:subsistence from it was three. A local gentleman bought the property, resold it in small holdings, and now it maintains fifty men. These small holders have not only maintained themselves but they have, in addition, repaid all the instal- ments of purchase money and in some instances erected dwellings for themselves. In another case, the provision of small plots of land practi- cally raised a parish out of pauperism. The common lands had been filched from the parishoners in the old bad style, and when a labourer wanted a patch of ground to cultivate he had to pay from four to eight pounds for what the farmers paid only twenty-five shillings. One of the results of this "dog-in-the-manger" policy was the presence in the parish of a large proportion of poor people who were partly dependent on out- relief for a subsistence. A scheme was started,on co-operative lines, for p roviding these people with allotments, and quickly all was changed. "Thera is now no poverty in the district," said the Rev. F. C. GREEN who read the paper in which these details were given. The whilom paupers have cul- tivated their allotments with profit and satisfac- tion to themselves, and have already built up a small reserve fund of forty pounds. All this, and much else that was disclosed at the !Conference— points clearly to the lines upon which the land reforms ot the future must proceed, and once again emphasizes the immense influence which the Parish and District Councils which are about to come into existence will have upon the develop- men t of rural England.
THE Railway Regulation Act Railwaymen's passed by the present Govern- Hours.

ment, is, judging from a report made to the Board of Trade,produeing satisfactory results. This Act was passed with the object of checking the excessive hours of labour which it had been proved were worked on some railways. By it the Board of Trade was given powers to reduce the hours of railwaymen to a reasonable point, compulsion, if need be, being brought to bear upon the Companies through the Railway Commissioners. Action is taken by the Board of Trade upon complaints made to them, and it appears that these complaints have been pretty numerous. Seventy-two cases have comae before the Board, and in practically every instance in which the evidence as to excessive hours, insuffici- ent intervals for rest, or inadequate relief from Sunday duty,was established, the Companies have undertaken to make the necessary changes. In fact, it is stated that there has been a widespread reduction of hours. The fashion in which the Act works is shown by the case of the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway Company. This Company agreed to reduce the hours of its signalmen from twelve to eight hours:at twenty-four cabins,from ten to eight at four cabins, and from twelve to ten at sixty- eight cabins. These were fairly large concessions, but the Board of Trade has not been quite satis- fied with them, and still further proposals are being prepared by the Company. It is quite clear, therefore, that the Railway Regulation Act has provided a piece of machinery from which railway. men are already freely benefiting.

div.head: " UNION " OF THE UNIONISTS
div.p: THE " UNION " OF THE UNIONISTS
STRONG SPEECH BY MR. T. W. RUSSELL.

Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., in an address to his constitu- ents at Clogher en Wednesday evening, said he believed that the Land Bill next session would finally settle the question of land tenure in Ireland. Proceeding, Mr. Russell made a remarkable reference to the' insult and slander" which had recently been showered upon him by the "hired scribblers of a venal and degraded press" —namely, the writers in the organs of Irish landlordism. These writers had been inspired, he said, by men who would prefer to see the most pronounced Nationalist representing South Tyrone rather than that it should be represented by him. I knew it all four years ago," he continued. "I knew the plot that was being hatched, and I wished to spare you and myself the worry and the danger of an inevitable contest. I desired to retire from Parliament—at least, from Ulster politics. My judgment was overruled by you and in London, and the decision had no sooner been given than this storm of insult, hatred, and abuse burst upon my head. I know its sources. And I tell its authors now they may do their worst. My back is to the wall in South Tyrone, and I shall fight it out with them at all hazards. The seat may be lost at the next election. I think this quite possible. But it will not be lost by any default of mine."

div.head: Y.M.C. A-OPENING OF THE SESSION.
div.p: Y.M.C. A-OPENING OF THE SESSION.

The annual cenversazione in connection with the above society was held in the Lecture Hall of the Association on Wednesday Mr. T. Jameson, of the Liverpool Ceatral Y.M.C.A. was the speaker, and Mr. R. Wyllie occupied the chair in the absence of Mr. William Owen, IP., who had been called out of town owing to a family bereavement. There were also present Councillor J. Shaw Green,Messrs. J. S. Garland and W. H. Bayley, the late hon. sec., and several other gentlemen who take a deep interest in the work of the Young Men's Christian Association in Warrington. The Chairman in his re- marks explained the reason he was called upon to occupy the chair on this occasion, after which it was decided to convey the sympathy of the workers to Mr. Owen in his bereavement. He made a few more remarks and then called upon Mr. Jameson, the Liverpool secretary for the Central Y.M.C.A. to give his address. Mr. Jameson first expressed hi a pleasure in the improvement which had been made in the hall, and congratulated the Warring- ton friends for their endeavours to increase the comfort and utility of the premises, and hoped the Association would now be able to establish regular gatherings. He said the history of the Christian Church clearly proved that special organisations had been guided to successful issues by Providential aid. He pointed out instances in the early life of the Jewish people. There was precisely the same need for organised effort on behalf of young men who throng our large towns and cities. The Y.M.C.A. work has grown wonderfully, and now there are over 5,000 branches with a membership in all lands of over 467,000. Mr. Jameson then referred to the appointment of the new secretary, Mr. Henry Stewart. Having known him for the last six years Mr. Jameson said he believed Mr. Stewart would do his part to help the workers. Up to the present the Warrington Association had been carried on very energetically. Mr. W. H. Bayley the late honorary secretary had worked hard. (Hear, hear.) In closing Mr. Jameson urged the young men present to take advaritage of the shorthand class which is prov- ing a success. Be hoped they would gather together and form classes in other commercial subjects and also to give their energies to the spiritual part. After the speakers helpful address refreshments were handed round, and the musical programme included selections by Messrs. Pearson and Payton, Miss Sent, Mr. W. H. Podrhore, Mr. Furness and Mr. F. Hickman. The items were excellently rendered, and were much appreciated by the audience. A vote of thanks was moved by Councillor J. Shaw Green, seconded by Mr. T. S. Sent, and carried unanimously. The meeting was then brought to a close.

div.head: INTERESTING LECTURE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INTERESTING LECTURE AT RUNCORN.

On TueAdav evening a large number of members con- nected with the Bethesda Literary and Social ClasS had the pleasure of listening to an interesting lecture, given by the Rev J. S. Simpson in the Bethesda schoolroom,on " A Tour through Switzerland." The rev. gentleman having but just recently returned from a tour in these mountainous regions was able to treat his subject with • Such a degree of freshness as to engage the attention of all present. limelight views were shown by a power- ful lantern operated by Mr. Turton of Frodsham. A NEGLIGENT PARENT AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court before Messrs. Philip Speakman, C.C., and F. J. Norman on Friday morning, William Radford, recently a labourer on the Ship Canal, Was charged with having, on the 20th March, deserted his two children, thus leaving them chargeable to the Runcorn Union.—Mr. Cooke, relieving officer, said the amount already expended on the children was £6. Defendant h3d for some time been going about under the assumed name of Bradshaw, and had consequently

given the authorities a great deal of trouble in tracing him. They at length found out that he was at Pendle- ton, and on the previous day he was arrested by P.C. Gregory in the presence of witness.—Defendaut was sentenced to two months hard labour. PROVIDENTIAL ESCAPE FROM DEATH AT RUNCORN. Mr. Peter Parr, engineer, residing at 6, Wivern-place Runcorn, and employed at the Sprinch Works, met with a very serious accident on Monday morning whilst following his employment. When decending a ladder, which was reared up to the roof of the smithy, a shaft Working below caught his coat. After being twisted 'round, Parr fell to the ground with considerable force. Dr. Mangan was instantly requisitioned, and when he arrived he found the man suffering from a fractured rib. Two other ribs were also staved in, and his system had sustained a severe shock. He was conveyed home, and is improving- as quickly as can be expected. Had the Than's coat not become disentangled from the shaft, he Would probably have been taken round with it and 'dashed to death. Mr. Robert' Yates, who was at the top of the ladder maybe also considered to have escaped very serious injury. Had the ladder not kept its position Ile would have been thrown a distance of 40 feet to the round. COLLIER'S BLACK BLENDED TEA, 2id. per quarter lb.—Adet COLLIER BREAD is the bast money can buy.—Advt. MEETING OF THE RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. The fortnightly meeting of the above Order was held O n Saturday evening in the Primitive Methodist school- room, Greenway-road, under the presidency of Mr. `George E. Sutton. An interesting paper was read by Idr. Edward Key, on the " Gothenberg system." He atrongly advocated the system,saying that it was within t„ be range of practical politics. He referred to the ad- sesion of the Bishop of Chester to the proposal,and to the increase of public opinion in its favour. After explain- ing the system at length, he pointed out that the com- Dany would be entitled to 5 per cent. of the profits and the rest would go to relieve the rates. One object would be to push the sale ef food and non-intoxicating drinks. The houses were open from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., and closed for the whole of Sunday. No seats were provided for the and attractions were conspicuous by their absence. The writer also referred to the Bishop of Chester's view that the present public-house system was failure. After the paper a short discussion ensued, in 'which the following took part :—Messrs. James Johnson, Itornas J. Holt, Thomas Cooke and John Williamson. .A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Key. on the proposi- tion of Mr. S. M. Temperley seconded by Mr. Daniel tisbrown. It was also decided to continue the discussion At the next meeting. TIE DECREASE OF DRUNKENNESS: COMPLIMENTARY REFERENCES TO RUNCORN. Lt the meeting of the Cheshire Standing Joint Committee .11-leld at Chester Castle on Saturday some complimentary 'references were made regarding the decrease of drunken- ness in Runcorn. After the Chef Constable had sub- tnitted bis report, Mr. Grayson said he was glad to see the decrease in drunkenness. This was the case at Run- corn more than any r ther place. He thought that such 14 fortunate state Of things had been effected by the in- 'ereased vigilance of the police, the strong action of the Licensing Bench, and the fear of the law entertained by publicane. (Arplause.)—Mr. Ralph Bates remarked that he was sorry to disagree with Mr. Grayson, but in thS records of Wirral and Runcorn there was an increase on the previous quarter.—Mr. Philip Speakman agreed with Mr. Grayson that publicans had an increased 'respect for the law. With regard to Runcorn, he might 'tell them as he had told them often before, that when the own had got rid of its surplus population caused by the 7hip Canal, there would be a still greater improvement. APplause). BRUNSWICE MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN. t. On Wednesday evening a very interesting and instruc- .;lre Paper was read by Miss Littler at the weekly meet- , gof the above class in the Brunswick schoolroom. `•Onsidering the counter-attraction in the form of a cycle 11,5rade outside, there was a fairly large aulience. Mr. • Simister presided. The subject of Miss Littler's paper " The value of self-reliance," and she dealt with it logically as to win every member present over to her A pleasing feature of the evenings proceedings *s that a few of the lady members broke the ice and .Pressed themselves as being thoroughly in accord with tne arguments of the essayist. A few of the gentlemen ernbers also glanced at ;the principal traits of the •;,',781, and eulogised the compiler. At the conclusion the ,n.airman also praised the work in a short and pithy .cidress. CONCERT AT THE RUNCORN SEAMEN'S 'INSTITUTE. .a The second of the series of "Penny Readings " which being held this winter in connection with the Run- , rn branch of the Mersey Mission to seamen took place • Tuesday evening in the lower room of the Institute. 41 ere was a fair attendance of seamen and watermen. e• W. Shaw, missionary, occupied the chair, and in tte_ning the proceedings he pointed out the objects of entertainments, namely, to give to all seamen and thatiermen coming to Runcorn an opportunity of passing I,e r evenings away in a cheap, enjoyable,and profitable tt;riner. He then expressed the great pleasure it orded him to introduce the Parish Church choir, the dueinbers of which had kindly consented, with their con- eet°r, Mr. James Littler.to sustain the programme that 514c1ng. (Applause.) The entertainment, which con- -11;; Pi of glees, duets, songs, etc., was then gone through ti,'„'he choir which comprised 25 membPrs.They rendered andlclieces allotted to them in a most praiseworthy style, were the recipients of several encores. Mr. Lancaster l3„--:coPanied with his usual ability on the pianoforte. layetikug the interval light refreshments were dispensed • e lady members of the mission. A vote of thanks sZsubsequently accorded to the choristers for their 'lees on the motion of the Chairman seconaed by 113,r W• pnl f fL•nn trr- latvti Liie singing ot the Nackuuat Atitneru.

ACCIDENT TO A LOCAL FOOTBALLER. During the progress of a football match between the Runcorn Victoria and St. Edward's teams on the ground of the former on Saturday afternoon, a youth named Samuel Caldwell, of 12, Water-st., of the St. Edward's Club,came into collision with an opposing player and had his collar bone broken. He was taken home and conse- quently attended by Dr. McKenzie. The injured young man is now progressing favourably, the limb having been set. WESLEYAN MEETINGS AT RUNCORN. On Tuesday evening at the Camden Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, a church meeting took place at which there was a large attendance. An excellent tea was prepared by the ladies and was partaken of by a numerous as- sembly. The Revs. T. Brackenbury, W. George, and W. Lite Stone, Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., Heath, Lambert, and Rowe were among those present. Mr. Beckett proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies for the care they had exercised in arranging matters. This was seconded by Mrs. Morris, and heartily accorded. On Wednesday evening the ladies of the sewing class, who are working assiduously for a coming bazaar, were entertained to tea by Mr. John Simpson. At the con- clusion of the proceedings, the Rev. W. George thanked Mr. Simpson on behalf of those present for his kindness, and the interest he had taken in the work. •

RUNCORN GRAYING Docx. A meeting of the Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Board room of the Runcorn Town Hall with reference to the above matter. Officials front the Manchester Ship Canal Company were interviewed and a discussion followed, the topic being whether the Commissioners would give the Company a further period of time to fully carry out the agreement if they made certain extensions of a tem- porary nature. The Committee emphatically declared that they were determined to have the agreement carried out but they would not hinder the Company if they made conditional and efficient facilities as speedily as possible for dealing with the present traffic, and con- veniences for the repairing of vessels. These expressions have been laid before the Directors of the Company at their last meeting, and the Committee are awaiting their proposals which are expected to be received in time for the next meeting of the Commissioners on Thursday next. A FORMER RUNCORN BOOT DEALER IN THE BANKRUPTCY COURT.

In the last issue of the" Gazette" is the announce- ment that John Peebles, Ducie-avenue. Whitworth Park, Manchester, formerly a boot dealer of Egerton-et. and Church-st. Runcorn, has been declared bankrupt. The first meeting of his creditors is fixed for November 2nd, in Ogden's Chambers, Manchester, at 3 p.m., and his public examination on the 16th November, at the Court House, Warrington, at n a. M. CONVERSAZIONE LT RUNCORN.

In connection with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, a conversazione was held on Tuesday evening in the new schoolroom, Greenway-road, Runcorn. There was a very large gathering present, and the chair was filled by the Rev. T. Bramall, pastor. A programme of carefully selected music was sustained and readings were also given. Songs were sung by Miss Stubbs ; Messrs. A. Shingler, F. Shingler, J. Stubbs, H. Woodward, and H. Pilgrim ; a duet by Miss Davies and Mr. A. Shingler, and readings by Messrs. R. Hillidge, S. Howard, and F. Stubbs. Mr. W. Grounds accompanied on the piano. At intervals refreshments were handed round by lady mem- bers of the choir. During the evening various kinds of games were indulged in, and a very happy evening spent. The entertainment was brought to a close by a vote of thanks being accorded the chairman and all who had assisted, on the motion of Mr. W. Gittens, jun., seconded by Mr. Wilson. Some PROSPECTIVE CANDIDATES FOR THE RUNCORN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

At a recent meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners held at the Runcorn Town Hall, for the purpose of considering the election of the District Council, a resolution was passed in favour of the election taking place on the 15th December, winch will be on a Saturday. This course was adopted for many reasons, the chief of which was that Saturday would be a most advantageous day for working people to register their votes. In the course of a discussion it was understood that Messrs. Taylor and Wiswall would contest Halton ward; Messrs. Lightburn, Pritchard and Speakman, Heath ward; Messrs. D. Biabrown, James Dobson and W. Leach, Newton ward; Messrs Imison and Collier, Central ward; and Messrs. Handley, Grice and Hankin- son, Mersey ward. Bridgewater ward is thus left open, no candidates having as yet come forward. It is thought that two of our present Commissioners will not seek positions on the District Council. A RUNCORN FLAT WRECKED: THE CREW LOST. News has reached Runcorn to the effect that the flat Rose, owned by Messrs. Philip Speakman and Sons, of Runcorn, was wrecked on Sunday morning off Penmaen Rock, Llandulas. Telegraphing on Sunday night, a Colwyn Bay correspondent says :—" When first seen from land, the sails being still above water, the small boat was attached to the sunken vessel, but at twenty past seven two men were seen pulling towards the shore, but when in the breakers the boat capsized and both were drowned. The boat came ashore, and had on the nameboard R. Abram, master.' The caps of both men were subsequently washed ashore, but the bodies have not been recovered. The Ada Mary, which belongs to the same owners, was lying close to the foundered vessel. A large concourse of people assembled on the shore awaiting the recovery of the bodies." On the previous Thursday afternoon the flat had left Runcorn for Llandulas with Captain Robert Abrams of 24 Albert-street,Runcorn, and Thomas Jones, Widnes, on board for the purpose of bringing back a cargo of lime- stone for Widnes. She arrived safely at her destination and was laden with the cargo. She then put out to sea, and was bound for Widnes when a gale sprung up and drove her on to the Rock where she sank. Both men were well known in Runcorn and Widnes. Captain Abrams would be about 27 years of age, whilst Jones, who acted as mate, was about 50. The former was a Wesleyan and leaves a widow and young daughter. Jones was also married, and leaves widow. Mr. Abrams was considered a very able captain, baying had a wido experience in the management of vessels. Up to a late hour on Thursday night last,no tidings had been received in Runcorn of the missing bodies.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
(BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR.)

The firm attitude struck by our Improvement Commissioners against the unreasonably:long delay of the Manchester Ship Canal Company in conform- ing to their promise to construct a graving dock at Runcorn, has not been without its good result. The directors of the company have, apparently, to a degree, been brought to their senses by the warn- ing note sounded by our local legislators, and are beginning to look upon our cause as being worthy of a little more of their attention. I have ascertained that the directors sent re- presentatives onTuesday to Runcorn to lay before the Commissioners certain propo- sals relating to the scheme. The Ship Canal officials were interviewed in the afternoon by the members of the Parliamentary and General Purposes Com- mittee, the last of whom expressed their determina- tion to have the agreement complied with, but if the Company would make conditional facilities as quickly as possible for the dealing with traffic, and would provide conveniences for the repairing of vessels, they would not hamper their movements. The Commissioners, if in their wisdom they accept the idea of temporary extensions, will not, we feel sure, allow the Company 'too much time to fulfil their obligations to the town.

We all linow that it is of course useless to at- tempt to get blood out of a stone, but the Com- pany is not exactly a stone, and because we may probably not be able to get at once the thing we want, we ought not to throw away our chances of obtaining it as soon as it is possible. The Ship Canal Company may not be in a very sound finan- cial state at present, but there is, of course, a pos- sibility of their enjoying such a state at no very distant date.

The latest honour to our townsman, Sir John Rigby, M.P., will be hailed by Runcornians with satisfaction. He has been promoted from the position of Chief Law Adviser of the Crown to a Lord Justiceship of Appeal, and as a consequence his seat in Forfarshire is now vacant. Sir John has undoubtedly built up a prodigious reputation in the legal world, and from all quarters have come opinions that he is eminently fitted for his new position. It must be pleasing to those of our towns- folk who have had the pleasure of being acquainted with Sir John whilst he was in Runcorn to now re- flect on the distinctions he has won and is still winning.

The recent Tonic Sol Pa concert was one of the most successful that the choir has ever held. It was not only so from a financial point of view, but it was, without mistake, a success from a musical standpoint. Year by year the choristers are climb- ing up the ladder, and if they continue their course in the future, as surely as they have maintained it in the past, then it will not be long before they reach the top. May that time soon arrive.

div.head: EXAMINER
div.p: THE EXAMINER
THE DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
MEETING OF TOWN HALL WARD.

A meeting of the electors residing in the Town Hall ward, was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening for the purpose of selecting three candi- dates to represent the ward on the new District Council. It will be remembered that at the public meeting held a few weeks back, committees were chosen for each ward, for the purpose of selecting suitable candidates, and if possible to avoid a con— test, and the expense on the rates entailed by a contest, and the meeting on Tnesday night as the result of this, and the candidates selected will be submitted to a general meeting of electors ,to be held later on. The Rev. T. R. Matthews presided, and there were with him on the platform Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, Messrs. G. Ratcliffe, W. Gilmour, D. Forrester, Stringer, Parr. Scott and Galligan. The Chairman, in opening, explained that each candi- date proposed, had been waited upon by members of the Committee, and a certain code of questions was put to them, and answers obtained. The gentlemen who had been nominated by the Ward Committee were Messrs.E. T. Evans. W. Gilmour, G. Ratcliffe, T. Scott, Rev. E.W. W. Kaye, and Dr. Handyside. He read a letter which had been received from Mr. Evans regretting his inability to be present, and saying that if chosen as a candidate that night, he would represent the ratepayers to the best of his ability. He also intimated that Mr. Forrester who acted as Secretary, could read the questions which had been submitted, if it was wished. Mr. Latham proposed that the list of questions be read, and this being the general desire, Mr. Forrester read the questions which were as under: —(1) Are you willing to represent the ward if selected? (2). Are you in favour of using the powers of the Coun- cil to institute an investigation into the ratepayer's dis- puted rights to Newton Common, and oppose any , encroachment thereon pending a settlement? (3). Will I you urge the Council to provide postal accommodation to meet the requirements of the Post Office authorities, with a view to despatching mails from Earlestown , station, and thereby carry out the wishes of the public las expressed in a recent petition ? (4). Will you insist , on all streets being made where dwellings are numerous? I (5). Are you in favour of using macadam or setts for this purpose? (6). Are you in favour of the building on corner of market being utilised for a public reading- room? (7). Dean Trust. Will you take steps to secure the appointment of trustees for this charity by the Council ? (8). What is your opinion regarding the establishment of a School Board in the district? (9). Are you in favour of the Council meetings held in the evening? Mr. Forrester, continuing, said Dr. Handyside had replied to the first question that if the electors thought fit to select him, he would do his best to represent them, but if there was a contest he would have nothing to do with it. Mr. Kaye would stand even if there was a contest. Mr. Gilmour was ready to stand, more particularly if he received the active support of the committee. No. 2. Dr. Handyside said if there was a good case he should be in favour of asserting the rights of the eommunity to the land. Mr. Kaye would rather compromise the matter, and if elected he would be one of a party tq approach Lord Newton, for the purpose of giving over a portion of the Common land to the com- munity, together with a sum of money, that it might be converted into a recreation ground for the people. Mr. Gilmour was of the same opinion as Dr. Handyside. He did not wish that they should go into the matter unless they had clear evidence that they would gain their point. (3) All the candidates were ia favour of better postal accommodation. Mr. Gilmour qualifying to the extent that they should not injure Newton. (4) All the candidates were in favour. (5) The candidates all approved of macadam. but Mr. Gil- mour wanted sets in those streets where the traffic was heavy. (6) Dr. Handyside wanted this building pulled down. Mr. Kaye was of the same opinion and also that the bricks might be used for pillars for covering in a portion of the market place. Mr. Gilmour was in favour of it being turned into a reading-room. (7) The can- didates were willing to do this. (8) None of the can- didates favoured this proposal. (9) Dr. Handyside was not in favour of this, as he thought the members might be sitting up all night. Mr. Kaye said that if working- men were elected on the Council he wraild be in favour of meeting in the evening. Mr. Gilmour was of a similar opinion to Mr. Kaye. Mr. Parr said the Chairman and himself formed a deputation to wait on the other three candidates, and the reply to all the questions was "yes," with the excep- tion of that relating to thefoundation of a School Board, which they did not think advisable. They were all in favour of macadam except one, who thought that setts should be used, where the traffic was heavy, they being more durable. Four of the candidates who were present, were then called upon to speak to the meeting. Mr. Gilmour expressed his gratitude for the honour conferred upon him in being selected as a candidate for the Town Hall Ward. In the contest in which he was to engage he did not wish to be personal with any can- didate. Secondly, he was not going to tight it politi- cally, and thirdly, he would not hit below the belt.. (Applause.) He then proceeded to deal with the ques- tions which had been put to him,seriatum. With regard to "common land," he said if it belonged to the people, as its very name suggested, then by all means let the people take it over. (Applause.) He did not think, however, seeing that it was a question which had been discussed for so many years, that they should rush at it headlong and take possession, but they should go about a thing of this sort in moderation. They must get to know the legal rights or claims they had on the land, and if they could get special advice from a Q.C. that Ithey had a legal claim to the land, then it should be given to them. (Hear, hear.) He had been in that neighbourhood as a ratepayer for over 30 years, and as a direct ratepayer for 15 years, and as that question of common land had been repeatedly before the people during that period, he thought it was a question which the Council out to settle. He did not wish to say any- thing against Lord Newton, and if he would give the Common up to the people to play games and walk about on, then it would be an everlasting credit to him. (Applause.) He would rather not fight the matter, hut that Lord Newton should hand the Common over to the people. With regard to the postal arrangements,he was certainly in favour of Earlestown having improved postal accommodation. There was a good central build- ing close to the station which might be converted into a first class post office for that neighbourhood, and he would do his best to get it if elected. He had got up a petition on the question of better postal accommodation, and since then there bad been wall boxes opened in various parts of the town. Referring to the Dean Charity Trust, he was in favour of the Council taking all charities over except the ecclesiastical property, and he was not in favour of taking anything from any church of any denomination. (Hear, hear.) On the School Board question, be was satisfied with the education he had given his children, and he did not see that a School Board was necessary. In addition to transforming the building on the market corner into a reading room, be thought it would be a great boon to have a reading room in the Town Hall. Touching the last question, if the meetings were held in the evening it would give an impulse to many a young man to go on the Council, and bear a part in the government of the town. During his long connection with Earlestown he had had practical experience in all the sanitary matters of the district. If he did get on the Board, and he hoped he would, he would keep no secrets.—(Applause.) The Rev. E. W. W.-Kaye could not claim to be as old a citizen as Mr. Gilmour, nevertheless he had beer: resident in Earlestown for about seven years, and that was a , short lifetime. Some people said that parsons ought I not to meddle with anything of that kind. The Act allowed working men the privilege of sitting on the Council, and be claimed to be a working man. Be worked as hard as any working man, and perhaps re- ceived less pay than many of them. Re then quoted , the authority of the Archbishop of Canterbury, who had 'recently advised every clergyman in every parish, where there was a district Council, to take an active part in them, and sit on them, if possible. He was going about all day in the houses, streets and alleys, and he thought the clergyman who was going about the streets, knew which needed repairing and paving, and which houses were in an insanitary condition. There might be other candidates who did not know all the streets in the place in which they lived, and had not been in all the entries and yards in Earlestown, in fact did not know they were there. He had answered all the questions put to him, and he intended.to keep his word, if the electors thought fit to elect him. His views were very much those of Mr. Gilmour, with the exception perhaps of the question relating to common land. He was certainly in favour of the people having the common land in their own right, but he was against them going into any law suit for it, and after an expenditure of £4OO or £500; getting beaten; he was in favour of a compromise, as be had stated to the deputation. He was interested in educa- tional matters, and of course as a churchman, he would not go in for what wascalled distinctive teaching. He thought he had a perfect right to get his views repre- sented on the Board. (Hear, hear.) Mr. G. Ratcliffe was not ashamed of what he had done as a commissioner, and was there to give them an account of his stewardship. With regard to the building on the market place, he thought it was nonsense to turn It into a reading-room. They had the 'num Hall, and he thought it ought to be used for that purpose, as the one at Newton was, for a nominal sum. As far as New- ton Common was concerned, the best thing was to take the opinion of an eminent counsel, and if counsel said they had a case then they could go on with it. The Commissioners had refused to pass the plans of six cottages to be erected on these lands, and had left the matter for the new Council to deal with, as they will have much larger powers. He thought that every part of the township should be fairly and honestly dealt with, and should pay an equal share of the rates, and have an equal share of the benefits, and if elected, he would serve them as he had before, to the best of his ability, and if not elected he hoped they would appoint a better Person in his place. (Apple use. ) Mr. T. Scott said he quite coincided with the views of the other candidates. The names were then ha,,lnted - upon with the following result :—Evans, 47 votes;
