ANNUAL SALE OF WORK.

A three days' sale of work was commenced in the I schooolrooms over Arpley Station, on Wednesday j afternoon,in aid of the general expenses of the Emm- anuel Reformed Churcb,Bold-st. There had not b, much decoration of the various rooms,buA thy stalls themselves presented a bright and attractivo lare appear- ance. Five stalls hsd been well arranged in the schoolroom, and the church parlour, blue room, and small schoolroom also Contained stalls. £lOO was the amount required to be raised, and from a prospectus issued by the Vicar (Rev. E. T. Reed) stating the work accomplished, we cull the following :—" There is much to encourage us in our work, fSpecially amongst the young, who, by means of our successful Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour, are being led to the Saviour and trained for Christian service through hav- ing definite work to do on the look-out, prayer meet- ing, borne and foreign missionary, relief, Sunday snaseel, or Other committees. During the past year a Junior Christian Endeavour Society has beesi com- menced for ebildred under 14 years of age ; the weekly Meetings are well atten,l4 and Meth, good is being clone. The debt opon the ofm'nell building has, during I thsepast 2 years, been reduced froth A3O to £lBO. in eur estunday schools a very 'Promising work s going on, oier aim is to lead the' little ones to the Sayoun, and ,51k eahe them up in Evangelical truth. Our church be- ;tete ntire:ly voluntary, is in a great measure dependent fog i,e sole of work for funds with which to Garry ut"t' -ork " on tire . me, foil, assisted at the stalls : Mrs& Reed's stall : \frslienry Gandy, Miss Eva Lees, tie. ; con- Mrs. Reed, s stall • • Mrs. Parsons Miss Tetlow, Mise gregational Masonnifiss sons, . •_ , &c., Sunday school stall : Mrs', .a Pa • A. Gandy,. Mrs. r°lln Allen, Miss Heald, Miss Lees, Miss Booth, Miss M. fle'ald, Miss Lloyd, &c. ; refreshment ABC°, stall Mrs. I`. irs. E. Allen, Mrs. E. Ditchfield, : . Miss Monks, Mies anih Miss Jessie Booth, &c.; dower Le. and fruit stall:: Miss M. E. Hindley, Miss Bibby, Miss Heron, Miss Iluattes7,4".e.; tea room : Mrs.Hallwood stall Christian En-cleavoue : Mrs. Norman, Misses E. and A. IL Nrding. Caenpiun, M. A. Blackburn, afinards, M. J. Bibby; Messrs. Norman Joseph CaVan, Win. Dickens, Joseph l Heron, jun., John Lloyd, Totn assam, Ben. Podmore, S Leonard Hope, Tom Lloyd, Ar, hur Ditchfield, &c. gentlemen's stall and jninble stall : Messre. J. T. and E. Allen, W. Atherton, H. Gandy, A. L. ndon, John Bibby, Arthur Dickens, George H.. Heald, syra, sk Lloyd, kc., Miss : Parsons, Miss Leach, Miss Clark, skc.• children's stall ' Misses Sandal!, Annie Harding, NeliieG 'nudn, Beatrice Carriage, Sarah Ellison, Sarah Sheethere ls M. and L. Hallwood, &c. At the opening ceremony there was a good attendance. After devotional exercises The Rev. E. T. REED said their own cengrega thin were quite aware as to the objects of thesale,but thos, 5 outside their church might net be so welt acquainted. Their object was to meet the current expenses of their "'hum"' and part of the expenses of their schools.. On the c.hurnn they had a very heavy ground rent to meet . year by year and as they had no premises of their own in connection with the Sunday inich.lol they had to pay rent for the rooms they occupie d that day which were used for Sunday school purposes. They could not forget that they were a voluntary church, having no endowments whatever to meet their expenses, and they were therefore dependent open the efforts of their congreeation,and aid from outside friends. Further, most of their congregation were not in a posi- tion to give much money towards helping forward the work. Their congregations were not large,but the great majority of the people gave very liberally of their means. Hence it was necessary to have a sale of work to help their funds. There were a great many who were willing te eive time and work to the church,and that sale of work efforded an opportunity to them of disposing of the work which they had been doing during the past twelve months. The ladies had worked hard and diligently at the sewing meeting,but he would be glad to see a larger number attending it. Others had done a good deal of w, ek in their homes. Various friends had kindly sent con- tr outiens towards their work in connection with that, sat, amounting to £l7 Os. 6d., which included a cheque of £5 from Mr. Joseph Davies, of the Old Warps. He had received letters of apology for non-attendance from thel Rev. D.W. Roberts and J.Yonge. The work they were endeav- ouring to do in connection with their church and schools was a lasting spiritual work. They were seeking to lead th.ir young people to a knowledge of their Saviour,Jesus Christ, and to build up a strong, earnest body of workers who would be willing to be spent in their Master's ser- vice in that town. 'As they were reformers, they had found, as all reformers had done,. that the way of reformers was hard. They had found difficulties which those congregations had not received who had been long established. But they did not complain of their lot. They had been areatly encouraged during the past year. They hs.d had the joy of seeing a great many of their young people brought to a knowledge of their Lord Jesus Christ, and by means of their Christian Endeavour Societies they were training up a band of workers, which they trusted in future years would be a great source of strength. (Applause.) Mr. CICERO SNITS, of Southport, in declaring the bazaar open. said he must first of all express his own Pleasure that they had again invited him to open their Sale of work. He received so much encouragement on the occasion of his bast visit, two years ago, that he had great pleasure in coming to see them again. There was another reason why he received with satisfaction the invitation to comes again and that was the kind of work they were tryine to do there. Their very existence was a protest against that kind of though t or practice at the present day which seemed to him would be in the future blockades to the great progress of spiritual worship. They were a protest against formalism or ritualism in the worship of God. They were also a protest by the very way in which they were trying to do their work against that wave of rationalism and indifferentism that semen so very prevalent at the present day. They had a vast number of people holding the opinion that the old ideas and old views were not necessary ; that the old book which had helped our fathers and had been. such a blessing to us. was not whet we once thought it was ; that Moses did not write those. first five books in trie Bible, that Daniel did not write the book, of-Deniel, nor David the Nelms. But they:ead shown there, that there was a power in the bible and in the preaching of Christ's _gospel-, and the work they were doing there was one of the best protests they could make against that state of feeling which he bad described.. There was also. feeling in the hearts and minds of people— s sort of struggling with what they called socialism. They felt in the nature of things that there must be something wrong in our present social Condition. They looked down en the misery, wretched- ness, squalor, and crime, and said there must be some- thing wrong. They said, we shall adopt tU& socialism whereby all will be equal, we will have a socialism to do away with this sorrow and suffering, and they were struggling with that grand ideal. He Wee speaker) thought much of this was due to the indifference and laziness of Christian peopTe themselves. Men had lost sisslat of that glorious movement Christ came to found— not in heaven—but here upon earth. They lost sight of the fact that all men were in God's sight equal,that if a man was a Christian he should show it by his life and his tenderness te his fellow men. If Christian men and christian women had carried out that grand ideal, had only known what the kingdom of God meant there would not have been any socialism to-day. These men we recalled extreme and fanatical, they would not have been if the rich man loved the poor man, a.nd the poor man loved the great, and men were like brothers. He wished to say a word of encouragement to the 'workers there. If they looked in the shop windows they would see numberless articles exposed for sale, but if they knew the history that lurked behind some of those. articles or garments' how they were made amidst squalor, disease, and starvation they would feel that there was a great deal in the world that wanted setting right. But when he came to look at their work on the stalls that day it called him to think of the love, and the devotion and the unselfishness that men, women and boys and girls had been giving for weeks past. He wanted them te remember that. , They served a master, and those who wanted so serve him well should look right behind the work and see the motive behind it. If they wanted to make the kingdom of God felt 'on this earth of ours, they muse- not merely look forward to the kingdom of heaven where all was joy, but a kingdom on earth. They had got to learn to be unselfish and learn to love one another as Christ had loved us. (Applause.) Mr. PAGE moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Smith for his address and for opening that sale of work. Mr. ALLEN seconded, stating that they were indebted to Mr. Smith for his inspiring address. The vote was carried unani- mously. The sale was then proceeded with. The result of the first day's sale amounted to £64 1&s. d.

The municipal elections have alter all resulted in nine councillors being elected unopposed. In the Whiteeross ward, the labour candidate has retired owing to a technical point which might result in causing him him to be unseated, in the event of his election. On only one occasion previously, since the borough was divided into the present wards,has there been na election, and that was owing to the smtkilpox epidemic two years ago, The mit result of the present elections has been an increase in the large number of gentlemen connected with the liquor traffic upon the Council for Councillor Lee who displaces Councillor Tinsley is a maltster., There are now eight out of the 36 members of the Council, who are directly connected with this trade, which every one will admit is an extremely unfair proportion. But r hear that yet another publican is spoken about as a possible candidate in the sear future.

The Young People's Society of Christian Endeav- our in connection with Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel has now been in exiatenee for twelve months, and the anniversary was :...elobrated on Sunday and Mon- day. The Society has. been 'a smecess, and there is a satisfactory number of members, The Work has been both spiritual and' educational,- and many who Iwould not perhaps otherwise hale taken up any church work have been induced by the meetings of , Society to do so. The edlcational Ipart'of the work h 1.8. been in the form of lectures, and many eminent lectiarers have been engagmd. An excellent pro- gramme haa been arranged' for the present season.

In going along Padgate am/ Fearnbead lanes-The other day, I wasr enrprised at the large quantity of property, which is, being or has been put up in that distric.t. The district is witlicut doubt s rapidly growing one, and along with Sztikey Briegee at the opposite, side it will no clenbt event.ually be incorporated in the borough.

THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. There was a good attendance on Thursday afternoon, when the sale was opened by the Rev. E. T. Reed, in the absence of Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., who was unable to be present. In his opening remarks, the rev, gentleman said that the previous day's takings had exceeded all their anticipations. Nothwithstanding the unfavourable weather they had taken more than in the previous two years, Two years ago they were greatly encouraged on taking £2 the firsb day. Last year the sale was held during the great coal strike, so that it was greatly affected, and they only took £35. This year, including subscriptions.they had taken £B. 18s. ld.,for which they were exceedingly thankful. Since the previous day £2 ss. had been received in subcrip- tions. He was sorry that the gentleman appointed to open the sale was. unable to be present that afternoon. One of Mr. Guest's oldest workmen had passed away—a man who had been in his employ for 20 years—and ai the funeral took place that day, Mr. Guest had felt bound onto! re.pect to attend it. He (Mt. Reed) wrote to him absolving him from coming under the circum- stances. Mrs. Guest would have been present but she was unwell, but Miss Guest was present. He earnestly hoped that the sale that day would be a great success. The sale was then formally declared open and the busi- ness was commenced.

div.head: GIIAN,D) GARS/VAL CYCLISIS AT' RUNCORN.
div.p: GIIAN,D) GARS/VAL CYCLISIS AT' RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening a grand .Isat-ml parade and fancy- dress carnival in aid ot the. Runccra, District Nurse Fund. and the Royal National Lit- boat Inst'Aution too*placeut Runcorn. As it vras no first chits kind;.the members of the Runcorst• Cycle Club,- by whom it had been originated, took the- greatest intsrest in the event,, and were engaged for several weeks previous u preparing their costumes and the decorations for theircnycles. Th 3 treasurer„Mr. H. ' Wright, and the secretaries, Messrs: 3. Mores and A. Riley were likewise very industrious. The cyclity clubs in the neighbouring districts were approached,•antr promised to assist them with their presence for tthe at- tainment of their commendable objects. Everything went on merrily, each meraberbeing indefatigable in his exertions to male as fine &show as ppssible. Their Nopes would certainly have been realised had the weather con- tinued fine, but,. alas Fon Wednesday morning, the-dar on which this auspicious event was to tike place, there- was a heavy downpour of rain. It is alfaelt needless-10. say that tne heartsof those who were to ,Jarticipate in that evening's proceedings at once sena within them as they glanced at the muddy thoroughfares and then at their machines which they were fast decorating. It must indeed have been a Dore disappointment to all,, more especially when it was- considered what an im- _ . . . _

mense amount- of time they had spent in preparing. The day wore on, and at noon the clouds broke and the sun 'shone ott. The streets were soon dried and the spirits of the processionists again rose. There was. every sign of the evening being a fine one,until about three o'clock, when the sky again became dark; and rain began once more to fail quite as,heaviiy as before. Adc.lecl to thi&. was a strong wind, which swept in very cold gusts through the streets. The rain continued to falEuntil about six o'clock. From this hour until seven ctofock the

cyclists could be seen making their way to the starting place, the Wilson's lintel, Bridge-3treet, accompanied by their machines. The crowds in the street 3- began to rapidly thicken, and when the procession .started there were two continual and dense li3es of spectators from the Wilson'o•Hotel, through the by streets to the-General. Post Office in Greenway-road. The procession, which measured nearly a mikl long took- the followingorder : Mr. R.. Mocrea-on horseback, as marshal! and represent- ing:Buffalo 3ill ;.band of the 2nd C. 11,17., uncler the con- dixtorship cf• bandmaster Outhwaite ;:army corps, with, their cycles,. from Orford Barracks, Warrington._ FoI-

lowing themtcame a supposed patient lying (If:jetty on an ambulance, with Is head bandaged, &c-. Then• in order came a trap containing three ladies, who wore dressed in cursingcostarnes ;.Runcorn Fire Brigade with, the large-engine and reel under Deputy-superintendent Wright. Nent followed the Eielsbv Church lia.ass Band members of the Helsby Fire Brigade on foot witb. lighted torches ; and a. lantern borne in, a cart, and by which Mr. C. Handley illuminated the proces- sion with limelight. Following these were numer- ous, cyclists whose festive-lookbg steeds seemed to have suffered somewhat from the wind and rain.. The lamps they carried could not be lighted, con- sequently they did not make such a pretty show as was anticipated.. The owners were attired, some is brilliant costumes representing a gay cavalier of the seventeenth centurv,a jockey, "two little girls in blue,'" a life guardsman Bed Indians, "Daisy Bell and her sweetheart ;whilst others were in ludicrous attire, per- sonating "Ally Sloper," Big Boancing Baby," a China-- man, policemen, "Mother Noblett," niggers and clowns. The remaining ones wore costumes representative of B. M. Stanley, sailors, jesters, etc. At the rear were the. members of the Mersey Mission Drum and Fife Band, conducted by Mr. W. Shaw, jun., a lifeboat containing" a full crew attired in oilskins and sou' westers ; lifeboat scenes thrown by means of a lantern upon a large screen. which had been rigged up in a waggon for the purpose. Mr. Hoxworth manipulated the lantern.

There were also several other men dressed in costumes of various descriptions, some of whom rode an horse- back. The procession paraded from the Wilson Ectei through several thoroughfares, under the captaincy of Messrs. G. Whinyates, and W. H. Machi, and returned to the Wilson Hotel. Flags and streamers hung from many of the buildings along the route, whilst in several windows numerous small lamps of various colours were placed. These had a very pretty effect when lighted, and added considerably to the scene. A largo number of collectors, including the members cf the Ituncorn Association Football Club, and several ladies were in attendance and did their utmost to obtain donations. Some of these were attired in different kinds of apparel. On arriving at the Wilson Hotel, refreshments.were par- taken of, and a smoking concert ensued. During the proceedings Mr. H. Wright announced that the total amount collected was £27. It might be of interest to know that the total number of coins was 5,002,made up as follows:—one &sovereign,. four 1 crowns, nine florins, 63 shillings, 152 sixpences, 113 threepenny pieces, 3374 pennies, and 1226 half- pennies. The result is exceedingly satisfactory consider- ing the very unpropitious state of the wecher which without doubt prevented hundreds of people visiting the t3wo. The cyclists are much indebted to many of the townspeople for the valuable assistance given. themint the shape of horses, traps, carts, and waggons.

div.head: AMERICAN LINER IN COLL/SION, LARGE SIIIP SUNK.
div.p: AMERICAN LINER IN COLL/SION, LARGE SIIIP SUNK.

The American liner Paris, which arrived from Newt York at midnight on Wednesday, reports terrine weather in the Atbmtic. Fier decks were swept by mountainous seas. On Wednesday morning, at 130, in the height of the storm, and when about eighty mile& from Scilly, the Paris ran into a barque or full-rigged ship, name unknown. It is believed the liner cut her completely in two. The Paris stood by for five bours until daybreaAt, with, boats in readiness, but no trace a the vessel ,-,cas seen. The ship was struck amidships, and it is thought she foundered immediately, with all hands. Ttie look out man believes that the ship was of about 2,30 tons. She was not seen until the Paris was close upon her, and nothing could then avert the colli- sion. The Paris is slightly indented at the bows, but otherwise she is uninjured.

div.head: DREAMS OF YOUTH.
div.p: THE DREAMS OF YOUTH.
The dreams of youth may fade away, As flowers that early bloom ; Like cutting winds, adversity May bring alas, their doom. •
Spring's gentle dews descend in rain; We nevermore behold The withered leaves expand again, Or frosted buds unfold.
But other flowers in beauty grow When winters cold is o'er, And other men more blest must be For noble lives before.
Oh maiden fair, heroic youth !

- May falsebooil ne'er destroy Sweet hopes of faithfulness and love, Of friendship, peace and joy. Our sorrows come without control, And *aging hopes decay, Till brightest dreams of happy youth Have vanished quite away.
And yet beyond this chequered life, Uncertain, tinged with care, Methinks that happy dreams foretaste A world so glad and fair.
Warrington, October, 1894.

div.head: EXPLOSIVES FOR MINING PURPOSES. EXPERIMENTS AT MESSRS. PEARSON AND KNOWLES' MOSS COLLIERY.
div.p: EXPLOSIVES FOR MINING PURPOSES. EXPERIMENTS AT MESSRS. PEARSON AND KNOWLES' MOSS COLLIERY.

A series of important tests were carried out on Wed- nesday at an experimental station, which had been put down at the Moss Colliery, near Wigan, owned by Messrs. Pearson, Knowles and Co., Limited, for the purpose of testing explosives used in coal mining opera- tions with regard to their safety under the conditions of a blown out shot coming in contact with coal dust, or an explosive mixture of gas and air in a coal mine, and also as to their relative strength as explosives, tested by the distance to which a projectile could be fired from a mortar. The experiments were witnessed by a number of Government mining inspectors, mining eneineers,and also by official representatives of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain. The various explosives which were put under test were dynamite, roburite, tonite, West- phalite, bellite,anamonite, Ardeer powder, and carbonite. As a guarantee that the conditions of the tests were strictly and correctly carried out, a committee, consist- ing of Messrs. J. Dickenson, late chief Inspector of Mines; D. H. F. Matthews, Inspector of Mines; J. Isher- wood, J.P., miners' agent; and J S. Burrows, of Messrs. Fletcher and Burrows, Manchester, was appointed to superintend the weighing of the various explosives and to record the results of the respective experiments. The general opinion expressed after the conclusion of the experiments was that Westphalite—which has already been largely adopted on the Continent, and in the mines of Saxony, which are very dangerous to work, is the only explosive the Gcvernment allowed to bused—had, under the canditions of the tests carried out, proved to be decidedly tl e safest explosive for mining purposes,

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES

Tin ALLEGED THEFT OF WHISKY. At the Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday morn- ing Andrew Sauce and Thomas Sauce, brothers, were charged on remand with stealing or receiving knowing to have been stolen, from a railway waggon stationed in Arpley siding on the evening of the 12th inst., a jar con- taining six gallons of Scotch whisky, the property of the London and North Western Railway Company and valued at £4 10s. Mr. James Fenna, solicitor for the London and Ishrth Western Railway Company, stated that Thomas Sauce was a goods porter, and had been in the employ of the London and North Western Railway Company, for over 18 months and Andrew Sauce worked as a puddler at Bewsey Forge. On the 11th of this month a jar of whisky was sent by a Liverpool firm to Mr. J. L. Jones, Moore, care of Mr. Savnpson, Norton Arms Hotel, Warrington. Mr. Fenna then repeated the evidence which, it was alleged, implicated the defen- dants and which has been given in a previous issue of the "Examiner." Several witnesses were also called, and the defendants were committed to take their trial at Li 'Quarter Sessions.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Trades Council was held at the liorsemarket-street Cocoa- rooms, on Tuesday evening, when there was a good attendance of delegates. The chair was occupied by the President Mr. Malkin). SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr. Buttocit, the secretary, said that in presenting their nineteenth annual report they could not, as at the last meeting. report an increase of membership. One society, the Bricklayers' Society, had seceded during the year, from some unexplained cause, and the Warrington Branch of the National Union of Boot and ShGemakers had become defunct, and therefore ceased to be repre- sented on the Council. He was pleased, however, to state that two other societies had become represented on the Council, viz., the Coachmakers, and Card and Blow- ing Room Operatives Societies, thus maintaining the same number which they commenced the year with, 24. In referring to the s'ate of trade, he regretted that there had been no improvement during the past year, and that there was great depression, causing a great number of people to be unemployed. In connection with the proposed Labour Bureau. the Council had decided early in the year that it would not answer the Purposes for which it was proposed, and that they take no action. He regretted that the Corporation contracts had not been carried out with proper recognition to the question of fair wages. The Council had also passed a resolution in favour of the Employers Liability Bill,and condemnatory of the House of Lords. They had also passed resolutions in support of the Factory and Workshops Act of Mr. Asquith. It was the desire of the Council that there should be direct labour representation upon the public bodies of the town, such as Town Council and Board of Guardians. A short time an, when there was a vacancy in the Howley ward, it was thought a favour- able opportunity to get a representative upon the Town Council, inasmuch as neither of the political parties were taking any part in the election. At the last moment., however, Mr. John Evans came out. Strong influences were brought to bear against Mr. Battersby, their candidate, and one of the political parties also used its induence with the re;.ult that Mr. Battersby was defeatd by a large majority. They were not without hope, however, that soon they would be successful in their object. On the motion of Mr. OAIDEN, seconded by Mr. DEVON, the report was adopted and ordered to.be printed.

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The following officials were elected for the ensuing year : president, Mr. T. Malkin. vice-president, Mr. J. Battersby, treasurer, Mr. J. oa.kden, geeretary. Mr. W. Bullock, committee, Messrs. Ogden, Devon, Gregson, Lang, and Barnes.

div.head: ADMISSION 01 TRADES-IJNIONISTS,
div.p: ADMISSION 01 TRADES-IJNIONISTS,

Mr.lilaTig;;;BY moved that all bosa-fide trades-unionists be admitted tr: the meetings of the Trades Council. He said that he thought that they had a right to be present. A great many people hardly knew what this Council was doing, and therefore it would be to its advantage to increase its publicity. It was carried out in other towns.—M-. OAKDEN seconded the :motion and after further discussion it was carried out.
THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS-WITHDRAWAL 07 MR. BATTEMSBY.

Mr. Barrnasny said that he wished to make an ex- planation with regard to its candidature for the White- cross ward. Arrangements had been made to enter into the contest, and they had worked hard ivdeed. He never knew a more favourable canvas. On Saturday morning be presented his nomination paper at the Town Hall, when be was informed by the Town Clerk that there was a certain barrier to his election which he was not previowly aware of, which would land him and the Council into difficulties and embarassments. The Town Clerk told him that his opponent had been to him and warned him that he (Mr. Battersby) had not presented his vouchers within the prescribed time, and that if he proceeded with the election his opponent would pro- ceed to law which would certainly unseat him on petition He (the speaker) would also be subject to pains and penalties which would be very heavy. He was surprised to fled this as the matter had been left entirely in the hands of the secretary of the Trades Council. Only one bill had not been sent in,but the error could not be recti- Aed. He therefore considered that the best course would be not to proceed with the contest. He had consulted a solicitor who also advised him to withdraw, but said that his opponent ought to have fought in a straight- forward manner. He left it in the hands of the Council, but personally he wished to withdraw. Mr. 0MED1427 moved a motion to this effect. Mr. OGDEN seconded and after a lengthy discussion the motion was carried.

The French are pushing on their preparations for the expedition to Madagascar. The force will be composed of nine battalions of infantry, ten batteries of artillery, and a detachment of Algerian spabis. The Princess Frederick Charles of Hesse (daughter of the Empress Frederick) has given birth to a son at Rumpenheim.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1894.
FOOTBALL.
RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.

About 500 Warringtonians left Warrington on Satur- day afternoon to watch how their favourites would play against the all-conquering Wigan team. As the Wiganers had not lost a match in the competition, and also had not had a single point scored against them—in this respect being superior even to Oldham—it was not with feelings of very great confidence that Warrington encountered them. The Warrington three quarter line was strengthened by the inclusion of Burton and Hee- som, and among the forwards, Savage took the place of Buckley who was unable to get off for the afternoon. The following was the composition of the two teams : Warrington: Full back, Boscow; three quarters, Burton, Heesom, Potts, and Cunningham ; half hacks, James T. Bate, and Clark ; forwards, Turner, Jolley, Dakin, Taylor, Nevins, Savage, Thornily and B3iley. Wigan: Full-back, Trow; three quarters, Flowers, Jago, Walkden, and Roberts half-backs, Barnwell, and Winstanley : forwards, Unsworth, Rigby, McNamara, Lowe, Benson, Webster, Brown and Munro. Referee: Mr. Dickenson, Carnforth. There was a moderate breeze along the field. and Barnwell, the Wigan captain upon winning the toss, decided to take advantage of it, and Nevins kicked off towards the railway goal before about 4,000 spectators. The ball was so quickly followed by the Warrington for- wards, that there was no return, and the visitors almost scored the first half minute of the game. Trow however just scored, and a scrimmage ensued on the line. The Wiganers who are noted shouters were struck dumb in this performance, and there was silence for the first three or four minutes, during which Wigan had all their work cut out to keep the" wire pullers "out. At length the hopes of the home team rose when a free kick was granted them, but by some of the team being off-side no relief came, and operations were again dangerously near the Wishn goal posts. Warrington were unable to score, and taking advantage of a momentary relaxation of the visitors, Wigan rushed the ball three parts the field, and for the first time in the match the spectators were able to indulge in a hearty shout. The onward rush was brought to an end by Boscow. From the ensuing scrim- mage, Bate smartly screwed to:half way, but Flowers taking possession passed to Jago, who was &send, and a dribble by Jolley, Turner, and Taylor, took play into Wigan quarters again, where Trow saved and returned to half way. At this portion of the game neither side could claim the superiority, for the ball kept travelling from one end of the field to the other, the defenders ia each case having plenty of work to do. Winstanley now by a tremendous punt sent the ball too far and a minor was the result. From the drop out, the ball got into the hands of the Wigan three-quarters, but their well meant attempts at passing were nipped in the bud by Nevins. Cunningham now broke away and was not far from scoring when he rushed into the embrace of Walkden. At the other side Burton was knocked into touch when near the scoring line. A most unpleasant incident now occurred. Halliwell made his mark, and elected to place it. Webster was chosen to attempt the place. Halli- well had put the ball on the ground, when Turner and Taylor rushed at the ball to charge it down, when Barn- well was accidently kicked in the upper part of the face. He was for a time unable to stand, and the game was delayed for about three minutes. The spectators were furious at the incident, and loud hootings and cries of " Order him off the field" were to be heard. As it was a pure accident, as everyone who could look at it coolly could see, the referee of course did nothing of the sort and the game was re-started,Halliwell having recovered. Cunningham had a grand sprint, and had bard lines in not getting over. Half-time arrived with no score, and with Warrington pressing considerably. McNamara re- started and Clark returned, and for the first few minutes Flowers and Jago pressed considerably, but found their match in Burton and Heesom. At length, Warrington gaining their second wind quickly turned the Wiganers to the right about, and obtaining a free kick, Burton made a good attempt at the goal, but only a minor re- sulted. Burton met the kick out and almost got in, as also did Bate a little later. Wigan had a most anxious time, for while Heesom and Potts were preventing them from breaking away, " Smack" Bite,Clark, Burton and Cunningham were continually giving them the greatest anxiety,and it is marvellous how a score was prevented. Turner made a good attempt at a kick at goal, and soon afterwards from a lofty kick by Jolley, Burton had a capital chance at scoring, but unfortunately lost the ball. The attack was at length brought to an end by Wigan conceding a second minor. Heesom met the kick out, and his kick was the means of another fruitless minor being gained. This was followed immediately afterwards by vet another minor. Wigan followed the drop out to half way, and looked like becoming danger- ous,when Burton got possession near the touch line at half way, and made a capital attempt to drop a goal, the ball just missing the uprights, and Warrington gained their fifth minor. The attack was still main- tained. and Jolley, Savage, and Dakin did some good work, but Wigan gradually recovered, and Flowers and Jago made some dangerous runs only to find Boscow safe. Flowers on one occasion almost wriggled through. " Smack " Bate and Clark respectfully non-plussed the opposing halves by their feints at passing, and on one occasion,Bate got free of his opponents,but having previ- ously'hurt his ankle, he was not speedy enough. A good chance of scoring was also spoiled by Heesom being accidentally knocked over by Potts. The concluding portion of the game was fought in mid-field, and when the whistle blew for the cessation of hostilities, neither side had scored anything tangible. The result of the game does not at all represent the play, for Warrington had by far the best, and ought to have won by two tries at least. It was simply their lack of scoring powers which robbed them of victory.

div.head: WARRINGTON " A " v. WIGAN" A."
div.p: WARRINGTON " A " v. WIGAN" A."

Another match was won by the Warrington " A " team against Wigan "A " team, on Saturday, on the Wilderspool enclosure, a large number of spectators witnessing the game. Randles kicked off for the home team towards the railway goal. As soon as the ball was set in motion, the visitors began to press their opponents, and brought the leather in the Warrington 25, scrim- mages and line-outs taking place. Soon afterwards Lawless got possession of the ball and carried it the length of the field, and scored a try ; the goal kick proving unsuccessful. After recommencing, Warrington improved in their play and several times entered the visitors, quarters, but without further scoring. The whistle was afterwards sounded with the half-time result : Warrington 2 tries, Wigan nil. After the inter- val the play seemed to be of an even character, the ball travelling from one goal to the other. The visitors became dangerous, having the leather several times on the Warrington line. The home team, received a penalty kick for snme unseemly behaviour on the part of Wigan but the kick proved a failure. After resuming, another try was added to the homesters' list. Play now began to be of an even character. The teams shortly afterwards retired, Warrington being the victors by points to nil. The teams were composed as follows : Warrington: Full back, Mannion ; three-quarter backs, Carey, Lawless, Gibson, Moores; half backs, Forster, Foden ; forwards, Berry, Willcocks, Bandies, Andrews, Houghton, Thornton, Barratt, Fairhurst. Wigan Full Back, Barton; three-quarter backs, Railton,Holden, Hasleden, Robinson ; half backs, Austin. Mitcheson ; forwards. Consin, Hampson, Derbyshire, Telford, Fors- ter, Blackburn, Marsh. McNamara. WARRINGTON ST. MANY'S V. PORT SUNLIGIIT.—PIayed at Warrington on Saturday. Sunlight won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. The Saints imme- diately pressed, and a smart passing movement by the home backs resulted in Warburton scoring, Dampson failing to convert. From the drop out they again in- vaded the visitors' quarters, when a few minutes later Hammon got over, W. Roughley doing the needful. Play settled at half way for some time, when O'Brien securing passed to Warburton, who rounded his oppon- ents in grand style and scored, Thomas failing at goal. A forward rush by the Saints gave the Sunlight backs trouble, who, however, managed to clear. Nothing daunted the homesters returned to the attack, and Hampson getting possession passed to Warburton, who secured his second try. Sunlight appealed for knock-on the point being disallowed. From the scrimmage Higginbottom ran in a try under the posts. T.Roughley failed. Nothing more was scored up to half time, when the Saints were leading by one goal three tries to no- thing. Oa changing ends, with the wind in the Saints' favour, they at once took the ball to the visitors' lines, and from a scrimmage under the posts Bennett scored. The kick proved futile. The greater part of the second half was spent in the visitors' quarters, and the Saints won by two goals six tries to nil.

WARRINGTON EXCELSIORS v. ROCHDALE rAßE.—Played at Rochdale. on Saturday. Warrington commenced hostilities, and some clever work by Woods and Leech for the Park saw the visitors busy defending. By steady work the home team forced the 'game on the visitors' lines. Chapman punted to half way, and the visitors, by the aid of Hughes and Sudlow, transferred play to the home lines, and experienced bad luck in not scoring a major point, eight minors resulting in as many minutes. They kept up the attack, and from a passing movement. W. Daniels ran in, the place kick proving s. failure. The visitors pressed up to the interval without any addition to the score. Resuming, the visitors were first to attack. Eventually Woods (Warrington) secured from a scrimmage, and passing nicely to R. Daniels. that player knocked aside all oppositien and scored a good try. Another bout of pacising by the visitors' backs saw C. Daniels securing, and he ran in at the corner, Brookes kicking a goal. Time:was now called, leaving the Excelsiors winne by one goal two tries to Rochdale Park nil.

ALL SAINTS V. BANK-ST. MISSION RESERVE.—PIayed on the ground of the latter. The Stints kicked off Against the wind, Muckley scoring ten minutes from the start. This early reverse roused the homesters who equalised from a corner. This ended the scoring till half time. The second half was all in favour of the Saints, E. Gandy and Hall scoring one each. The game finished : All Saints, tkree goals ; Bank-street, one goal.

RUNCORN RECREATION V. LOSTOCK ALKALI.-0111 Satur- day afternoon these teams tried conclusions at Lostock, and in the end the visitors proved themselves the masters by two goals, two tries, three minors against nothing. RUNCORN V. Sr. HELENS RECREATION.—These teams met on Saturday afternoon before a very large " gate " at St. Helens and engaged in their first encounter this season. Hitherto, Runcorn has generally succeeded in vanquishing the "Saints," but such was not the case on Saturday. The visitors were unable to place any- thing like a representative team in the field, whereas the homesters had a very choice team. The clubs were represented as follows :—Runcorn : Houghton, back ; Richardson, Warder, Robinson, and West, three-quarter hacks; Abrams and J. Faulkner, half-backs; Langley, Farmer, G. Moores, Davies, Stubbs, Johnson, Lightfoot and F. Gayter, forwards. Recreation: Crossley, back; Archer, Seddon, Traynor and Massey, three-quarter backs ; Mullineux and Orford, half-backs; Mousdale, Fildes, Reynolds, Briers, Chapman, Winstanley and Potts, forwards. The kick-off was taken by Lightfoot, and after a little give and take play rain began to fall heavily. In the first half Runcorn pressed their opponents for sometime until the homesters pulled themselves to- gether and from a scrimmage gained a penalty kick. Seddon was entrusted with the place and executed it beautifully, the ball sailing over the bar in grand style. Runcorn tried in vain to score, but owing to the slippery state of the ground, many good chances were spoiled. In the second Portion of the game, play was not so ex- citing. The visitors made great efforts to gain some advantage, but could not, and the match ended in a victory for the. homesters by one penalty goal (three points) to nothing. RUNCORN V. ST. HELENS RECREATION " A " TEAMS.— Though the senior team of the Runcorn Rugby Club was unfortunate enough as to be beaten on Saturday at St. Helens, the junior team of the same club inflicted a severe defeat upon the Sc. Helens men at Runcorn. Although they were somewhat weak, three of their men playing with the first team at St. Helens, the Runcornians man- aged to score two goats (one dropped) and two tries, against one dropped goal, in the first portion of the game. In the second half they scored two more goals, making twenty-five points in all. Some capital passing was seen on the part of the homesters, who completely non-plussed their opponents. The defence of the visitors was very good, and the Runcorn men were repulsed and placed en the defensive many times. • 'I here was, how- ever, an absence of combination iR the visiting team, but with the homesters combined play was a feature of the game. WARRINGTON GYMNASTS AT LOSTOCK visit was paid to Lostock Gralam on Saturday, by eigh members of the Warrington Gymnasium, under the direction of Mr. J. Kinsley, director of the Warrington Gymnasium. A fine display was given in the schools before a very appreciative audience. Mr. J. J. Howitt (supported by the Vicar and Mr. J. Lord) was in the chair, and spoke of the great benefit to be derived from a systematic course of Gymnastics. He felt sure that after the display they were about to witness the people of Lostock would acknowledge the great usefulness of such an institution, and expressed the hope that the members of the Lostock Gymnasium would strive to emulate the deeds of the visitors. The display consistet of dumb-bell, bar-bell and Indian club exercises (td musical time), parallel bars, horizontal bars, and higo jumping. The whole of the display was excellent, thh several efforts of the performers being heartily applauded Mr. J. Podmore coming in for special notice in the high jump, clearing sft. lin. before he retired. At the close Mr. J. Kinsley, the director, gave an excellent exhibi- tion with the Indian clubs, and well merited the ap- plause which his play elicited. A vote of thanks to the performers for providing such a pleasing display was moved by the Chairman, and supported by Mr. Lord. Mr. J. Davies, in returning thanks on behalf of the visitors, spoke of the pleasure with which they had ac- ceded to the request to visit Lostock, and expressed a hope that the inhabitants would be benefited by the formation of a gymnasium in their midst. A hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Howitt for presiding brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: ASSOCILTION.
div.p: ASSOCILTION.

WARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S V. RUNCORN.—PIayed at Arpley on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the Run- corn team. In the first half the visitors played a goad game, rarely letting the homesters get a chance, and at the interval were leading by three goals to one. In the second half the game was of a more even character. St. Mary's missing several good chances. The visitors succeeded in putting on two more goals, while J. Richardson scored for St. Mary's. and at call of time the score stood—Runcorn, five goals ; St. Mary's, two goals. ST. PAUL'S RESERVE V. FLETCZER RUSSELL'S Est- , PLOYEES.—This match was played on the ground of the former. The visitors kicked off against a strong wind, 'and C. Longshaw for the home team getting possession of the ball, dribbled down the field, and from a rush in front of coal the former forced a goal. Good play was now witnessed between the forwards, and a second goal was scored. Bate, Crosby, and Bossward having shots at the goal resulted with six goals at half time. Fall time score—St. Paul's 13 goals. Fletcher Russell's Em- nloyres nil. The scores for St. Paul's were as follows—. J. S. Bate 4, C. Longshaw 4, W. Leach 2, H. Crosby 2, A. Bossward I.

RUNCORN RESERVE V. ASTON HALL—Played on Satur- day afternoon at Runcorn. The score at the finish of hostilities was, Runcorn four goals, Aston Hall nothing. LANCASHIRE ALLIANCE—EARLISTOWN V. HAYDOCE.— The return fixture in the alliance competition, between Earlestown and Haydock, tee& place on Saturday after- noon, on Earlestown ground, in the presence of between 3000 and 4000 persons. A fortnight ago, the teams played a draw of one goal each, but it was then seen that the play of the Earlestown men was much superior to that of Havdock, and it was freely asserted that Hay- dock would be easily beaten at the next meeting. A treat surprise was the result,and as the match progressed a feeling of disgust appeared to pervade the breasts of the Earlestown supporters, whilst the Haydock people, of whom there was a goodly number present were in the same degree jubilant. Axcepting Siddeley and Taylor, the half backs, not one of the Earlestown players dis- played anything like their season's form, whilst the whole of the Fia.ydnck team played as if they meant to win, and win they did in a most decisive fashion. Hay- dock won the toga, and unlike other teams which visit the ground they chose to play uphill during the first half. Topping kicked off, and play became at once of a desultory character. The kicking on the part of the Earlestown backs was faulty, which the Haydock for- wards took advantage of. After play had been in progress a few minutes, rain descended in torrents, both teams being soon wet through,end they retired to the pavilion. The ground was rendered slippery and the ball greasy, and when play was resumed, it was of rather pcorer description than before the rain, Haydock got away, and Baines shooting, defeated Sudworth. This roused the Earlestown players, and for a brief space they showed some of their old form, but Wainwright and Greenhalek were able to avert all danger, and the home forwards were sent to the right about. A pretty bit of head play brought ,to down again, but Lee cleared. A visit to the home goal was reveled, and Siddeley by a well placed kick passed to Lee, but the slippery state of the ground prevented correct shooting. Visits were paid to each goal in turn, Haydock RS a result of one of these visits, lowering the Earlestown goal a second time. Havdock pressed and made several assaults on the Earlestown goal, but they were unable to score. Hay- dock now worked up and some good football gave them an opportunity of scoring which Worsley improved upon and scored the third goal for Haydock. tlntil half-time Haydoclehad matters all their own way, and led by 3 goals to nil. On changing ends, matters did show the slightest improvement, and in a very few minutes Hay- dock had registered their fourth goal. After playing for some time without anything occurring of notice,Siddeley passed to the right wing, and Lee getting possession eluded his opponents, scored the first goal for Earles- town. Haydock, however, shortly afterwards retaliated by shooting a fifth time and the game ended—Haydock 5 goals, Earlestown 1. Teams :—Earlestown: Goal, Sudworth ; hacks, Peet and Wilkinson; half-backs, Taylor, Siddeley and Clarke; forwards, Conway, Lee, Topoine, Jenkins and Fluehes. Flavdock : Goal, Lee; hacks, Wainwright and Greenhalgh ; half-backs,Stocklev. Harrison and Preston; forwards, Meyer, Shaw, Fielding, Baines and Worsley. WARRINETON BASEBALL RESERVE Y. ST. BAUL'S.—This match was played on the ground of the former at Gorsey-'ane. The Saints winning the toss played with the wind. The first ten minutes play was very equal, hut with the help of the wind the Saints scored. At half- time the score was—Saint. two goals ; Baseball. one. In the second half the Baseball pressed, and soon scored two more goals. The final result was—Baseball, three goals; S. Pa.il's. two. NF.WTON-LE-WILLOWS RESERVE V. BANE-ST. MISSION.— The junior League match was played en the Mesnee Ground, Newton, on Saturday last, before a few spe:ta- tcrs. After a good passing movements by the home for- wards S. Boardman scored the first goal for Newton, the visiting goalkeeper making a very good clearance directly after from a shot by Bartley. Tl,s visit ors then made tracks for the other end, and defeating the home backs Duckworth equalised with a good shot. The home team by means of Cameron put on No. 2. Bank-st. not to be denied scored again. Beresford and Boardman each added to the score for the homesters, and the teams turned round with Newton leading by four goals to two. Play in the second half was of a very fast description, the goalkeepers on both sides being called upon to de-

fend, Rigby at last putting the home team another point ahead. Owing to the poor defence of Newton, the visi- tors scored two more goals. Their hopes of equalising were soon dispelled, however, as S. Boardman scored the sixth goal for the home side with a grand shot, and the whistle sounded " time" directly after, leaving the home team winners of a very poor game by six goals to four.

LYMIK V. HIGHER CRIIMPSA.LL.—At Lymm the Man- chester Leaguists played their full strength, and Lymm were well represented. The home team kicked off, and smart play by Leah, Martin, and Peters resulted in the last-named scoring a goal in the first minute of the game This was followed a few minutes later by one from Martin. After this reserve the visitors improved, and attacked strongly, and by means of some grand for- ward play scored twice in quick suceession. The game now became very fast, both ends being visited, Leah putting the home team ahead. Lymm continued to have slightly the best of the game, and a good run by Martin and Peters forced a corner, which was headed out, but Peters returned with a low shot and scored. Good play by the Lymm half-backs transferred play to the other end, Leah again scoring. From the kick off the visitors 'got away, and after some pretty passing Armstrong scored with a long shot. A fast and pleasant game ended Lymm, five goals ; Higher Crumpsall, three goals.

div.head: WARRINGTON HAIRDRESSERS AND
div.p: WARRINGTON HAIRDRESSERS AND
SUNDAY SHAVING.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Friday, a number of hairdressers in Warrington were sum- moned at the instance of the Warrington Hair- dressers Association for keeping their establish- ments open on Sunday for the purpose of trade. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, prosecuted, and Mr. Knowles, solicitor,Widnes,appeared on Vehalf of the defendants. The first case taken was that of John Davies,who was charged with having on the 7th October, it being the Lord's Day, carried on his ordinary calling as a barber, it not being a work of necessity. Mr. Knowles stated that the HairJressers' Asscciation, he was informed ,was amalgamated with the Warrington Trades and Labour Council. He understood that two magistrates Messrs. S. Wright and J. W. Hayward were connected with that council and if those two gentlemen were on the bench he thought that the Clerk would advise them not to ad- judicate in the case.—Mr. S. Wright said he was not in- terested in the transaction of the Hairdressers' Associa- tion. Mr. Knowles said if the Hairdressers' Associa- tion was amalgamated with the Trades and Labour Council that body was prosecuting. Mr. S. Wright said so far as his knowledge went the proceedings were not with the consent of the Trades Council of the town. He would use his own discretion as to sitting on the Bench. The case was then proceeded with. Mr. Browne said the Hairdressers' Association did not take those proceedings from a faddists point of view, but they'were for the protection of the members of the Association. Where the defendant and several others who had not joined the Association, carried on business, there were several shops, the pro- prietors of which were members of the Hairdresser's Association, and in consequence of these men opening on Sunday morning several had had to close their shops. On Sunday, the 17th inst. Mr. E. Smith and Mr. Jos. Hedgcock and another man watched the defendant's shop in Tanners-lane because of certain information Twelve months ago Mr. Davies, the defendant, gave a promise on him (Mr. Browne) withdrawing the summons against him that he would not open again on Sundays. They did not even ask for any costs on Mr. Davies giving that assurance. But on the date named from ten minutes to nine to 11.15 a.m. seven persons were seen to go to the defendant's shop, and to come out shaved. One of the men came out rubbing his chin. The de- fendant came out to Mr. Smith and Mr. Hedgcock and used filthy language to them, and threatened them. He also told them to watch others as well as him as there were others carrying on the business was well as he was on a Sunday. He asked that after the warning on the last occasion a fine should be inflicted. There were only three in the town who kept open on Sundays.—Mr. E. Smith and Mr. Hedgcock corroborated air. Bruwne's statement, and Mr. Knowles cross-examined them at some length. Mr. Hedgcock stated that 99 out of every 100 who got shaved on Sundays were persons who were too drunk to get shaved on Saturday nights. For the defence Mr. Knowles contended that shaving was a thing of necessity. Cleanliness was next to odliness. On Sunday mornings a number of men of the Roman Catholic religion came into the town from the district and before they went to church they went for a shave. Possibly, as a witness had said they were on the " spree " the previous evening, but they would as soon think of going to the church in their dirty clothes as without a shave. Their hands were too rough to shave themselves, and therefore they went elsewhere. The prosecution was taken by a set of people who wanted to coerce those outside their associa- tion. He also contended that there was no evidence to prove that the defendant had shaved the seven people mentioned. They might have shaved themselves, and he asked the magistrates not to convict on such evi- denee.—The Chairman (Alderman Wright) said the magistrates could not help referring to the fact that twelve months ago the defendant made a promise in that Court not to open again on Sundays. He would be I fined ss.

James Green, Bostock-street, was summoned for a similar offence on the same date. Mr. Browne said it was the first case against the defendant and if he would give an undertaking to close on Sundays the case would be withdrawn. As the defendant would not give his consent to such an undertaking the case was proceeded with. Mr. Browne stated that the defendant worked at Messrs. Houghton's during the day-time and did shaving and haircutting at nights. Saturday afternoons, and Sun- days. On Sunday, the 7th inst., nine persons were seen to enter his premises and seven were seen to leave, one with his lip cut. They had all been shaved.—Mr.McClew and Mr. Joseph Podmore, jun., bore out Mr. Browne's statement.—Mr. Knowles stated that the defendant was not following his ordinary employment when shaving. He was a wire polisher by trade, and he had quite as much right to shave on Sundays as he had to go a walk. He had also done a great deal of shaving for charity, having shaved 1,160 for nothing during the coal strike. They could not convict unless it was proved that defend- ant had been paid for shaving.—The magistrates asked the defendant to promise not to open again on Sunday, which he ultimately did, and Mr. Browne then withdrew the case.

Gr.gory Murphy, Scotland-road, was summoned for a similar offence on the 7th inst. Mr. Browne stated that the defendant gave an undertaking twelve months ago to close his shop on Sundays. On the morning in question eight persons were seen to go to the defendant's shop and to come out shaved. One gentleman who came out was well-known, and closed his premises at nine o'clock on Saturday night.—Mr. Wm. Podmore cave evidence as to watching Murphy's place on the date named. He corroborated Mr. Browne's statement as to the number of persons he saw enter and leave the shop.—Councillor Roberts asked for the name of the gentleman who had been mentioned. —Mr. Browne said it was Mr. Jchn Thomas Woods, oTocer.—Mr. Knowles thought Mr Browne had followed an improper course.—Mr. Chas. Wainwright and Mr. Titchett also gave evidence for the prosecution. —For the defence Mr. Knowles contended that it was a work of necessity in many cases, and that such was the case with regard to Mr. Woods. Defendant was fined 53.

div.head: ST. HELENS THEATRE ROYAL. VISIT OF MR. WILTON BARRETT.
div.p: ST. HELENS THEATRE ROYAL. VISIT OF MR. WILTON BARRETT.

As will be seen from an advertisement in another column the eminetit actor Mr. Wilson Barrett and his celebrated company will visit St. Helens on Monday next for a week's engagement at the Theatre Royal and Opera House, Corporation-st. Mr. Barrett's fame as an histrionic artiste is world-wide and assisted, as he is, by one of the best, if not the best, all-round companies, now touring the provinces. The lovers of a fine, real, dramatic representation are assured of a splendid treat next week. Mr. Wallace Revill, the .respected proprietor of the Theatre Royal, has completed the engagement at a great expellee and recollections of former visits by Mr. Wilson Barrett and his famous company encourage the hope that his enterprise on the present occasion will receive, as it merits the support of the theatre-goers of St. Helens and 4,he surrounding districts. On Monday and Wednes- Jay the latest and greatest successful play of IThe Manxman," adapted from the novel of that title by Mr. Hall Caine, will be produced, when Mr. Barrett will take the character of "Pete Quilliam " and Miss Maud Jeffries, whose charm and grace as an actress are uni- versally admired will portray the part of" Kate." The classical play of " Claudian," which has gained Mr. Barrett an enviable renown in past years, will be given on Tuesday and Saturday; the interesting drama of " Ben-my-Chree " (girl of my heart), a story of the Isle of Man, will be presented on Thursdsy, and Shakespeare's grand tragedy of "Hamlet " will be given on Friday. In addition to Miss Maud Jeffries already mentioned, Mr. Barrett's company includes such well-known lights of the profes- sion as Miss Daisy Belmore. Miss Alice Gambier, Miss R. Pendennis, Miss Maud Hoffman, Miss Cissie Rogers,Miss Marie Dorey, Miss Annie Bedford,Miss Kate Barton. Miss A. Martin, Miss B. Elma, Miss Cecilia Wilman, Mr. T.W. Percyval, Mr. Austin Malford, Mr. Horace Hodges, Mr. Ambrose Manning, Mr. G. Howard, Mr. T. Bolton, Mr. Stafford Smith. Mr. H. Mellor, Mr. C. Derwood, Mr. W. Grainger. Mr. E. Lyncl, Mr. F. Derward, Mr. T. Bolton, Mr. A. Rivers. Mr. Franklyn McLeay, Mr. Edward Irwin. Mr. T. Bainbridge, Mr. H. Barber, Mr. W. Ford. &c. Owing to the great expense attached to Mr. Barrett's visit the prices of admission have been slightly re-arranged. as will be noticed from our advertising columns. It may be stated that intending visitors from Earlestown, Newton, &c., will find the passenger train arrangements very convenient.

WESLEYAN Y.P.S.C.E. ANNIVERSARY.

The anniversary services in connection with the Wesleyan Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour were held on Sunday at Bold-st. and Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapels. The pulpits were occupied by the Revs. J. Kirtlan and G. D. Mason, and there were excellent services at each chapel. In the afternoon the annual service known as the chil- dren's service was held,at which special efforts were made to bring the children to decision for Christ. The service at Bold-st. chapel was conducted by the Rev. J. Kirtlan, and there were very encouraging results. The Rev. G. D. Mason conducted the service at Bewsey-road chapel, and the service was additionally impressive, owing to a terrible accideat in the preceding week hav- ing caused the death of one of the scholars. Mention was made of this to show the brevity of life, and a large number of children came out and publicly joined the church. At Ellesmere-st. mission, where the service was conducted by the workers on the spot, very encourag- ing results were obtained, and at Sankey Bridges Wes- leyan Chapel, Mr. J. R. Allen, of Lymm, also had a good meeting.

On Monday evening an "aggregate young people's meeting" was held in Bold-st. Wesleyan ehapel at which the scholars from the various schools in the circuit were invited. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Kirtlan. The programme of the evening consisted of speeches, singing, and a quartette, " When peace like a river," which was very impressively sung by Miss Pigot, Miss Tunnicliffe, the Rev. G. D. Mason, and Mr. G. Perkins, Miss J. E. Pigot accompanying. Miss Tunnicliffe was the accompanist in the other pieces._ _

The CHAIRMAN said that that gathering was represen- tative of the young life of the various congregations in the circuit. He was glad that there had been such en- couraging results at the meetings on the previous day. There was a considerable amount of spiritual influence at all the various schools of the circuit. They had been battling against sin, and against indecision, and be felt thankful for the results which had been achieved. There was no work in which they were engaged which was more important than the work among the young people. There was a grand body of young people in the town, and he was sure that the best society was that of Chris- tian young men. He considered that it was highly desirable that they should have a united gathering of young people sometimes, and there was no better time than to have it the day, after the Young People's Sunday. The Rev. G. D. MASON said that they were met toge- ther primarily as members and friends of the Young People's Soniety of Christian Endeavour. It was about that time last year that the society was commenced,and they therefore thought that if they did nothing more than advertise the fact that they had been a year in existence, and were celebrating their birthday, it would do good to the society by directing the thoughts and sympathies and practical help of many persons to the society. The object of the Ended.vour Society was not doctrinal, and in that respect it was as broad as the Y.M.C.A. or the Y.W.C.A. They were endeavouring to press the claims of the young people upon the Christian Church. There were manifold temptations and oa qger, which beset the young people on every hand,and it w, the desire of every preacher and teacher to keep them clear of them. He had been struck by several state- ments he had read. There was no less a number than 400,000 lads alone between 13 and 17 years of age who passed yearly through the Sunday schools, not into the church but into the world to swell the number of the degraded, drunken and impure masses. The vast mass of drunkards were recruited from the young men and young women who attended the Bunday schools, or otherwise the number would decrease. A great deal of this was Cue te bad company. He urged those before 'him to keet) clear of the public-house and bad company of every kind. Let them have no connection with the class of people who went into the public-houses. He held that education of itself was not sufficient to keep anyone in the paths of rectitude.as many criminals were men of education. Without religion it was impossiblel to live aright. He therefore urged everyone to join the church, and follow in the principles laid down by the blessed Master.
The meeting was brought to a close 19y the pronounc- ing of the Benediction.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON..
F &REWELL SERMON OF TNE REV. J. W. VARLZY

The Rev. J. W. Varley, pastor of Latchford Baptist Church, who is leaving the district to undertake the pastoral duties at the Baptist Church at St. Anne's-on- the-Sea, near Blackpool, preached his farewell sermon ea Sunday evening. There was considerable evidence of the rev. gentl3man's popularity among his people, for the chapel was crowded, and during the course of his mermen, several members of the congregation exhibited signs of great emotion. The rev, gentleman based his remarks upon Acts 3 c.. 25 v., "Ye are children, or the scns of the prophets." In the course of his remarks Mr. Varley said there were prophets who saw, felt and worked in the nineteenth century. The prophets of this century were the preachers,and reformers and preachers. They were the Spurgeons, Wilberforces and Sir Wilfred Lawions. They were men to do and to act, and the people were the sons of the prophets. They required good men as well as great men. He wished those before him to rise to that prophetic enthusiasm, insight, and daring. The past was full of examples, encouragement, and inspirations. They at that church inherited a holy heritage. At the time of his departure, he wished to centralise his thoughts upon those who were connected with that place. It was a little over nine years since he was called to be their pastor, and one-eighth of the span of life allotted to most individuals had been spent in their midst in ser- vices for the divine Christ. Was it too much for him to say to them that he had joyed with them and sorrowed with them? He had walked with some of them to the graveside where they had buried those who had been as the apple of their eye. Was it too much to say that he had entered into their hearts and lives as pastor and been their guide? When he contemplated the separa- tion, it was a separation that could not be expressed. If he had had his wish, there would have been no ser- vice like that. Those things were better felt than spoken about. He left college a raw inexperienced lad to undertake‘ the charge of brethren and sisters older far in Christian experience than himself, and was it not likely that when he came to think of the nine long, happy years of service: that those nine long years would live, and live forever? And he trusted that when they saw his face no longer, and some other brother came to take his place, they would give that brother the f•arn, faithful, earnest affection as they had extended to him. During the course of the service the choir rendered the anthem " Lord be merciful "very efficiently. PRAYER FOR SUNDAY SCHOOLS. - -

Sunda; Ta4.-1-9ein-g—t-h-e—diy appointed for special prayer for Sunday Schools throughout the country, special intercession on their behalf was made in the various Sunday schools and places of worship in the town. The Warrington Sunday School Union also arranged an inter-visitation of the various Sunday schools connected with the Union,and addresses suitable to the occasion were delivered at the afternoon services. At Wycliffe Church the Rev. J. Yonae preached special sermons. At the morning service his sermon was more particularly for Sunday school teachers. In the evening he preached a special sermon to elder scholars and young people.
ST. PAUL'S CI:JUROR.

Special sermons were preached in the above church on Sunday on behalf of the Sunday schools, the pulpit in the morning was occupied by the Rev. A. H. Towns- end, curate, and in the afternoon and eveniqg by the Vicar, the Rev. H.V.Pigot. In the course of his sermon In the evenirm,the preacher,without pressing the matter unduly on the congregation, who had at the present time many calls upon them, hrought before them the importance of Sunday school work. Upon him (the Vicar) was laid the duty of instructing all the young in the parish that they might come forward to the perfec- tion of Christian fellowship, although in a large parish like that, as well as in others, it could not be done without the help of Sunday schools. Great anxiety existed now with regard to the fate of the schools which the Church established in the time when the State took no care for education. They (the clergy) therefore needed the prayers and sympathy of the people in the ereat work which the Church began at the beginning of the century. A collection was made at the close of each service, a satisfactory amount being obtained.

div.head: " OFFERe " TO LABOUR If.P.'S.
div.p: " OFFERe " TO LABOUR If.P.'S.

Mr. B. Pickard. M.P., speaking at a Liberal bazaar at Barnsley, on Wednesday, said he could not agree with the methods and tactics of the Independent Labour Party. Referring to a cartoon which, he said, had been Published representing John Burns crawling on his knees gathering momer, and himself looking on, he sup- posed, extremely desirous of having. a portion, with Lord Rosebery acting as their leader, Mr. Pickard stated that he had not been long in Parliament before certain offers which it would have been warth his while to accept were made to him to become a director of public companies. But he felt that if a working' man lent him- self to such schemes he could not go clean-handed to his own werk, and he had tried to be independent in both his political and non-political actions. But if it had been a question of money-grabbing he could have had a fair share of it.

It is reported that a suit has been commenced at Salta against Jabez Balfour on a charge of having carried on fraudulent commercial operations in Argentina. The charge is believed to have been trumped up as a coun- terfoil to the extradition in the event of its being granted.

JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health. MORE NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT
WARRINGTON.

John and Annie Barnes, of 6 Cropper's Brow were also charged, yesterday, with neglecting their four chil- dren. Inspector McAteer sail that the children were Winifred aged ten years, John, eight years, James, three years, and Annie, four weeks. On the 15th of last month, witness was with P.C. Delahey in Buttermarket-street at 9.30 p.m., and saw James sitting on the pavement crying bitterly. He was half naked at the time. He took the child home and there found the other children sitting over the fire place. There was no fire, and both father and mother were away. When the mother came in several questions were put to her, and she said that she had only just gone out. Witness further visited the house with Detective Monaghan the following morning and examined the children. They were badly clad. Winifred was wearing a couple of old garments, and had not been washed for some time,and her hair was :matted with dirt and vermin. John was also in a similar state to his sister. James was sitting on; the floor almost naked only wearing an old shirt. He found nothing for the children to eat, and the room was very filthy and appeared as if it had not been washed for some time. The bed on which defendants and two children slept upon:consisted of two dirty old mattresses, and an old sheet. In the corner was an old broken down squab in which the re- mainder of the children slept. The reom smelled abomin- ably. Toe male defendant was a rni.n of II drunken habits, and his wile and he were always quarelling. She had used the poker for ill-treating her during the last few weeks, and his head had had to be bandaged. He was employed at Mr. Connor's, undertaker, Sankey-st. The wife was as bad as her husband. Detective Monaghan and P.C. Deiahay gave corrobor- ative evidence, and the prisoner said that he had always been a hard worker and only got 183 a week. There were seven or eight to keen out of this. He could not keep tlyan in proper clothing out of the money. Alderman Wright (presiding magistrate) advised the defendant to take the pledge. The case would be ad- journed for one month to give them another chance,and if they were brought up again they would be severely dealt with.
