ELECTION. Sir,-4,was rather amused at " Merlin's." description in last Sattrday's" Examiner.," of how the result of the Birkenhead election was received at Warrington, and I see front Wednesday's " Observer "that 4e has roused the ire of one of the "Tory .bloods." This is not sur- prising.if " TaryUood" is a typical member of that Ilk, as they are all more or lese excitable, but what I am surprised at is that the "Observer "should tpublisb such rabblaes that.contained in the aforesaid letter. It is -evidently the contribution ,:cf a young member of the Tory fraternity .as the general tone of it is very juvenile. The trorrow majority of Kr. Lees cameas a surprise to no sneall number of Tories, but it seems to have affected the Warrinstton set mast of all.—Yours &c., "A 1123ERAL." Warrisgtori, October 25,104.

THE WATCH ,COMMITTRE AND GAMBLING. Sir,—Whenever I read .a speech of Mr. Councillor Zenry Roberts :I expect.to.ment with a large surnant of 'shrewd sonmensense.,tinged (of course) more or less with bigoted bias against beer,•of which, by his own ac- count, he never tasted in his Wel But for ()mean a way be was not in his usual forrn, when, as chairman of a 'religious meeting held last week, he dilated on the sin of rardbling. Tie said rthere was no gambling in theiGarden ot Wei ' • but howdoes he knew*' I might as safely as- SerrthatAdam and Eve .di bet, and who shall deny it '? The asiolent puritanical tirades against betting that have taken place in my time, have moct certainly tended to increase it and the whole social purity school put to- gether stay as well try to stop it as to dam up Niagara with a troth ladle ! They only make matters ten times worse. I see also Councillor Roberts falls foul of a por tion of die Council. because., forsooth, -they will not be. dictated to by a set of TM Purity" faddists, with himself as the leader. I wonder it he ever heard of that old pro- verb. "Its a dirty bird that fouls its own nest." Judg- ing by his speech against brother councillors, I should nay not. (am simply delighted that the Watch Com- mittee treated him and his co-meddlers with the con- tempt they richly deserved,and I hopefuls lesson will do them good, though I fear not. But what shall I say of what I read in the next column.? Sir, my gorge rose at the fulsome adulation throws at Mr. D . W. Roberta. for doing what not one of itis beslaverers would have done, namely, act the part of a spy. I pity the poor fellow from the bottom of my 'heart, and I add, that a Bussianizing system of espion- age will not go down here, unless and until my towns- men have lost all self-respect, and are willing to be driven like slaves by a very small set of ultra-bigoted Pharisees of the most nauseous order, Warrington, Oct. 24th, 1894.
NO-SPY.

THE NEW GUARDIANS AND VACCINATION Sir„---In a little over a month we shall be in the midst of a contest for the election of guardians. One, and an increasingly important, duty of theirs, in the light of awakening public opinion is to concern themselves with vaccination. Since 1873 over 40,000 persons have been proceeded against under the "Vaccination Acts " ; how strong must be the conviction then of the thousands who regularly fly in the teeth of these acts which they characterise as brutal and inhuman. A census recently taken of some 60 towns and villages elicited the opinion of 125,000 persons, of whom 109,200 (88 per cent.) were against compulsory vaccination, and 84,858 (68 per tent.) did not believe in vaccination at all. Notwith- - standing the progress of enlightenment thus evinced, all England is stilt suffering from the infliction of a medical rite which hara3ses and injures those who could prevent the injury by a proper use of their votes. It is of vast importance that all guardian candidates' opinions on this question should be clearly expressed and among others for these three reasons : (a) The preponderance of evidence, new to the last few years, is against vaccination and all the older evid- ence more nearly scrutinised gives the same lesson. (b) The "Vaccination Commission" has reported against the infliction of repeated penalties which is the effect also of the Evesham circular of the Local Govern- -meat Board. (e) The same Board has allowed it to become known that the guardians will not be compelled to enforce vaccination, pending the final report of the "Corn- mission.,, However, the Board's kindness is of little use since guardians cannot be compelled to enforce vaccioation except by a new act of the legislature, which even our friends the enemies would scarcely have the hardihood to propose. It is true the 27th section of 30 and 31 Vict. Cap. 84 (1867) provides that guardians "shall cause proceedings to be taken against persons in default." Clerks' law in many cases seems made up of this section alone, and seldom leaves Guardians any dis- cretion at all. But the schedule to the 1871 Act (17th section 34 and 35 Vic. Cap. 98) repeals this section ; so Guardians now prosecute defaulters, not because bound to, but to provide themselves the pleasure of subjecting others to a filthy and degrading rite. The Local Gov- ernment Board has, however, succeeded in re-enacting this compulsory sections—in cases where it has cowardly and ignorant Guardians to deal with by Article 16 of its order. " The Guardians shall in all cases in which the previsions of the Vaccination Acts for enforcing vaccina- tion have been neglected, cause proceedings to be taken azainst the persons in default." Just so the powers of this Board (Vaccination Act, 1874) include "making of rules . . . for enforcing the provisions of the said Acts" and since that 27th sec. 30 and 31 Vic. Cap. $4 is no longer one of tll-.1 provisions, and the Board's powers are limited by the bounds of the 1874 Act that Board cannot and does not make any rule to compel the Guardians to move in the matter. Having shewn that Guardians need not move perhaps you will allow me a word to show why they should not -move. We are too apt to take our medicine from doctors on faith. We accept the doctrine of vaccination on trust on the understanding that doctors are the likeliest to know and to propound the best remedies for our ills— Are they? Well, yes! perhaps, if they were more than buman—else ? As we are on a medical dogma let us adopt the dogmatic formula of three reasons why : (1) Medicine is not an exact science though we little -suspect the fact in our intercourse with its professors— who have even been know to swear to blood-stains as human!! There can be produced no opinion of a medical man on this question of vaccination, to which I cannot produce a flat denial on the authority of an equally eminent medical man. (2) It is to the interests of the profession to foster vaccination. £lOO,OOO a year are paid out of the rates alone in vaccination fees £3,250,000 have been paid in all and it is estimated directly and indirectly the faculty profits £2,000,000 annually, 25 per cent. of the total earnings. (3) Doctors have been more unanimous and equally forcible and dogmatic in propagating ideas now long since exploded, to wit, vivisection and Inoculation. What guarantee then have we that this body of men

which has been committed to practices which are scanted to ‘3ay by the merest tyro in the profession, shall not, ere another decade, as completely denounce the practice which is now imposed on us by the sole weight of its authority ?—Yours sincerely, BIBLIOTHEVUE. Runcorn Oct. 23, 1894.

div.p: FOOTBALL.
CUESHIRE v. MIDLAND COUNTIES. VICTORY OF THE MIDLANDERS.

On the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn, the above teams eontested under Rugby Union Rules on Wednes- day afternoon, for the mastery. Rain had fallen heavily for several .hours in the morning,but at noon the weather cleared, and there was every promise of a goodly day. The ground was in a very bad state, and would not allow of much sure running. Shortly before the kick off rain began again to fall ; slightly at first, but after- wards very heavily for a few minutes. Notwithstanding these unfavourable conditions the players took up their positions in the following order : CHESHIRE.—S. Houghton (Runcorn), back ;W. Bailey and Saville (Stockport), Fenton (Birkenhead Park), and Jones (New Brighton), three-quarters; J. Faulkner and Robinson (Runcorn), half-backs; W. Faulkner, Taylor, Langley, Davies (Runcorn), Bailey, Mottershead, King (Stockport), and R. Ould (Birkenhead Park), forwards. MIDLAND COIINTIES.—J. F. Byrne (Moseley), hack; A. H. Frith, F. R. Lovett, G. Tuke (Coventry), and F. A. Byrne (Moseley), three-quarters; R. H. Cattell (Mose- ley), and W. J. Foreman (Leicester), half-backs; 7. Evershed (Burton), G. Carpenter, W. Lamb (Coventry), A. Henshaw (Derby), E. Redman, G. Jones (Leicester), W. H. Rowlands, and P. J. Ebsworth (Moseley), forwards.

It will be seen that the original teams chosen were much altered, and at the last moment only was J. P. Ebsworth (Moseley) selected to fill the place of A. E. Cooke (Leicester) in the Mid- land team as forward, and R. Ould (Birkenhead Park) instead R. Brown, (Tranmere Wanderers) forward for Cheshire. Mr. J. H. Smith, of Widnes, acted as referee. Last year the contest between these counties resulted in a victory for the Midlands by one goal and a try to one goal. At 3.30 prompt J. Faulkner kicked off for Cheshire against a strong wind, and before about 3,000 spectators. Scrimmaging at once ensued in mid- field, but before long the Cheshire forwards secured the leather and troubled the visiting backs sorely. Some dangerous rushes were successfully repelled by Tuke and J. F. Byrne. Robinson passed very badly and almost let in the Midlanders. Again obtaining the ball the Cheshire men ran well into the Midland territnry but Byrne with a powerful kick sent the oval into the Cheshire 25. Here it was met by the Cheshire backs and made a good return and play for some time in the Midland /5. Saville then became prominent. With a good kick he sent the leather beautifully over the Mid- land crossbar amid loud applause. This was soon silenced, however, when it was found that the goal was negatived because simultaneously with the kick the whistle had sounded for a previous infraction by a Midlander. Pressing was still continued by Cheshire and the outcome of some clever passing was a try capi- tally secured hy J. Faulkner between touch and the goal posts. The place was taken by Saville who shot very well but the ball was borne wide with the wind and nothing resulted. The Midlanders, after Cheshire had been twice penalized, gradually assumed the aggressive, and the result of a fine concerted movement among their forwards was a good try obtained by Frith who out- stripped Saville in the running. F. Byrne converted this into a goal. The Midlanders continued to have the: best of the play until half time arrived with the score Midland Counties one goal ; Cheshire one try. On the resumption of play, the midland men pushed en vigourously and maintained the upper hand. Cattell had a chance, but was too slow. A penalty kick was given to Cheshire, and Saville made a splendid attempt at goal. Some good work was put in by Houghton, his sure kicking and tackling being very bright features in the game. The visiting team, more especially their for- wards,played in magnificent style and from a pass Lovett scored a try. The same player failed to improve this advantage, though in a very easy position. Even play followed, and Cheshire might have equalized if their halves had only acted coolly. Several chances of scor- ing fell to them but their passing was very ill-judged and precipitate. The Cheshire forwards in comparison were smarter than the visitors, but they could not make any headway owing to the weak support given them by the halves. Some time before the finish of the game Cheshire went at it very spiritedly, but could not score so superb was the defence of the Midlanders. The enal score was—Midland Counties, one goal, one try ; Che- shire, one try.

MVI VAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY LECTURE.—OR Mon- day evening und.r the auspices of the above society, a lecture on "life Underground" was delivered in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, by Mr. James Tonge, C.E.,F.G.S. The lecture was illustrated by limelight views from photographo taken in the mine by the electric and mag- nesium lights. Mr. James Dodds occupied the chair,and the audience included the Rev. Ed wardes-Evans, M.A., the Rev. W. T. Lewis, M.A., and Messrs. G. H. Watson and C. H. Kerry. The Chairman remarked that the gentleman who was going to deliver the lecture was fully qualified to deal with the subject and, further, was an old friend of theirs. Mr. Tonge then proceeded with his lecture. At the outset he remarked that there were about three-quarters of a million persons employed in coal getting, and the amount of coal raised in one year was abouttwo hundred million tons. Therefore it was a very important industry. It was also a most danger- ous occupation. Views were then thrown on the screen of an ideal forest in the period when coal beds were formed, namely, about a million years ago. 'Views various parts of the workings of a mine were shown with men at different kinds of work,and the lecturer ,ex- plained the processes of getting coal. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer.

A SUCCESSFUL WARRINGTON ANGLER. So far as sweepstakes are concerned the angling season was practically brought to a close on Mon- day. when the majority of the crack anglers of Sheffield and several others hailing from other parts of the country met at Crowle Wharfe and competed in the waters of the Kenny Canal in a competition open to all England. The affair was really pro- moted for crack anglers, and only those who were experts competed. The entries totalled 63. A special train left the Victoria Station on Monday morning at9.4'5, and after the draw for stations had taken place at •the South Yorkshire Hotel, the anglers distributed themselves along the bank of the ohne' ten yards apart. Fishing commenced at 12 o'clock and continued for three hours, or until three o'clock. During this time the sun shone forth brizhtly, with the water in good condition, but ilPsDitt, the conditions the catches were only light, the first prize of .£5 being won by T. Wild, of Sheffield, with a catch weighing 11b. 940 z. With the exception of the third, ninth, and eleventh prizes (which were won by J. Barrow, Mexborouch ; W. Bolton. Warrington; and W. Harper.( WorAbor'ough Dale) the other nine were won by Sheffield maulers. _ _ _

THE ALLEGED ASSAULT BY A PUBLICAN.—At the Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday morning before Messrs. A. Thom•is and Philip Speakman, C.C., the case of Ellen Simpson v. John Simpson, was called upon. It will be remembered that as reported in our last issue, this was a charge of assault preferred by Ellen Simpson, against John Simpson, her husband, and landlord of the Castle Hotel. Halton. The assault was alleged to have been committed on the Bth inst., when the defendant according to the complainant's story, threw a candle- stick at her head when she was retiring to bed.—Mr. Burton again appeared for the defendant, and Mr. Allen represented the complainant, who did not appear.—Mr. Burton asked their worships to grant an adjournment of a fortnight as both parties desired to settle the matter out of Court.—Mr. Allen made no• objection and the application was granted. A PLEASANT GATHERING.—More than one hundred of the teachers and elder members of the Parish Church Sunday School, Halton, assembled on Friday evening and partook of an excellent tea in the girls' schoolroom. The meal was succeeded by a concert. Mrs. Wray was present and at the outset apologised for the absence of the Vicar who had gone to preach at Aston Church, on the occasion of the harvest festival. She expressed the pleasure it gave her to see so many smiling and happy faces, and felt sure that they should all be very thankful for the rapid and enormous increase in their numbers. The vicar and herself felt very thankful for the many earnest lay workers they had around them. A pro- gramme of appropriate music was-then admirably sus- tained, and the proceedings were at length brought to a happy conclusion by the singing of the National Anthem.

SINGING CLassas.—On Tuesday evening singing classes fur adults and juveniles were opened in the Halton Library by Mr. John Holford, Runcorn. There was a fair attendance of pupils, who seemed to take the keenest interest in the remarks of their tutor, and it is confidently anticipated that before very long the classes will prove very successful.

Sir,—l should like to call the attention of the Newton Commissieners to the disgraceful condition of Mercer- st. and the bye street leading from High-st. across the Menses, as it is disgraceful tint the tenants mad the public of Newton, that are obliged to use the streets, should have to walk through such mire. It is bad enough at present,but what will it be if nothing is done to alter the condition of it. —Yours &c., S. DAVENPORT. Mercer-st., Newton-le-Willows, Oct., 24, 1894.
AN APPEAL ON BEffALF OF GENUINE LABOUR CANDIDATES (MUNICIPAL).

Sir,—Labour representation has during recent years made such remarkable progress, and public sympathy is now so strongly with it that it is not surprising that persons who have little identity with the woaking classes should be run as "Labour" candidates. It is due to the pubKc and to the working classes themeelves that some efforts should be made to clearly define the term "Labour candidate." No person can attend the Trades Union Congress as a delegate unless he is ivow,or has been a workman, Even in cases where the men are not working at their trade they are paid by their fellow toilers to look -after their interests. Acting on the same principle the Labour 'Electoral Association—which is the offspring of the' Trades Union Congress—has again and again advised the 'electorate not te recagnise anyone as a labour .candidate nless they are now or have been werkmen. Although there are hosts of people outside thezonks df the labour- ing classes who are ,prepared to assist in the•elevation ct: the toilers it is obvious that the woeking,peeple must in the main work out -their own salvation and this can only be done by sending to the public bodies not merely men pledged to a certain class of opinions but men who having toiled in workshop, factory., mine, &c., and hay- ing;no dual interests to serve, can speak with an experi- ence and a knowledge of the wants.und hardships of the people to which no one who has never worked, however socialistic his opinions, can attain to. Although the entension of ritual:A[3ot government has during the last SC-vears done much for the liberties and well-being of the people it is a regrettable fact that until a few years ago the administration of 'octal affairs has 'been -wholly in the hands of the commercial classes. /Even now they ferns the overwhelming majority on .every Town Council-in the United Kingdom. While they -have not wished to. crush the working classes their inter- testfi, their training, and a false reading of the claims of economy have made them buy their labounin the cheap- est-market, irrespective of the claims of humanity or of the truer interests of the people. They have too often ,unwittingly encouraged those who think that a living wage-for workmen is the very last thing,nn employer should think of. iniact many municipalitiesinstead of -being model employers of labour have been the re- verse. Sloppily a change,is coming over the minds of many members of local authorities and this is showing itself ha more sympathetic policy towards labour. It is a significant feet that in those towns where genuine work- men have been elected,and where they have,by common- sense action, gained the respect of their colleagues the position of labour, whether employed publicly or priv- ately has been correspandingly improved. On the prin- ciple that a bird in the-hand is worth two in the bush it is infinitely better tha labour should improve its lot now, rather than that it should have to be satisfied with hopes that possibty E-0 years hence such a change of affairs may be brought about as will secure greater happiness all round. The mission of the Labour Electoral Association is to secure the-eleetion ef iona fide workmen to all public bodies, and. however much they may -differ in opinion, that associatien asks the electors generally to support them, providing of course they place the claims of labour first and let any particular " ism " to which they may be attached occupy a subordinate position. The time has arrived when the working classes by their action should protest against the Labour and Trades Union movement being sacrificed in order to promote a PTitieular class of opinion. The opportunities whereby bows fide workingmen re- presentatives put forward by Trades Councils. Labour Electoral Associations, and genuine labour bodies can assist the labouring people are legion. By supporting the proper carrying out of the fair contract resolution they can strike a severe blow at sweating, and improve the rate of wages and ths conditions of toil ; they can prevent the police being used as an engine to assist any particular section of the community and can help to secure even-handed justice to all ; and they can do much to bring about a municipal eight Mute day and to secure a minimum living wage for corporate werkmen. All this, of course, as great influence upcas the commercial world, for private employers are naturally enough prone to follow the example of the local Town Council. Then, as a matter of course, genuine labour representatives are invariably in favour of better housing of the poor—and who is so likly to understand this question as they—and the whole of their influence must be cast on the side of the labouring poor. Having no interests to serve but those of the people,being seldom if ever property owners, and invariably trained as officials in the Trades Union ranks the bona fide workman makes an ideal representa- tive and ratepayers generally who wish to secure good government with economy; and the removal of these blots which deface our present social system will be acting wisely by voting for such Labour. candidates as are indicated above. I shall be glad to supply any in- formation on the points raised or where possible give any suggestions.—Yours truly, T. R. TEIRELFALL, Secretary, Labour Electoral Assaciation of Great Britain and Ireland. 19, Sussex-road, southpert, Oct. 23, 1894.

div.head: "TURNING ON" OF WATER AT PADGATE.
div.p: THE "TURNING ON" OF WATER AT PADGATE.

--- The ceremony Of" turning on" the water into the mains recently laid down by the Warrington Corporation for the water supply of Padgate and the neighbourhood, was performed on Wednesday morning by the deputy mayor (Alderman Fran- comb) who is also chairman of the Water Committee of the Warrington Town Council. The work of laying the mains was commenced about three months ago, and has been performed by the War- rington Corporation under the superintendence of Mr. Ross the water engineer. The work was done at the request of the Rural Sanitary Authority who agreed to pay a rental at the, rate of Btli per cent upon tke total outlay, but as the Cheshire Lines Railway Committee are expected to require a good supply, it is not thought that the work will cost the Authority a large figure. There is also an increasing population up to the borough boundary, and also in Padgate, and at Fearnhea.d Cross and it is to supply these inhabitants with water that the scheme has been taken in hand. Tite Orford water scheme will also be carried out oa similar terms. The Orford scheme, however, was only commenced a few weeks ago. In the larger Padgate scheme, the pipes go along Gorsey-lane, and are eight inches in diameter. They then proceed to the borough boundary in Padgate- lane,and then up to Fearnhead Cross where they are of six inches diameter. A service pipe of three inches diameter isthen taken along, Fearnhead-lane for about 150 yards, and there terminates, but will of course be continued should the increase of population require it. A service pipe ofithe same dimensions also branches off at Bruche Avenue. Hydrants are placed at different portions of the length of the pipes which will be useful in case of fire. The total length of the pipes is about 2700 yards, and within the last few weeks plumbers have been busy "laying on" water to a number of houses. The weather on Wednesday morning was of a wretched description, and as a consequence the only members of the Water Committee to put in an appearance were Alderman Francomb and Councillor Garner. Messrs. T. Longdin (borough surveyor) and ROSS (water works engineer) also joined the party, who proceeded by 'bus from the Town Hall as far as the Cemetery, where the drainage scheme of the Town Council in Manchester- road was inspected. They afterwards drove along Pad- gate-lane to Fearnhead -Cress, where the six-inch pipe terminates, and here a hose pipe was attached to the hydrant, and on the Deputy-Mayor turning it on, a fine stream of water was sent forth to mingle with the rain which was descending in torrents. Although the water I was not at its full force, it rose high above the houses round about. The party then proceeded under the most depressing sircumgances to the end of the three inch service pipe, where an equally streng jet of water was obtained. Tke ceremony then concluded, and the inhabitants of the district can now have a water supply as good as that enjoyed by the Warrington ratepayers. The weather was toe bad for any speeches and the party returned home via Winwick, and arrived at their journey's end at about 12.30. As an instance of the growth of the Padgate popula- tion, it may be mentioned that Mr. Hindley of Padgate, has built a shop and two villa residences, and is erecting two other houses at the Cross. Mr. Bywater is just completing five bow-windowed houses, and is also busy at work with six of a similar character in Fearnhead- lane. He has also land sufficient for eight other houses, which will be commenced as soon as possible. In addi- tion to these, a large number of villas and semi-detached houses are in the course of erection. There is therefcre every indication that this district will become a popular and populous suburb of Warrington. The Cheshire Lines Committee are recognising this fact, as a better train service is promised for November.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL

'Warrington considerably astonished, the football world, themselves included, by making a. draw with Wigan on I.4.aturday. The Wigan teani 'nave been doing so well, that they looked upon Warrington as almost a certain victory for them, but they had reckoned without their hest. Not only did they fail to secure a victory., but daisy were tacky indeed even to be let off with a draw, for Warrington -were pressing much the greater part of the game. Fortune is at present very unfavcrur- able to Warrington, and she was especially En on Satur- day, for none of the Players could utilise their chances to give their side the:tlead. Wigan of. course had hard hick once or twice, but nothins., like the quantity which Warringteit had. This lack of ability to put on the finishing touches is at present Warm,ngtod's great weak- ness.

The Wigan spnctators were anything but 'pleased to see the!r team having the worst of: it. They have been so accustomed to seeing them winning all before them, that,they cannot tolerat3 a team which ,pres,ames to get the better of them. Consequentrty the referee came in for a great deal of abir3e from the crowd who could net understand why free kicks were not given to the Wigan team whenever they were hard pressed. The game was rendered very unpleasant by the persistent hootings' which carnerprinciptlly from the grad stand. There was one unpleasant incident in the game when Hallidwell was kicked while placing a ball for a shot at the goal. The spectators were very demorntrative at this, but as it was ,a pure accident, there was a little teo much made of

To come to the players, it was Enticed by everyone that there was an all-round improvement in the War- rington'team, which promises very well for the future. If they keep up their form, they will make a good num- ber of the teamsin the,competition,quake to meet them. One of the causes of this great improvement is due to the three-quarter rank being strengthened. Burton was an acquisition on Eaturday, and if he will play regularly with the team, the committee need choose no better man. He completely " bottled up" the speedy , Flowers on Saturday. Heesom, although not properly recovered from his injuries, playe& a splendiid defensive game on Saturday, in conjunction with Potte, both of them tackling well. Cunningham on the opposite end to Burton, promises to become a good player, for he has a good amount of speed. He has improved immensely of late.

Boscaw played a grand game at full back, although he commenced a bit "shaky," but this was only during the first five minutes, and he never made a mistake after- wards. Bate and Clark were superior by far to their opposing halves, and they baled them time after time with their feints at passing. "Smack" has long been an adept at this, and all other half back tricks, and now Clark is following suit,so that before long wemay expect to see them play as well together aa "Smack" and "Jack" Bate.

The most surprising point in the match was the way in which the Warrington forwards beat the Wigan lot. Wigan are supposed to be exceptionally strong among their-forwards, but they met a better lot on Saturday. Even in the " serum" Warrington held their own, but immediately the ball became loose, they quite ran away with the Wlganers. It quite took the breath away from the spectators the way they commenced the game, tak- ing the ball to the line the first half minute. The opinion was freely expressed that they had commenced too strong to last., but they lasted as long as their op- ponents nevertheless.
The draw on Saturday again took Warrington to the fourth'place in the League for which they were displaced by St. !galena last week. The results up to date are appended herewith :

For. Agst. Phi. Won. Lost. Drn. G. T. G. T. Pts Oldham Wigan 4 3 0.. 1 ... 6 5 ... 0 0 ... 7 Tyldeeley Warrington St. Helens *Salford Broughton Rangers 4 ... 1 ... 3 ... 0 ... 3 2 ... 6 6 ... 2 Swinton Rochdale Hornets *Leigh * Leigh, having been suspended for professionalism, will not take any part in the competitionthis season.. Salford. on October 16, were struck out of the competition for the same reason.

To-day, the Swinton team are due at Warrington. Warrington were the only team last year to beat the "Lions." In fact they were able to extract three points out of the four from them. The Swintonians, how- ever, have not done as well as usual this year, but not- withstanding this fact, and given a fine day, there will be no doubt a monstre gate. As Warrington have not yet suffered defeat at Wilderspool at the bands of this famous team, I expect them to gain another couple of points.

To get these two points, the following players have been chosen : Bescow, full back : Burton, Hampson, Potts, and Cunningham, threequarters ; "Smack" Bate, and Clark, half-backs ; Turner, Jolley, Dakin, Berry, Taylor, Thornily, Buckley, and Nevins, forwards,

The " A " team obtained a victory at the expense of Wigan "A " to the tune of three tries to nil. This is a great improvement upon last year for then Wigan were the victors. In fact the two principal teams of War- rington made great strides upon last year's results, for then they were both beaten,whereas neither were beaten this time. Our A team have as yet only Iren beaten once in the A team competition and that was at the hands of Oldham, whereas they have won victories over Wigan, St. Helens, and Broughton Rangers, so that they have a very satisfactory record indeed. They will be at the top,or not far from it when the competition closes— that is if all the other teams of the competition are not suspended for professionalism, as is not at all unlikely. In that event.Warrington will win both cups with a walk over.

The St. Mary's team were not long in finding that they had an easy thing on with Sunlight on Saturday, and they made the most of their opportunities. Although they were without Barton, they gained the victory by two goals, six tries to nil. The goal kicker would do with a little improving, however.

The Warrington Excelsiors gained the verdict over Rochdale Park, on Saturday, by a goal and two tries to nil, notwithstanding that they were in " furrin parts." Each of the Warrington scorers was named Daniels.

Stockton Heath and the Rangers met for their first fixture at Stockton Heath, on Saturday. Although such rivals, a very pleasant game was the result, and Stock- ton Heath won by a goal and a try to nil. The Rangers did not do as well as St. Mary's, but wait till the Heathens come to Lovely-lane. The Heathens thus far have a splendid record, for that little affair with the St. Mary's is the only defeat they have yet suffered,

At a meeting of the Governors of Seamen's Moss Charity on Saturday. reference was made to the death of the late Rev. On Saturday a man working on the Ship Canal at Lower Walton was nearly drowned in a very singu- lar manner. The wash made by the passage of the steamship Magnetic caused the pontoons on which men were employed repairing the sides of the canal, to heave so much that John bricklayers' labourer was pitched overboard. Roberts,de fell between the canal bank, which is verticle, and the pontoon, and was in imminent peril of being sucked under the latter when Josiah Hickman, a dumb labourer, from Warrington, pushed the pontoon from the bank, and seized Roberts by the hair of the head and held him there till more help came'and Roberts was drawn out not much the worse for hie immer- sion.

On Saturday the members of the St. Barnabas' Church choir had their annual excursion the place chosen being Liverpool. During the day, the museum, art gallery, and other places were visited. Miss Lonsdale kindly took the boys on to New Brighton fora run on the sand, the adult members joining them at four o'clock, when they all sat down to a substantial knife and fork tea, and after partaking of the good things the party re-crossed to Liverpool. The boys were then sent home by the 7.30 train under the care of one of the masters, the adult members remaining to hear Mr. H. Irving in the "The Merchant of Venice." The Vicar accom- panied the party. Mr. W. Woodcock Acted as , treasurer, and Mr, Stacey as secretary. SEWING. MICTINES Hand £2 18s. 6d. Treadle £4 4s. with handsome walnut cover.—.l. and W. DUTTON, 16 and 13, San key-st. , Warri ngton. —Advt. CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' QUARTERLY

MEETING. The quarterly meeting of the members of the Church Sunday School Teachers' Association was held on Tuesday evening in the new Eairfield Schools, Manchester-road. There was a large at- tendance of clergy and laity, and the meeting was one of the best which has been held. The chair was occupied by the Rector, who briefly introduced the Ttev. G. B. Thurston, senior curate of the War- rington Parish Church, who proceeded to read a paper on the best arrangement and use of the Sun- day morning school. lie said that a Sunday school was the central organization in a neglected work- ing-class parish or mission district, for the state of a home might be pretty accurately guaged by the state of the children from that home. Their sub- ject was limited not only to the best way of con- ducting a Sunday school, hut to the still narrower choice as to whether the Sunday school or a chil- dren's service was the better means of employing the Sunday morning. In conclusion, Mr. Thurston gave an account of a children's service on the above linos, and showed that it had worked most successfully in the parish where be resided for five years. An interesting discussion followed.

BUCKLEY-STREET BAND OF HOPE. The first of a series of limelight entertainments, in connection with the above, was given in the Buckley-street Schoolroom on Saturday evening, by Mr. Simpson. Mr. Th3mas Trow presided. and readings were given by the following: Mr. Trow, "Buy your own Cherries " : Mr. Scott, "Under Canvas"; Mr. Tavlin, "The effects of Gambling." Miss. E. Simpson, and Mr. Bate rendered songs. There was a large audience. WYCLIFFE YOUNG PEOPLE'S SOCIETY. A well-attended meeting of this society was held on Monday evening when the chair was occupied by Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., L.L.B. The programme for the evening was "Stray Leaves" which con- sisted of a number of papers on various topics con- tributed by members of the society. Eight papers were sent in bearing the following titles : "Can jEngland feed herself?"; "Up-to-date Literature "; "Types of men and how they changej';" Home"; " Friendship " ; " A Dream" ;" Is it right to attend a theatre ? ; and" Sunday Cycling." Interesting dis- cussions followed the reading of the papers and a most pleasant evening was spent. ALL HOUSEHOLD LINEN, hemmed and marked free of eharge.-4. and W. DUTTON'. Sankey-st., Warriagton.—Advt. TENNIS REQuIBITII9.—OARLAND, 51. Bridge-street, War- rington.— Advt. EMMA.NUEL CHURCH, BOLD-STREET. On Sunday special services were held in this church on the occasion of the Sunday School anni- versary, the preacher both morning and evening being the Rev. T. W. Gladstone, of Trinity C'hurch, (Reformed Church of England) Eccles, who also held a children's service in the afternoon and gave an interesting and instructive address to the children. Preaching in the evening from the words "I must work," (John 9.4) the reverend gentleman said that a divine necessity had been laid upon Christ to work, and that the same necessity was laid upon all true Christians. A lazy Christian was he said, an anomaly. He also pointed out the different fields of labeur wherein Christians might enter active service such as the Sunday School, &c. and urged I.is hearers to be diligent in the work of leading souls to the Saviour. Special hymns were rendered by the children, and the services were well attended. ORGAN RECITAL AT Sr. PAUL'S CHURCH. An organ recital was given on Wednesday even- ing at the St. Paul's Church, by Mr. Martin Schnei- der, of Liverpool. There was a good congregation, who listened with great attention to the pieces which were splendidly executed by the organist. The following were the pieces which he rendered: —Festal March, Sir G. Elvey ; cavatini, Raff ; cuckoo and nightingale concerto,Handel ; Romance sans Paroles, Gounod ; Fantasia Pastorale, Wely grand fugue in G major. Krebs ; overture, Poet and Peasant, Von Suppe. In addition to these pieces, Mr. Schneider gave a clever rendering of a piece of his own composition entitled, "Echo," and also the well-known hymn, "Christians awake," with varia- tions. During intervals in the recital Miss May Wayman, of Liverpool, who has a capital contralto voice, sang with great effect, "The King of Ages," "Ora Pro Noble," and "Star of Bethlehem." An offertory was taken at the close in aid of the organ fund. The service was brought to an end by the pronouncing of the Benediction by the Vicar, the Rev. H. V. Pigot. It was opened by a pianoforte solo brilliantly played by Lady Synge, who at a later period of the even- ing gave another selection on the same instrument. Miss P. Reynolds (Sankey-st.) contributed "Kitty of Coleraine" and "Should he Upbraid " ; Miss Coubrough, "Grandma " ; Miss Shawcross, "Dolly's Revenge"; Miss Philip , a pianoforte solo; Mr. Armstrong, a cornet solo; the Rev. A. H. At the conclusion of the programme, on the motion of Dr. Adams, seconded by Mr. Chantry, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Vicar for presiding over the meeting, and the vocalists and instru- mentalists for their services. The singing of "God Save the Queen" brought a very enjoyable evening to a close. No charge was made for admission, but a coll3ction was made amounting to .B 2 6s. 10d. Mrs. Adams was the accompanist. WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.—COUNTY SCHOLARS. It will be remembered that during the last three years four students of this school have gained scholarships offered for competition by the Lan- cashire County Council. These scholarships are of the value of £6O a year and may be renewed twice, if in the opinion of the Council the student is making satisfactory progress, and it will be inter- esting to note the progress of the local scholars. Mr. John W. Dooley, who obtained his award in 1892, after studying for two years in one of the great life schools in Paris, has recently moved to Ant- werp for his third year, and is now working at the Government School of painting there. Students of this school are only admitted after submitting a number of drawings, as evidence of fitness, and passing a special examination. Mr. H.Woodier,also a scholar of 1892, has also spent two years at Paris, and has now been granted a free studentship at the National Art Training School, at South Kensington, in order to study modelling from the life under M. E. Lanteri. The county scholarship in each of the above cases has only one year to run. Mr. Oswald Garside, a scholar of 1893, is still prosecu- ting his studies at the Academie Jullien, at Paris, where he has been joined recently by Mr. John Millard, the last addition to the list of local county scholars. SERVICE OF SONG AT THI3I3I7TTERIdiRKI4T- . ST., MISSION. On Saturday evening the Latchford Wesleyan Choir ably rendered at the above room a service of song, entitled " Eva," in aid of the funds of the Tern- perance Hall. The attendance was good. Mr. Thos. Morris was the chairman, and Councillor Henry Roberts rendered the connective readings in an excellent manner. Mr. Morris made a few remarks at the commencement. The choir then sang the opening piece, after which the Chairman called upon Mr. Roberts, who briefly explained the service of song, which was based on the immortal book "uncle Tom's Cabin," by Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe, who had rendered good and lasting service to the coloured race. The book should be read by all. The service was most interesting and impres- sive. Mr. R. Storey proposed, and Mr. John Drury seconded. votes of thanks to Mr. Morris and Mr Roberts for their services, and spoke in high terms of the help rendered to the temperance mission from time to time by those gentlemen. Messrs. Morris and Roberts responded, and the latter stated that Mr. Morris had always been a warm and true friend of his; indeed one of the best friends he had ever bad. Ile thought the singers merited great praise for the sweet and able manner in which they had rendered that service of song. Mr. 3. Rigby moved a hearty vote of thanks to the choir, which was warmly accorded. On Sunday evening the usual gospel temperance meeting was held. The usual Band of Hope meeting was held on Monday even- ing when Mr. Downs, of Church-st., gave a magic- lantern entertainment, which was highly appre- ciated WARRINGTON GYMNASTS AT LC/STOCK GRALAM A visit was paid to Lostock Gralam on Saturday, by eight members of the Warrington Gymnasium. under the direction of Mr. J. Kinsley, director of the Warrington Gymnasium. A fine nisplay was given in the schools before a very appreciative au- dience. Mr. J. .1. Howitt (supported by the Vicar and Mr. J. Lord) was in the chair, and spoke of the great benefits to be derived from a systematic course of gymnastics. He felt sure that after the display they were about to witness the people of Lostock would acknowledge the great usefulness of such an institution. and expressed Cie hope that the members of the Lostock Gymnasium would strive to emulate the deeds of the visitors. The display consisted of dumb-bell, bar-bell, and Indian club exercises (to musical time), parallel bars, hori- zontal bar, and high jumping. The whole of the

div.head: TERRIBLE DEATH AT THE WHISTON:
div.p: TERRIBLE DEATH AT THE WHISTON:
COLLIERY.

Shortly after four o'clock on Wednesday afternoon,. whillit the cage ascending No. 2 pit, known as Bottom. Place,belonging to the Wigan and Whiston Colliery Corn- pany,was near the top, one of the men, William Johnsont a man about sixty, was missed, and immediately Mr. Madew, manager, and Rutter, underground manager, went in search. They first found a foot cut off at the ankle in one of the landings, and the body terribly mutilated in the water of the dibhole at the bottom. There were eight men besides deceased in the cage when it started, and they covered their faces with their caps in coming up,on account of the sulphurous fumes in the shaft, but the end man remembered feeling a grazing of his leg when about midway, and deceased must have fallen about 200 yards, as the pit is nearly 400 yards, deep. On recovery of the body Police-Constable Francig- had it removed to the Seel Arms, fluyton Quarry, to await an inquest. Deceased, who lived at William-st., Prescot, leaves a widow and grown-up son.

div.head: NEWS OF THE PEARY EXPEDITION
div.p: NEWS OF THE PEARY EXPEDITION

GHASTLY DISCOVERY IN AN ESQUIMAUX CAMP. Whalers arrived at Dundee bring letters from the Peary expedition received from Esquimaux in the vicinity of Cape York on the Greenland coast. The. letters stated that the Peary party left M'Cormick Bay in March and proceeded inland, but encountered terrific storms and privations. The doctor and other members of the party were frost bitten and had to return to M'Cormisk Bay,where they will winter. The vessels also bring intelligence of a ghastly discovery made by the crew of the Balena in Prince Regent's Inlet. A boat's crew landed in Elvin Bay, and near the water's edge found an Esquimaux camp, with a number of corpses of men, who had died from starvation. The party had evidently been driven to cannibalism by their sufferings, some of the bodies being partially eaten, while clean picked bones were lying about. One corpse was decapi- tated, and the head was found some distance away. It is supposed that the party had been surprised by winter and been unable to get away from the island, which iS quite barren and destitute of game. The bodies were in a good state of preservation.
